papers.title: Human Papillomavirus and Prostate Cancer: A Controversial Association
papers.abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a sexually transmitted virus which infection can be asymptomatic or appear as mucosal lesions. HPV infection is estimated to contribute to approximately 5% of all cancers worldwide and is strongly associated with the development of most cervical cancers, as well as a substantial proportion of oropharyngeal, penile, and vulvar cancers. The viral HPV proteins E6 and E7 promote the development of tumour cells by disturbing the cellular signalling pathways involving the retinoblastoma protein (pRB) and cellular tumour antigen p53. Due to the established role of HPV in several anogenital cancers, a possible association between HPV infection and prostate cancer (PCa) risk has also been investigated. Recent studies and meta-analyses have reported an association between HPV infection and PCa in some populations. However, the available evidence remains inconsistent, and HPV infection cannot currently be considered an established risk factor for PCa. Further studies are needed to determine whether HPV infection plays a causal role in prostate carcinogenesis and whether HPV detection has clinical or prognostic utility in PCa.

papers.title: Distribution of Human Papillomavirus Genotypes and Co-Infection Patterns Across Anogenital Sites in Female Patients: A Microarray-Based Study
papers.abstract: Background: Cervical cancer is the most common and prevalent health problem, and the leading cause of cervical cancer worldwide is human papillomavirus (HPV). There may be missed opportunities in conventional approaches due to genotype-specific risk and multiple infections. This study aimed to describe the distribution of each genotype and co-infection at anogenital sites in symptomatic Iraqi women. Methods: In this prospective cross-sectional study, 100 women with clinically suspected HPV infection were consecutively enrolled between December 2025 and July 2026. A single specimen was collected from one of seven cervical, vulval, anal, or perianal sites. DNA was extracted using an automated magnetic-bead system, followed by post-PCR microarray hybridization for simultaneous detection of 35 HPV genotypes. Associations were assessed using exact and nonparametric tests. Results: HPV DNA was detected in 65.0% of participants (95% CI, 55.3–73.6%), comprising LR-only (48%), HR/PHR-only (9%), and mixed LR/HR-PHR infections (8%). HPV-6 and HPV-11 predominated, accounting for 40.9% and 30.7% of genotype detections, respectively. Multiple-genotype infections occurred in 20%. Age and sampling site were not significantly associated with HPV risk category. Among HR/PHR detections, 63.2% comprised non-avalent vaccine-covered genotypes. Conclusion: LR genotypes predominated, consistent with a wart-associated profile, while HR/PHR and mixed infections indicate clinically relevant oncogenic risk. Genotype-resolved microarray profiling may strengthen molecular surveillance and risk-informed HPV screening and vaccination strategies in Iraq.

papers.full_text: Abstract Cervical cancer, a significant global health challenge, is strongly associated with persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly HPV-16. The viral oncoproteins E5 and E6 are critical to HPV-mediated carcinogenesis, as they promote cell proliferation, immune evasion, apoptosis resistance, and genomic instability. E5 contributes to tumor progression by modulating growth factor signaling and promoting cell survival. E6, on the other hand, primarily drives malignant transformation by targeting the tumor suppressor p53 for degradation. Given their pivotal roles in cervical cancer, both oncoproteins are promising therapeutic targets. Recent advancements in gene-silencing technologies have provided novel opportunities for the selective inhibition of HPV oncogenes. Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and CRISPR/Cas-based genome-editing systems have demonstrated significant potential in suppressing E5 and E6 expression, restoring tumor suppressor functions, inducing apoptosis, and enhancing the sensitivity of cancer cells to conventional therapies. This narrative review summarizes the biological functions of HPV16-derived E5 and E6 in cervical carcinogenesis, and discusses recent developments in gene-silencing strategies targeting these oncogenes. Furthermore, it highlights current challenges, therapeutic limitations, and future perspectives for developing targeted molecular approaches aimed at cervical cancer prevention and treatment. papers.title_original: Targeting HPV16 E5 and E6 through gene-silencing approaches: mechanisms, preclinical evidence, and therapeutic perspectives

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on the biological functions of HPV16-derived E5 and E6 in cervical carcinogenesis and explores gene-silencing strategies targeting these oncogenes for therapeutic applications. The central question is whether targeting E5 and E6 through gene-silencing approaches can effectively prevent or treat HPV-associated cervical cancer.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of preclinical studies on gene-silencing approaches targeting HPV16 E5 and E6. It does not report on systematic search methods, databases, or meta-analysis. The evidence is derived from the biological mechanisms of E5 and E6, their roles in carcinogenesis, and the outcomes of gene-silencing interventions in experimental models.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that E5 and E6 are critical to HPV-mediated carcinogenesis, with E5 modulating growth factor signaling and promoting cell survival, while E6 primarily drives malignant transformation by degrading p53. Gene-silencing technologies, such as siRNAs and CRISPR/Cas-based systems, have shown significant potential in suppressing E5 and E6 expression, restoring tumor suppressor functions, and enhancing cancer cell sensitivity to conventional therapies.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights challenges in translating preclinical findings to clinical applications, including the need for more research on the long-term safety and efficacy of gene-silencing strategies. It also notes the lack of data on the impact of these approaches in diverse populations and the need for further exploration of their mechanisms in vivo.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that future research should prioritize the development of safe and effective gene-silencing therapies targeting HPV16 E5 and E6, with a focus on clinical trials and long-term safety assessments. It also emphasizes the importance of expanding studies to include diverse patient populations and exploring the potential of these strategies in combination with existing treatments.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines the roles of HPV16-derived oncoproteins E5 and E6 in cervical carcinogenesis and evaluates gene-silencing approaches as potential therapeutic strategies. It highlights the critical functions of E5 in promoting cell survival and E6 in driving malignant transformation through p53 degradation. Preclinical evidence supports the use of siRNAs and CRISPR/Cas systems to suppress these oncogenes, restore tumor suppressor functions, and enhance cancer cell sensitivity to conventional therapies. However, the review identifies challenges in translating these findings to clinical practice, including safety concerns and the need for more research on diverse populations. Future research should focus on clinical trials, long-term safety, and combination therapies to advance targeted molecular approaches for cervical cancer prevention and treatment.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述重点关注 HPV16 衍生的 E5 和 E6 在宫颈癌发生中的生物学功能,并探索针对这些癌基因的基因沉默策略的治疗应用。核心问题是通过基因沉默方法靶向E5和E6是否可以有效预防或治疗HPV相关的宫颈癌。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述是对针对 HPV16 E5 和 E6 的基因沉默方法的临床前研究的叙述性综合。它不报告系统搜索方法、数据库或荟萃分析。证据来自 E5 和 E6 的生物学机制、它们在致癌作用中的作用以及实验模型中基因沉默干预的结果。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 该综述得出的结论是,E5 和 E6 对于 HPV 介导的癌变至关重要,其中 E5 调节生长因子信号传导并促进细胞存活,而 E6 主要通过降解 p53 驱动恶性转化。基因沉默技术,例如 siRNA 和基于 CRISPR/Cas 的系统,在抑制 E5 和 E6 表达、恢复肿瘤抑制功能以及增强癌细胞对常规疗法的敏感性方面显示出巨大的潜力。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该综述强调了将临床前研究结果转化为临床应用的挑战,包括需要对基因沉默策略的长期安全性和有效性进行更多研究。它还指出,缺乏关于这些方法对不同人群的影响的数据,以及需要进一步探索其体内机制。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 该综述建议,未来的研究应优先开发针对HPV16 E5和E6的安全有效的基因沉默疗法,重点是临床试验和长期安全性评估。它还强调了扩大研究范围以纳入不同患者群体并探索这些策略与现有 治疗 相结合的潜力的重要性。

papers.title: Partial sequence of L1 gene in HPV 16 and HPV 18 isolated from head-neck squamous cell carcinoma tissues in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Human papillomavirus is one of the most crucial determinants responsible for the progression of head-neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Here, we report partial L1 gene sequences of two high-risk etiological agents, HPV-16 and HPV-18, extracted through biopsies from multiple head-neck tissue regions of HNSCC patients in Bangladesh.

papers.full_text: Abstract Based on the transmission mechanism of HPV, this paper establishes a dynamic model that includes sexual and non-sexual transmission. First, the threshold \(R_{0} \) of the model is obtained using the next-generation matrix method. It is found that when \(R_{0} < 1 \), the disease-free equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable, while when \(R_{0} > 1 \), the endemic equilibrium exists. Subsequently, numerical simulations verify that vaccination strategies targeting susceptible populations are more effective than input measures for vaccinated populations. Furthermore, sensitivity analysis is conducted on threshold \(R_{0} \), and the corresponding optimal control problem is considered. It is found that when implementing a single measure, sexual contact control is the most effective, followed by non-sexual contact control. In addition, vaccination measures should not be ignored. Data availability This research does not involve real data. No data were used, and no new data were created. analysis.summary_en: This study presents a dynamic mathematical model of human papillomavirus (HPV) transmission that incorporates both sexual and non-sexual routes. The model calculates the threshold $R_0$ using the next-generation matrix method, revealing that when $R_0 < 1$, the disease-free equilibrium is globally stable, while an endemic equilibrium exists when $R_0 > 1$. Numerical simulations indicate that vaccination strategies targeting susceptible populations are more effective than input measures for vaccinated groups. papers.full_text: Most existing studies focusing on human papillomavirus (HPV)-microbiota interactions are confined to the cervicovaginal tract, while mucosal microecological crosstalk at oral, anorectal and penile sites remains insufficiently summarized. This mini-review provides a narrative synthesis of current sequencing and epidemiological evidence regarding potential bidirectional interactions between HPV infection and site-specific mucosal microbiota across extra-cervicovaginal niches in both males and females. Oral HPV reshapes microbial composition in a sex-, race- and population-dependent manner; periodontal dysbiosis, high-risk HPV and Candida albicans jointly form a tripartite oncogenic axis that may contribute to oral squamous cell carcinoma, and periodontal inflammation independently elevates oral HPV susceptibility. Among men who have sex with men, pro-inflammatory anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis and Sneathia accumulate in anorectal HPV-related lesions, and concurrent HIV or sexually transmitted bacterial co-infections worsen mucosal dysbiosis and viral persistence. On penile skin, Corynebacterium is associated with a lower prevalence of HPV, whereas anaerobe-dominant community state types increase high-risk HPV risk, with HIV-induced baseline dysbiosis masking HPV-specific penile microbial signatures. Collectively, tissue-specific mucosal dysbiosis may represent an important co-factor linked to persistent HPV infection and subsequent malignant transformation. This review offsets long-standing sex-related and anatomical research bias, clarifies multi-site host-virus-microbe mechanisms, and provides theoretical support for developing microbiota-based biomarkers and microecological interventions to prevent non-cervical HPV-associated malignancies. 6ConclusionThis mini-review provides a narrative synthesis of observed associations and potential bidirectional interactions between HPV and mucosal microbiota in oral, anorectal and penile niches beyond cervicovaginal tissues. Site-specific microbial dysbiosis is associated with impaired mucosal immunity and may facilitate persistent HPV colonization and may contribute to oncogenic progression; meanwhile HPV infection can reshape local microbial composition. Distinct protective and pathogenic bacterial taxa are identified across three anatomical sites. Nevertheless, the supporting evidence is far more robust for the oral cavity, whereas evidence from anorectal and penile mucosa is limited and heterogeneous. Therefore, a uniform mechanistic model for all three anatomical sites cannot be assumed. Future longitudinal cohorts and functional experiments are required to clarify causal mechanisms and develop microecology-based preventive strategies for extragenital HPV-related malignancies. 1IntroductionHuman Papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection globally, with the most sexually active men and women estimated to have been infected with genital HPV at least once during their lifetime (Bruni et al., 2023). HPV can be transmitted in many ways through different abrasions, with sexual intercourse, when the newborn passes through an infected genital tract, and from a variety of self-inoculation positions (Erickson et al., 2013; Muzio et al., 2021). HPVs are capable of infecting multiple human anatomical niches including the skin, vagina, cervix, oral cavity and gut. Distinct dominant high-abundance HPV genotypes are enriched at separate body sites, exhibiting prominent tissue-specific tropism (Ma et al., 2014).The mechanisms underlying persistent HPV infection remain incompletely elucidated, with mucosal microbial dysbiosis emerging as an important contributing factor. Studies have shown that microbial imbalance is associated with sustained HPV inflammation and may contribute to the initiation and progression of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) (Song et al., 2020; Lebeau et al., 2022). Certain bacterial metabolites can activate epithelial inflammasomes, amplify inflammatory cascades, and potentiate the activity of HPV oncoproteins, thereby reinforcing persistent viral infection (Song et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025). Each individual harbors a unique microbial fingerprint. Organ-specific microbiotas regulate host immunity and mucosal physiological functions (Kilian et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2022).Extensive research has delineated the complicated interplay between cervicovaginal microbiota and HPV, confirming its pivotal role in cervical carcinogenesis (Usyk et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2024; Oyedokun et al., 2026). However, bidirectional crosstalk between HPV and mucosal flora at oral, anorectal and penile sites remains insufficiently characterized, and few reviews have provided a summary of these extra-cervicovaginal microbial niches. This narrative mini-review integrates available evidence for extra-cervicovaginal mucosal niches in both sexes to mitigate the historical cervix-centered research bias (Table 1). The overall prevalence of oral HPV among healthy general populations ranged from 0.67% to 11.89%, and infection rates were higher in males than females (Maltseva et al., 2025). Chronic inflammation linked to the oral microbiome may induce abnormal immune responses and interfere with the clearance of oral HPV infection, which could potentially contribute to carcinogenesis (Tezal, 2012). HPV infection is a significant risk factor for oropharyngeal cancer (McQuillan et al., 2017). Approximately 70% of oropharyngeal cancer are associated with oral HPV infection (D'Souza et al., 2007; Marur et al., 2010; Joseph and D'Souza, 2012). full_text_sections.abstract: Most existing studies focusing on human papillomavirus (HPV)-microbiota interactions are confined to the cervicovaginal tract, while mucosal microecological crosstalk at oral, anorectal and penile sites remains insufficiently summarized. This mini-review provides a narrative synthesis of current sequencing and epidemiological evidence regarding potential bidirectional interactions between HPV infection and site-specific mucosal microbiota across extra-cervicovaginal niches in both males and females. Oral HPV reshapes microbial composition in a sex-, race- and population-dependent manner; periodontal dysbiosis, high-risk HPV and Candida albicans jointly form a tripartite oncogenic axis that may contribute to oral squamous cell carcinoma, and periodontal inflammation independently elevates oral HPV susceptibility. Among men who have sex with men, pro-inflammatory anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis and Sneathia accumulate in anorectal HPV-related lesions, and concurrent HIV or sexually transmitted bacterial co-infections worsen mucosal dysbiosis and viral persistence. On penile skin, Corynebacterium is associated with a lower prevalence of HPV, whereas anaerobe-dominant community state types increase high-risk HPV risk, with HIV-induced baseline dysbiosis masking HPV-specific penile microbial signatures. Collectively, tissue-specific mucosal dysbiosis may represent an important co-factor linked to persistent HPV infection and subsequent malignant transformation. This review offsets long-standing sex-related and anatomical research bias, clarifies multi-site host-virus-microbe mechanisms, and provides theoretical support for developing microbiota-based biomarkers and microecological interventions to prevent non-cervical HPV-associated malignancies.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 6ConclusionThis mini-review provides a narrative synthesis of observed associations and potential bidirectional interactions between HPV and mucosal microbiota in oral, anorectal and penile niches beyond cervicovaginal tissues. Site-specific microbial dysbiosis is associated with impaired mucosal immunity and may facilitate persistent HPV colonization and may contribute to oncogenic progression; meanwhile HPV infection can reshape local microbial composition. Distinct protective and pathogenic bacterial taxa are identified across three anatomical sites. Nevertheless, the supporting evidence is far more robust for the oral cavity, whereas evidence from anorectal and penile mucosa is limited and heterogeneous. Therefore, a uniform mechanistic model for all three anatomical sites cannot be assumed. Future longitudinal cohorts and functional experiments are required to clarify causal mechanisms and develop microecology-based preventive strategies for extragenital HPV-related malignancies.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionHuman Papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection globally, with the most sexually active men and women estimated to have been infected with genital HPV at least once during their lifetime (Bruni et al., 2023). HPV can be transmitted in many ways through different abrasions, with sexual intercourse, when the newborn passes through an infected genital tract, and from a variety of self-inoculation positions (Erickson et al., 2013; Muzio et al., 2021). HPVs are capable of infecting multiple human anatomical niches including the skin, vagina, cervix, oral cavity and gut. Distinct dominant high-abundance HPV genotypes are enriched at separate body sites, exhibiting prominent tissue-specific tropism (Ma et al., 2014).The mechanisms underlying persistent HPV infection remain incompletely elucidated, with mucosal microbial dysbiosis emerging as an important contributing factor. Studies have shown that microbial imbalance is associated with sustained HPV inflammation and may contribute to the initiation and progression of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) (Song et al., 2020; Lebeau et al., 2022). Certain bacterial metabolites can activate epithelial inflammasomes, amplify inflammatory cascades, and potentiate the activity of HPV oncoproteins, thereby reinforcing persistent viral infection (Song et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025). Each individual harbors a unique microbial fingerprint. Organ-specific microbiotas regulate host immunity and mucosal physiological functions (Kilian et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2022).Extensive research has delineated the complicated interplay between cervicovaginal microbiota and HPV, confirming its pivotal role in cervical carcinogenesis (Usyk et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2024; Oyedokun et al., 2026). However, bidirectional crosstalk between HPV and mucosal flora at oral, anorectal and penile sites remains insufficiently characterized, and few reviews have provided a summary of these extra-cervicovaginal microbial niches. This narrative mini-review integrates available evidence for extra-cervicovaginal mucosal niches in both sexes to mitigate the historical cervix-centered research bias (Table 1). analysis.summary_en: This mini-review explores the bidirectional interactions between HPV infection and mucosal microbiota in non-cervicovaginal sites such as oral, anorectal, and penile regions. It synthesizes evidence from multiple studies, highlighting sex-specific differences in oral microbiota associated with HPV infection, particularly in males. The review also discusses the impact of HIV-driven oral dysbiosis on HPV-specific microbial signatures and the role of microbiota in HPV persistence and pathogenicity. However, the findings are limited by small sample sizes and restricted populations, such as pregnant women and HIV-negative men. The review emphasizes the need for further research to understand these interactions across diverse populations and their implications for HPV-related diseases.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 这篇小型综述对当前测序和流行病学证据进行了叙述性综合,涉及男性和女性宫颈阴道外生态位中 HPV 感染与特定位点粘膜微生物群之间潜在的双向相互作用。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 阐明宫颈阴道外微生物群与 HPV 感染之间的相关性将进一步阐明粘膜 HPV 易感性和相关的 宿主-微生物-病毒相互作用。健康普通人群口腔HPV总体患病率范围为0.67%至11.89%,男性感染率高于女性(Maltseva et al.,2025)。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 观察数据表明,口腔微生物群的成员可能通过改变 HPV 的致病性或细菌群落行为来与 HPV 相互作用(Ghannoum 等,2010;Muzio 等,2021)。大规模 NHANES 横断面数据 (n=5496) 进一步证实,口腔微生物 α 多样性减少和独特的群落特征仅与男性中的高危口腔 HPV 显着相关,这种基于性别的差异与男性对 HPV 相关头颈恶性肿瘤的易感性较高一致(Park 等人,2022 年;Gaeta 等人,2023 年;Feng 等人,2024)。据报道,口腔 HPV 不会诱导独特的口腔微生物分类群或生态型,而是通过协调的毒力网络定殖预先存在的口腔生态系统(Chambuso 等人,2026)。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 这些发现受到样本量小和仅招募怀孕受试者的限制,这限制了这些结论对更广泛人群的普遍适用性。另一项横断面研究分析了 5000 多个口腔冲洗样本,报告显示 HPV 阳性个体中韦荣菌科的相对丰度较高,双粒菌减少。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 这项工作表明,由 HIV 驱动的先前存在的口腔生态失调掩盖了 hrHPV 的微生物特征,而 hrHPV 通过扩大致病类群进一步扰乱粘膜微生态。据报道,口腔 HPV 阳性孕妇的口腔微生物丰富度较高,其中硒单胞菌属、巨球菌属和 TM7 相关类群的相对丰度较高(Tuominen 等人,2018a)。另外,来自同一组的婴儿口腔微生物群数据显示,口腔 HPV 阳性改变了属和科水平的细菌谱,但没有改变整体 α 多样性(Tuominen 等人,2018b)。

papers.source_body_en: This mini-review provides a narrative synthesis of current sequencing and epidemiological evidence regarding potential bidirectional interactions between HPV infection and site-specific mucosal microbiota across extra-cervicovaginal niches in both males and females. This review offsets long-standing sex-related and anatomical research bias, clarifies multi-site host-virus-microbe mechanisms, and provides theoretical support for developing microbiota-based biomarkers and microecological interventions to prevent non-cervical HPV-associated malignancies. 6ConclusionThis mini-review provides a narrative synthesis of observed associations and potential bidirectional interactions between HPV and mucosal microbiota in oral, anorectal and penile niches beyond cervicovaginal tissues. This narrative mini-review integrates available evidence for extra-cervicovaginal mucosal niches in both sexes to mitigate the historical cervix-centered research bias (Table 1). analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 这篇小型综述对当前测序和流行病学证据进行了叙述性综合,涉及男性和女性宫颈阴道外生态位中 HPV 感染与特定位点粘膜微生物群之间潜在的双向相互作用。
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 阐明宫颈阴道外微生物群与 HPV 感染之间的相关性将进一步阐明粘膜 HPV 易感性和相关的 宿主-微生物-病毒相互作用。健康普通人群口腔HPV总体患病率范围为0.67%至11.89%,男性感染率高于女性(Maltseva et al.,2025)。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 观察数据表明,口腔微生物群的成员可能通过改变 HPV 的致病性或细菌群落行为来与 HPV 相互作用(Ghannoum 等,2010;Muzio 等,2021)。大规模 NHANES 横断面数据 (n=5496) 进一步证实,口腔微生物 α 多样性减少和独特的群落特征仅与男性中的高危口腔 HPV 显着相关,这种基于性别的差异与男性对 HPV 相关头颈恶性肿瘤的易感性较高一致(Park 等人,2022 年;Gaeta 等人,2023 年;Feng 等人,2024)。据报道,口腔 HPV 不会诱导独特的口腔微生物分类群或生态型,而是通过协调的毒力网络定殖预先存在的口腔生态系统(Chambuso 等人,2026)。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 这些发现受到样本量小和仅招募怀孕受试者的限制,这限制了这些结论对更广泛人群的普遍适用性。另一项横断面研究分析了 5000 多个口腔冲洗样本,报告显示 HPV 阳性个体中韦荣菌科的相对丰度较高,双粒菌减少。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 这项工作表明,由 HIV 驱动的先前存在的口腔生态失调掩盖了 hrHPV 的微生物特征,而 hrHPV 通过扩大致病类群进一步扰乱粘膜微生态。据报道,口腔 HPV 阳性孕妇的口腔微生物丰富度较高,其中硒单胞菌属、巨球菌属和 TM7 相关类群的相对丰度较高(Tuominen 等人,2018a)。另外,来自同一组的婴儿口腔微生物群数据显示,口腔 HPV 阳性改变了属和科水平的细菌谱,但没有改变整体 α 多样性(Tuominen 等人,2018b)。

papers.full_text: Background and objectiveAdults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are screened for cervical cancer at substantially lower rates than adults without disabilities. Communication differences, sensory sensitivities, and difficulty tolerating speculum-based examination all contribute. Deferred screening is frequently recorded as patient refusal rather than as an unmet need for adapted care. Human papillomavirus (HPV) testing on self-collected vaginal specimens is now recognized as an acceptable screening option, but published implementation strategies for this population are limited. The objective of this study was to evaluate respondent-reported acceptability, tolerability, and level of assistance required for a nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model in an interdisciplinary primary care clinic serving adults with IDD.MethodsWe conducted a prospective, single-site, minimal-risk observational study at the Program for Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (PAIDD) at University of Florida Health Jacksonville. Vaginal specimens for HPV testing were collected in the clinic by the patient under nurse guidance, with hands-on assistance from a trained program nurse or a caregiver as needed. The model also included structured pre-visit planning, an animated patient education video, and caregiver engagement. A structured post-visit survey administered in REDCap assessed the level and appropriateness of assistance, patient tolerance, observable distress, acceptability, and support for future use. The survey was designed as a caregiver proxy instrument and was completed directly by the patient where able; outcomes are therefore described as respondent-reported, with proxy and direct responses distinguished explicitly. Results are reported as n (%). Recruitment is ongoing toward a planned enrollment of 30, and these are preliminary findings.ResultsOf 23 patients identified as eligible, 18 (78.3%) were offered the pathway. Among those offered, 14 (77.8%) completed collection, and four (22.2%) declined; zero (0%) attempted collection without completing it. Uptake was 14 of 23 (60.9%) among those identified as eligible. All 14 specimens (100%) returned negative high-risk HPV results. Complete survey data were available for 13 of the 14 completed collections. Among these 13 encounters, tolerance was rated very good in 11 (84.6%) and good in two (15.4%), with zero (0%) rated fair, poor, or very poor; no distress was observed in 12 (92.3%) and mild distress in one (7.7%), with zero (0%) moderate or severe. All 13 encounters with available assistance data (100%) required hands-on assistance, provided by the nurse in nine (69.2%) and by a caregiver in four (30.8%); zero (0%) were completed unaided or with verbal coaching alone, and zero (0%) were unable to be completed despite assistance. All 13 respondents (100%) judged the level of assistance appropriate, rated the process acceptable or very acceptable, and would support offering it again.ConclusionsA nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model was well tolerated and highly acceptable to respondents in an academic primary care clinic for adults with IDD. Every encounter with available assistance data required hands-on assistance, indicating that nursing support is integral to the model rather than incidental. Clinic efficiency, physician time, and scalability were not measured and remain hypotheses for future evaluation. Recruitment continues. Materials and methodsStudy design and settingThis was a prospective, single-site, minimal-risk observational study evaluating the feasibility and acceptability of an adapted cervical cancer screening workflow offered as part of routine clinical care. It was conducted at the Program for Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (PAIDD) at University of Florida Health Jacksonville, an interdisciplinary primary care medical home led by a physician medical director, operationalized by a registered nurse (RN) program coordinator, and delivered by advanced practice providers, physicians, and nursing staff in close partnership with caregivers. The program was established in 2013 and serves approximately 350 adults with IDD, many of whom are nonverbal or minimally verbal and have significant sensory sensitivities and anxiety related to clinical examination. Approximately 40% of the program population are women, and approximately 80% of those fall within the 25- to 64-year screening age range, giving an estimated 110 potentially eligible patients. These are program-level estimates rather than counts from a verified screening registry. Data were collected between February 3, 2026 and August 25, 2026. Recruitment is ongoing.Participants and eligibilityPatients were eligible if they were adults aged 25-64 years receiving care at the PAIDD clinic, had a diagnosis of intellectual and/or developmental disability, had a cervix, were due for cervical cancer screening per clinic practice, and if a caregiver was available and willing to complete a proxy survey. The age range was chosen to align with American Cancer Society guidance recommending initiation of screening at age 25 years [4,5]. Screening was deferred where there was a medical contraindication to HPV testing, where the clinical team determined that screening was not appropriate that day, or where the patient exhibited behavioral distress such that proceeding was not clinically appropriate. Patients for whom an HPV-only pathway is not appropriate under current guidance, including those with HIV infection or another immunocompromising condition, a history of high-grade cervical dysplasia, or in utero diethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure, would have been managed with alternative screening strategies; 0 patients (0%) in the screened population met any of these criteria.InterventionThe model was designed to address the barriers most commonly encountered in patients with IDD: difficulty tolerating speculum-based examination, communication differences, and reliance on caregivers for coordination and decision-making. HPV-based screening was prioritized because it identifies high-risk HPV infection before cytologic change and, on a self-collected vaginal specimen, avoids speculum insertion entirely. Patients screened through this pathway are advised to repeat testing at three years following a negative result, consistent with the interval recommended for self-collected vaginal specimens, rather than the five-year interval that applies to clinician-collected primary HPV testing [5]. In the HPV FOCAL randomized trial, primary HPV testing on clinician-collected specimens resulted in a significantly lower likelihood of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 or higher at 48 months than liquid-based cytology; invasive cervical cancer incidence was not an endpoint of that trial [8]. A meta-analysis of HPV testing on self-collected compared with clinician-collected samples found lower pooled sensitivity and specificity on self-collected samples overall, with the difference concentrated in signal amplification assays; the authors concluded that some polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based assays could be considered for routine screening after careful piloting [9]. The assay used in this study is PCR-based.The model had four components: (1) adoption of HPV screening on a self-collected vaginal specimen to reduce procedural burden; (2) structured pre-visit planning to identify eligible patients and anticipate support needs; (3) patient self-collection of the specimen as the default, with expansion of nursing roles to include patient preparation, positioning assistance, real-time coaching, and assisted collection when needed; and (4) integration of caregivers to support communication, facilitate the consent and assent process, and enhance patient comfort.Implementation proceeded through a multidisciplinary process. Attending physicians, resident physicians, nursing staff, and caregivers were engaged early to identify workflow barriers and inform intervention design. Clinic workflows were modified to include pre-visit identification of patients due for screening and to allocate additional appointment time for encounters requiring enhanced support. Nursing staff received targeted training on HPV screening workflows and on strategies for supporting patients with IDD, including communication techniques and assistance during specimen collection. Roles and responsibilities were delineated in advance to promote consistency across providers. Figure 1 illustrates the adapted clinic workflow.Figure 1Adapted clinic workflow for nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening.Adapted clinic workflow incorporating pre-visit identification of screening-eligible patients, nurse-delivered education using accessible language and visuals, structured consent and assent, and specimen collection performed by the patient with hands-on assistance from the program nurse or a caregiver.Specimen collectionVaginal specimens were collected using the OneSwab collection kit (Medical Diagnostic Laboratories, Hamilton, NJ, USA), a snap-swab device with a screw-cap design permitting room-temperature storage and transport. Collection took place in the clinic examination room rather than at home, so that support was available at the point of collection.Specimens were processed by Medical Diagnostic Laboratories, a CLIA-certified reference laboratory, using the HPV Type-Detect 4.0 multiplex real-time PCR assay. The assay identifies and simultaneously distinguishes 13 high-risk HPV genotypes: 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, and 68. This assay is a laboratory-developed test; its performance characteristics were determined by the laboratory, and it has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. FDA.A graded approach to collection was used, with support matched to the individual patient rather than withheld until failure. Collection was performed by the patient under nurse guidance, in privacy, and with verbal coaching. The PAIDD program nurse, trained in the protocol and in supporting patients with IDD, provided hands-on assistance or completed the collection where the patient could not do so independently, which was anticipated for a substantial proportion of this population. Caregiver assistance was used where the patient preferred it or where caregiver presence was necessary for the patient to proceed. Nurse assistance was preferred over caregiver assistance where either was acceptable to the patient, as the nurse is trained in specimen adequacy and in de-escalation. No patient was required to undergo speculum insertion to complete screening. Because hands-on assistance was required in every encounter for which assistance data were available, the specimen is described throughout as nurse-assisted self-collected rather than as unassisted self-collected.Patient education materialsPatient preparation included an animated education video explaining the self-collection procedure in accessible, trauma-informed language. The video uses an animated character rather than clinical photography or live demonstration, conveying the steps of the procedure without exposure to imagery that patients with sensory sensitivities may find distressing. It was developed from an original concept and storyboard by the senior author (RF) and produced with University of Florida Health Jacksonville Media Relations. The video was shown to patients and caregivers before the encounter and was available for repeat viewing at home. Video 1 presents the education video in full.Video 1Patient and caregiver education video for nurse-assisted self-collected HPV cervical cancer screening.Animated education video shown to patients and caregivers before the screening encounter, explaining the self-collection procedure in accessible, trauma-informed language. The video uses an animated character rather than clinical photography or live demonstration, conveying the steps of the procedure without exposure to imagery that patients with sensory sensitivities may find distressing.HPV, human papillomavirusDeveloped from an original concept and storyboard by the senior author (RF) and produced with University of Florida Health Jacksonville Media Relations.Data sourcesTwo data sources were used. Respondent-reported outcomes were obtained from the post-visit survey described below. Counts of patients identified as eligible, offered the pathway, completing collection, and declining were compiled from the clinic’s pre-visit planning records maintained as part of routine clinical operations and are reported here in aggregate without identifiers.Survey instrument and data collectionA structured post-visit survey was completed at the end of the encounter. The instrument assessed the level of assistance required from nursing staff and from caregivers, whether the level of assistance provided was appropriate, overall tolerance of the self-swab process, observable signs of distress, overall acceptability of the method, and willingness to use the approach again. The instrument was investigator-developed and was not formally validated. It was administered by the program nurse through an anonymous REDCap link immediately following the encounter, with REDCap being a secure, institutionally hosted electronic data capture platform. Study data were collected and managed using REDCap electronic data capture tools hosted at the University of Florida [10,11]. The full instrument is presented in Appendix A.The instrument was designed as a caregiver proxy survey, and caregivers responded as proxies for most encounters, reporting their own observations rather than the patient’s direct report, as many patients in this population are nonverbal or minimally verbal. Where the patient was able to respond, the patient completed the survey directly rather than through a proxy. Because the dataset therefore combines proxy report and direct patient report, outcomes are described throughout as respondent-reported rather than as caregiver-reported, and the distribution of respondent roles, including the proportion responding directly, is given in the Results.In REDCap, a survey record is created at the moment a survey link is generated rather than at the moment a response is submitted. Links were generated at the time of pre-visit planning for encounters at which screening was anticipated, before eligibility and the offer of the pathway were confirmed at the visit, and a further link was generated where a patient returned at a later visit. The number of records generated therefore exceeds the number of patients identified as eligible and the number offered the pathway, and the records correspond to survey link generations rather than to unique patients.Consent was documented separately in the patient’s medical record; survey responses recorded in REDCap contained no names, medical record numbers, or other identifiers and were not linked to the consent documentation. All caregivers present at an eligible screening encounter during the evaluation period were invited to complete the survey.Statistical analysisOne record submitted during instrument testing, containing non-substantive free-text entries and predating the first patient encounter, was excluded before analysis. Survey links generated but never opened were treated as non-responses. Responses were summarized using descriptive statistics and are reported throughout as n (%), with the denominator stated for each domain; missing responses were not imputed. Because the survey dataset is anonymous and cannot be linked to the clinical record, outcomes for the one completed collection without complete survey data could not be recovered from another source, and assistance, tolerance, distress, and acceptability results are therefore reported against the 13 encounters with available data rather than against all 14 completed collections. Given the pilot design and small sample, no inferential testing was performed, and no comparison group was used. A subset of these data was presented previously in preliminary form; the proportions reported here differ from those presentations because the test record described above was excluded from the present analysis.Clinic-level cervical cancer screening completion rates before and after implementation are being collected in parallel and will be reported separately. The study has a planned enrollment of 30 participants. Recruitment had not closed at the time of this report, and the results presented here are preliminary, reflecting the first 14 completed screenings and the survey responses returned for them.Ethical considerationsThis project was reviewed by the University of Florida Institutional Review Board and determined to be exempt under 45 CFR 46.104(d)(2), which covers research involving survey procedures where responses are recorded without identifiers (IRB202501845). The materials submitted to the Institutional Review Board comprised the study protocol, the consent documentation, and the caregiver proxy survey instrument presented in Appendix A.Consent for participation was obtained from the patient where the patient was capable of providing it, and otherwise from a power of attorney, legally authorized representative, or healthcare surrogate. Consent was documented separately in the patient’s medical record and was not linked to the de-identified research dataset. Patient assent was sought in all cases, including for nonverbal patients through observable acceptance or refusal cues, and collection was paused or stopped if the patient showed escalating distress or indicated refusal. full_text_sections.abstract: Background and objectiveAdults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are screened for cervical cancer at substantially lower rates than adults without disabilities. Communication differences, sensory sensitivities, and difficulty tolerating speculum-based examination all contribute. Deferred screening is frequently recorded as patient refusal rather than as an unmet need for adapted care. Human papillomavirus (HPV) testing on self-collected vaginal specimens is now recognized as an acceptable screening option, but published implementation strategies for this population are limited. The objective of this study was to evaluate respondent-reported acceptability, tolerability, and level of assistance required for a nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model in an interdisciplinary primary care clinic serving adults with IDD.MethodsWe conducted a prospective, single-site, minimal-risk observational study at the Program for Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (PAIDD) at University of Florida Health Jacksonville. Vaginal specimens for HPV testing were collected in the clinic by the patient under nurse guidance, with hands-on assistance from a trained program nurse or a caregiver as needed. The model also included structured pre-visit planning, an animated patient education video, and caregiver engagement. A structured post-visit survey administered in REDCap assessed the level and appropriateness of assistance, patient tolerance, observable distress, acceptability, and support for future use. The survey was designed as a caregiver proxy instrument and was completed directly by the patient where able; outcomes are therefore described as respondent-reported, with proxy and direct responses distinguished explicitly. Results are reported as n (%). Recruitment is ongoing toward a planned enrollment of 30, and these are preliminary findings.ResultsOf 23 patients identified as eligible, 18 (78.3%) were offered the pathway. Among those offered, 14 (77.8%) completed collection, and four (22.2%) declined; zero (0%) attempted collection without completing it. Uptake was 14 of 23 (60.9%) among those identified as eligible. All 14 specimens (100%) returned negative high-risk HPV results. Complete survey data were available for 13 of the 14 completed collections. Among these 13 encounters, tolerance was rated very good in 11 (84.6%) and good in two (15.4%), with zero (0%) rated fair, poor, or very poor; no distress was observed in 12 (92.3%) and mild distress in one (7.7%), with zero (0%) moderate or severe. All 13 encounters with available assistance data (100%) required hands-on assistance, provided by the nurse in nine (69.2%) and by a caregiver in four (30.8%); zero (0%) were completed unaided or with verbal coaching alone, and zero (0%) were unable to be completed despite assistance. All 13 respondents (100%) judged the level of assistance appropriate, rated the process acceptable or very acceptable, and would support offering it again.ConclusionsA nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model was well tolerated and highly acceptable to respondents in an academic primary care clinic for adults with IDD. Every encounter with available assistance data required hands-on assistance, indicating that nursing support is integral to the model rather than incidental. Clinic efficiency, physician time, and scalability were not measured and remain hypotheses for future evaluation. Recruitment continues.
full_text_sections.methods: Materials and methodsStudy design and settingThis was a prospective, single-site, minimal-risk observational study evaluating the feasibility and acceptability of an adapted cervical cancer screening workflow offered as part of routine clinical care. It was conducted at the Program for Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (PAIDD) at University of Florida Health Jacksonville, an interdisciplinary primary care medical home led by a physician medical director, operationalized by a registered nurse (RN) program coordinator, and delivered by advanced practice providers, physicians, and nursing staff in close partnership with caregivers. The program was established in 2013 and serves approximately 350 adults with IDD, many of whom are nonverbal or minimally verbal and have significant sensory sensitivities and anxiety related to clinical examination. Approximately 40% of the program population are women, and approximately 80% of those fall within the 25- to 64-year screening age range, giving an estimated 110 potentially eligible patients. These are program-level estimates rather than counts from a verified screening registry. Data were collected between February 3, 2026 and August 25, 2026. Recruitment is ongoing.Participants and eligibilityPatients were eligible if they were adults aged 25-64 years receiving care at the PAIDD clinic, had a diagnosis of intellectual and/or developmental disability, had a cervix, were due for cervical cancer screening per clinic practice, and if a caregiver was available and willing to complete a proxy survey. The age range was chosen to align with American Cancer Society guidance recommending initiation of screening at age 25 years [4,5]. Screening was deferred where there was a medical contraindication to HPV testing, where the clinical team determined that screening was not appropriate that day, or where the patient exhibited behavioral distress such that proceeding was not clinically appropriate. Patients for whom an HPV-only pathway is not appropriate under current guidance, including those with HIV infection or another immunocompromising condition, a history of high-grade cervical dysplasia, or in utero diethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure, would have been managed with alternative screening strategies; 0 patients (0%) in the screened population met any of these criteria.InterventionThe model was designed to address the barriers most commonly encountered in patients with IDD: difficulty tolerating speculum-based examination, communication differences, and reliance on caregivers for coordination and decision-making. HPV-based screening was prioritized because it identifies high-risk HPV infection before cytologic change and, on a self-collected vaginal specimen, avoids speculum insertion entirely. Patients screened through this pathway are advised to repeat testing at three years following a negative result, consistent with the interval recommended for self-collected vaginal specimens, rather than the five-year interval that applies to clinician-collected primary HPV testing [5]. In the HPV FOCAL randomized trial, primary HPV testing on clinician-collected specimens resulted in a significantly lower likelihood of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 or higher at 48 months than liquid-based cytology; invasive cervical cancer incidence was not an endpoint of that trial [8]. A meta-analysis of HPV testing on self-collected compared with clinician-collected samples found lower pooled sensitivity and specificity on self-collected samples overall, with the difference concentrated in signal amplification assays; the authors concluded that some polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based assays could be considered for routine screening after careful piloting [9]. The assay used in this study is PCR-based.The model had four components: (1) adoption of HPV screening on a self-collected vaginal specimen to reduce procedural burden; (2) structured pre-visit planning to identify eligible patients and anticipate support needs; (3) patient self-collection of the specimen as the default, with expansion of nursing roles to include patient preparation, positioning assistance, real-time coaching, and assisted collection when needed; and (4) integration of caregivers to support communication, facilitate the consent and assent process, and enhance patient comfort.Implementation proceeded through a multidisciplinary process. Attending physicians, resident physicians, nursing staff, and caregivers were engaged early to identify workflow barriers and inform intervention design. Clinic workflows were modified to include pre-visit identification of patients due for screening and to allocate additional appointment time for encounters requiring enhanced support. Nursing staff received targeted training on HPV screening workflows and on strategies for supporting patients with IDD, including communication techniques and assistance during specimen collection. Roles and responsibilities were delineated in advance to promote consistency across providers. Figure 1 illustrates the adapted clinic workflow.Figure 1Adapted clinic workflow for nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening.Adapted clinic workflow incorporating pre-visit identification of screening-eligible patients, nurse-delivered education using accessible language and visuals, structured consent and assent, and specimen collection performed by the patient with hands-on assistance from the program nurse or a caregiver.Specimen collectionVaginal specimens were collected using the OneSwab collection kit (Medical Diagnostic Laboratories, Hamilton, NJ, USA), a snap-swab device with a screw-cap design permitting room-temperature storage and transport. Collection took place in the clinic examination room rather than at home, so that support was available at the point of collection.Specimens were processed by Medical Diagnostic Laboratories, a CLIA-certified reference laboratory, using the HPV Type-Detect 4.0 multiplex real-time PCR assay. The assay identifies and simultaneously distinguishes 13 high-risk HPV genotypes: 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, and 68. This assay is a laboratory-developed test; its performance characteristics were determined by the laboratory, and it has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. FDA.A graded approach to collection was used, with support matched to the individual patient rather than withheld until failure. Collection was performed by the patient under nurse guidance, in privacy, and with verbal coaching. The PAIDD program nurse, trained in the protocol and in supporting patients with IDD, provided hands-on assistance or completed the collection where the patient could not do so independently, which was anticipated for a substantial proportion of this population. Caregiver assistance was used where the patient preferred it or where caregiver presence was necessary for the patient to proceed. Nurse assistance was preferred over caregiver assistance where either was acceptable to the patient, as the nurse is trained in specimen adequacy and in de-escalation. No patient was required to undergo speculum insertion to complete screening. Because hands-on assistance was required in every encounter for which assistance data were available, the specimen is described throughout as nurse-assisted self-collected rather than as unassisted self-collected.Patient education materialsPatient preparation included an animated education video explaining the self-collection procedure in accessible, trauma-informed language. The video uses an animated character rather than clinical photography or live demonstration, conveying the steps of the procedure without exposure to imagery that patients with sensory sensitivities may find distressing. It was developed from an original concept and storyboard by the senior author (RF) and produced with University of Florida Health Jacksonville Media Relations. The video was shown to patients and caregivers bef…
full_text_sections.results: ResultsScreening completionThese are preliminary results from an ongoing study. Twenty-three patients were identified as eligible for cervical cancer screening through pre-visit planning during the reporting period. Of these, 18 (78.3%) were offered the nurse-assisted self-collection pathway. Among those offered, 14 (77.8%) completed collection and four (22.2%) declined; zero (0%) attempted collection without completing it, and zero (0%) were unable to complete collection despite assistance. Uptake was 14 of 18 (77.8%) among those offered and 14 of 23 (60.9%) among those identified as eligible. The screening cascade is presented in Table 1.Table 1Screening cascade for nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening.Number of patients at each stage of the screening pathway during the reporting period, compiled from clinic pre-visit planning records. Percentages are shown relative to the 23 patients identified as eligible and to the 18 patients offered the pathway. No specimen (0%) was reported by the laboratory as inadequate or unsatisfactory for testing, and no patient (0%) required referral for colposcopy or speculum-based evaluation.Survey responseTwenty-seven survey records were generated in REDCap. As described in the Methods, a record is created when a survey link is generated rather than when a response is submitted, and links were generated at pre-visit planning before eligibility, and the offer was confirmed at the visit, so the number of records exceeds the number of patients identified as eligible and the number offered the pathway. Of the 27 records, 11 (40.7%) links were never opened, and one (3.7%) was a test submission excluded before analysis, leaving 15 (55.6%) records with data: 14 corresponding to completed collections and one documenting an encounter at which collection was not attempted. Complete experience data were available for 13 of the 14 completed collections (92.9%); one respondent (7.1%) recorded the encounter but did not submit the remaining items. Denominators are reported accordingly, and missing responses were not imputed.Among the 15 records with data, respondents were family members in four (26.7%), direct support professionals in four (26.7%), legal guardians in two (13.3%), and others in five (33.3%). Caregivers or other proxies were therefore the respondents in 12 of the 15 records with data (80.0%), and the patient responded directly in three (20.0%). No observable signs of distress were reported in 12 (92.3%), and mild distress in one (7.7%), manifesting as agitation; zero (0%) were rated moderate or severe distress, and in no case was the procedure stopped or nearly stopped because of distress.All 13 encounters with available assistance data (100%) required hands-on assistance to complete collection, provided by the program nurse in nine (69.2%) and by a caregiver in four (30.8%). full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis work demonstrates that a nurse-assisted workflow can be used to deliver HPV cervical cancer screening on a self-collected vaginal specimen to adults with IDD in routine primary care. Self-collected HPV screening is now recognized in national guidance as an acceptable option for average-risk individuals, but its implementation in populations with significant sensory, cognitive, and behavioral barriers remains limited. This report describes a pragmatic implementation strategy rather than a novel diagnostic or technological intervention.A key feature of the approach is the integration of nursing staff into the screening workflow to support patient preparation and specimen collection. Caregiver involvement supports communication, patient comfort, and completion of screening within a single encounter, which is relevant in a population for whom additional visits carry transportation, scheduling, and anxiety burdens.Among patients offered the pathway, 14 of 18 (77.8%) completed collection, no attempt that began was left unfinished, and no patient proved unable to complete collection despite assistance. Four patients (22.2% of those offered) declined. Declination is reported here as a legitimate outcome of a model built on assent rather than as a failure of the workflow. These proportions describe completion among patients offered a specific pathway at a clinic encounter and are not comparable with population-level cervical cancer screening coverage estimates, which use different denominators, timeframes, and ascertainment methods; no such comparison is drawn here.The most consequential finding is that no encounter with available assistance data was completed unaided or with verbal coaching alone. All 13 such encounters required hands-on assistance, from the nurse in nine (69.2%) and from a caregiver in four (30.8%). Self-collection in this population is therefore better understood as nurse-assisted collection: the term describes who holds the swab less than it describes a procedure that removes the speculum, the stirrups, and the clinician-directed examination while retaining hands-on support. This distinction matters for anyone planning to replicate the model, because a clinic that budgets for unassisted self-collection will not be able to deliver it. It also means that the accuracy literature on self-collected specimens [9] bears on the specimen type used here rather than on the staffing model.Acceptability was uniform among respondents. Every respondent rated the process acceptable or very acceptable, judged the assistance provided appropriate, and would support offering it again, and tolerance was rated good or very good in every encounter with survey data. Observable distress was rare and mild where present, with no encounter requiring the procedure to be stopped. In a population where speculum examination is frequently deferred or performed under sedation, a screening pathway that no respondent found unacceptable is a substantive result even in a small cohort.The model requires no additional equipment or capital investment beyond the collection kit and aligns with existing preventive care reimbursement structures, which suggests it may be transferable to other primary care settings, including academic clinics, federally qualified health centers, and community practices. Clinic efficiency, physician time, staffing cost, and screening uptake at the clinic level were not measured in this study; however, the scalability of the model therefore remains a hypothesis rather than a finding. The requirement for hands-on nursing assistance in every encounter with available data is itself a resource implication that any replicating site would need to plan for.The animated education video is a low-cost component that is independently transferable. Accessible preparation materials address a barrier that procedural adaptation alone does not, since informed assent requires that the patient understand what the procedure involves. The video is publicly available and can be adopted by other clinics without cost, although its independent contribution was not evaluated in this study.The approach supports more inclusive, sensory-informed care for patients who may otherwise be unable to tolerate or complete speculum-based examination. It emphasizes structured assent, caregiver partnership, and minimization of distress, consistent with principles of patient-centered and disability-affirming care.LimitationsThis evaluation has several limitations. It was conducted at a single academic site with an established interdisciplinary IDD program, and the findings may not generalize to settings without comparable nursing capacity or caregiver engagement. The sample was small, with 14 completed collections against a planned enrollment of 30, and surveys were completed at the end of the encounter, which may favor positive reporting. One respondent recorded the encounter but did not submit the experience items, so those outcomes describe 13 of the 14 completed collections (92.9%); because the survey dataset is anonymous by design, the missing outcomes could not be recovered from the clinical record, and that encounter may have differed from those reported. The uniformly positive ratings should also be read with the setting in mind: respondents were reporting on a service delivered by a team they know, in a program they have chosen to remain with, which is a context that discourages criticism. The survey instrument was investigator-developed and was not formally validated or pilot-tested, so its measurement properties are unknown. Experience was reported largely by caregivers acting as proxies rather than by patients directly, a limitation in a population whose own preferences are underrepresented in the literature, although three respondents were patients reporting on their own experience. There was no comparison group and no pre-intervention acceptability measure, so the results describe acceptability of the adapted approach rather than improvement relative to usual care. Clinic-level screening uptake data were still being collected at the time of this report, so effectiveness cannot yet be assessed. No high-risk HPV infections were detected in this cohort, so the downstream pathway for managing an abnormal result, including speculum-based evaluation or anesthesia-assisted follow-up, was not tested in practice.The HPV assay used here is a laboratory-developed test rather than an assay cleared by the FDA for primary cervical cancer screening. It detects 13 high-risk genotypes and does not include HPV 66, which is covered by some FDA-approved primary screening assays. Pooled accuracy of HPV testing on self-collected specimens is lower than on clinician-collected specimens overall, with the difference concentrated in signal amplification rather than PCR-based assays [9]. The assay used here is PCR-based, but clinics replicating this model should confirm that their laboratory has validated its assay for self-collected vaginal specimens. Clinically, the approach does not eliminate the need for speculum-based evaluation when HPV results are abnormal, and some patients may still require anesthesia-assisted procedures for follow-up. Because the recommended repeat interval following a negative self-collected result is three years rather than five, the reduction in lifetime procedural burden relative to clinician-collected primary HPV testing is smaller than the avoidance of a single speculum examination might suggest [5]. Individuals with HIV infection or immunocompromising conditions may have impaired viral clearance and are not ideal candidates for HPV-only screening pathways. Patients with prior high-grade cervical disease or in utero DES exposure likewise require alternative screening strategies.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsCervical cancer screening disparities among adults with IDD are driven substantially by modifiable system-level barriers rather than by patient refusal. A nurse-assisted model of self-collected HPV screening was feasible within an existing interdisciplinary primary care clinic and was well received: 14 of 18 patients offered the pathway (77.8%) completed collection, tolerance was rated good or very good in all 13 encounters (100%) with complete survey data, observable distress was rare and mild, and all 13 respondents (100%) judged the process acceptable and would support offering it again. Every encounter with available assistance data required hands-on assistance, which should be planned for rather than treated as an exception, and the model is therefore more accurately described as nurse-assisted self-collection. Whether the model improves clinic efficiency, preserves physician time, or is scalable beyond this setting was not measured and remains to be tested. Recruitment toward the planned enrollment of 30 is continuing, and final results will be reported on completion. Further work should evaluate screening uptake before and after implementation, downstream clinical outcomes, patient-reported rather than proxy-reported experience, and sustainability across diverse care settings.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionInclusive cervical cancer screening is a critical health equity issue. Adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are substantially under-screened for cervical cancer. A population-based study comparing women with and without IDD found significantly lower participation in cervical screening among women with IDD, leading the authors to question whether screening programs are delivered equitably to this population [1]. This disparity is multifactorial and reflects both patient-level and system-level barriers. Traditional speculum-based pelvic examination may be intolerable or distressing for some individuals with IDD. Deferred screening is then often mischaracterized as patient refusal rather than as a need for adapted care approaches. A prior review examined barriers to pelvic examination for cervical cancer screening in women with cerebral palsy, a group that overlaps substantially with the population served by this clinic [2].Multiple patient-level and structural barriers contribute to this gap, including sensory sensitivities, communication differences, mobility limitations, anxiety related to pelvic examination, and limited availability of clinician time and training to support adapted screening workflows in primary care settings. A systematic review of cancer screening behavior among people with intellectual disabilities identified barriers and facilitators operating at the patient, caregiver, and health system levels, indicating that screening uptake in this population is shaped by modifiable factors rather than by patient preference alone [3].In practice, options offered to patients who cannot tolerate speculum examination have included modified examination technique, sedation or anesthesia in selected cases, and greater caregiver involvement. Each is resource-intensive, and none is easily scalable in routine primary care.Human papillomavirus (HPV) testing on a self-collected vaginal specimen offers an alternative pathway, and current guidance distinguishes it from clinician-collected primary HPV testing. The American Cancer Society recommends that individuals with a cervix begin cervical cancer screening at age 25 years and continue through age 65 years, with primary HPV testing on a clinician-collected cervical specimen every five years as the preferred strategy [4]. In a 2026 update, the American Cancer Society concluded that clinician-collected cervical specimens remain preferred, but that self-collected vaginal specimens are acceptable for cervical cancer screening in average-risk individuals aged 25-65 years, with repeat testing recommended at three years rather than five years following a negative self-collected result [5]. The World Health Organization recommends HPV DNA detection as the primary screening method for the general population of women and, as a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence, suggests that HPV DNA testing may be performed on either a provider-collected or a self-collected sample [6]. A US Preventive Services Task Force draft recommendation statement addressing patient-collected high-risk HPV screening was posted for public comment on December 10, 2024; that draft has not been finalized and does not represent a current Task Force recommendation [7]. Published implementation experience describing how self-collected HPV screening can be operationalized for patients with significant sensory, cognitive, and behavioral barriers remains limited.The aim of this work was to evaluate respondent-reported acceptability and tolerability of a clinic-based, nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model for patients with IDD within an academic primary care setting and to characterize the level of assistance required to complete collection.Portions of this work were previously presented as a plenary presentation at the Society of General Internal Medicine Southern Regional Meeting (Inclusive Cervical Cancer Screening: Nurse-Led, Self-Administered Swab Model for Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities, 2026, New Orleans, LA, USA) and as a poster at the Down Syndrome Medical Interest Group-USA (DSMIG-USA) Annual Symposium (Implementing Nurse- and Caregiver-Supported Self-Collected HPV Screening in Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities, 2026, Orlando, FL, USA).

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the acceptability and tolerability of a nurse-assisted, self-collected HPV cervical cancer screening model in adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD). The research aimed to address the lower screening rates observed in this population. The model included structured pre-visit planning, an animated patient education video, and caregiver engagement.
elements_en.main_results: Of 23 patients identified as eligible, 14 (60.9%) completed collection. All 13 respondents (100%) judged the level of assistance appropriate, rated the process acceptable or very acceptable, and would support offering it again. No patients met criteria for alternative screening strategies.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating that the nurse-assisted self-collected HPV screening model was well tolerated and highly acceptable to respondents in an academic primary care clinic for adults with IDD. This is a novel approach to addressing screening barriers in this population.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that this model could improve cervical cancer screening rates among adults with IDD, potentially enhancing early detection and prevention efforts. They inform the development of more accessible and patient-centered screening strategies for this vulnerable group.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Given the pilot design and small sample, no inferential testing was performed, and no comparison group was used. The evidence is therefore limited in scope and strength, with a moderate confidence assessment due to the preliminary nature of the findings.
