papers.full_text: IntroductionThis retrospective, single-center study aims to analyze the prevalence and genotype distribution of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection in women undergoing HPV testing at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China.MethodsA total of 13,492 females, 18–85 years, undergoing HPV testing at the physical examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou, China, were recruited. Cervical cast-off cells were collected for HPV testing by low-density gene chip and flow hybridization technology using HPV typing test kit. A total of 27 kinds of HPV types were detected using this method, including 17 kinds of high-risk HPV (HR-HPV) and 10 kinds of low-risk/uncertain oncogenic significance HPV (LR-HPV).ResultsThe overall HPV infection rate was 16.86% (2,275/13,492), with 12.59% (1,699/13,492) females detected as single HPV-type infection and 4.27% (576/13492) females detected as multiple HPV-type infection. Among all 27 detected HPV types, HPV52 exhibited the highest prevalence (3.58%, 483/13,492), followed by HPV53 (1.76%, 237/13,492) and HPV81 (1.71%, 231/13,492). The most common HPV coinfection pattern was HPV52 + HPV53 (12/2,275). Overall HPV prevalence showed a “two-peak” age-related distribution, with the first peak in the ≤29-year age group (19.69%) and the second peak in the ≥60-year age group (24.45%), respectively. It decreased in the 40- to 49-year age group (13.64%). The prevalence of single/multiple HPV and HR-HPV/LR-HPV infection also exhibited age-related trends similar to those described above. Binary logistic regression analysis revealed a non-linear relationship between HPV prevalence and age (p < 0.05).ConclusionOur study revealed the basic genotype- and age-specific distribution of HPV infection among females attending the physical examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou. These results emphasized that the specific population should strengthen regular HPV surveillance and improve awareness of vaccination, especially for the highly prevalent HPV types (HPV52,53,51). In addition, our findings provide valuable insights for the measurement of HPV prevention interventions. 2Materials and methods2.1Ethics statementThe study involving humans was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhangzhou Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University (Ethics approval number: 2026LWB202) on 4 June 2026. The study was conducted in accordance with the local legislation and institutional requirements. Written informed consent for participants was not required from the participants or the participants’ legal guardians/next of kin because this is a retrospective study, and all the participants’ results were retrospectively collected.2.2Study design and populationsInitially, a total of 23,650 participants with HPV testing data were retrospectively retrieved from the laboratory information system (LIS) at Zhangzhou Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University, from January 2025 to August 2025. Participants who underwent HPV testing at the health examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou were included (n = 13,492). Meanwhile, the participants attending other clinics in this hospital, including gynecology, urology, and obstetrics, were excluded (n = 10,029). We excluded male participants (n = 129). Duplicate records were checked using unique participant IDs. Among the 13,492 included participants, no duplicate subjects were observed. In addition, no cases with incomplete data were observed. Therefore, the number of final included participants was 13,492, aged 18–85 years. The participant selection flow diagram is shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Participants’ selection flow diagram.Flowchart illustrating participant selection: from 23,650 initial participants, 10,029 attending other departments and 129 males were excluded, leaving 13,492. No samples were excluded due to incomplete data or duplication, resulting in 13,492 final included participants.2.3HPV genotypingTo collect the cervical cast-off cells, a vaginal dilator was used to expose the cervix. Cervical mucus was removed with a cotton swab. The cervical brush was placed at the cervical opening and gently rotated clockwise for 3–5 times. The cervical brush was slowly removed and placed into a sample tube containing cell preservation solution. The brush head was left in the sample tube, and the bottle cap was tightened. The sample tubes were labeled with number and date and then transported to the laboratory for immediate DNA extraction or stored at 2–8 °C for no more than 2 weeks.To extract the HPV DNA, 0.5–1.0 mL of cell preservation solution containing cervical cast-off cells was centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 1 min, and the supernatant was discarded. Then HPV DNA was extracted using cell lysis buffer (Kaipu Biotechnology, China, Catalog: 20150019) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Then, 1 μL of extracted DNA sample was served as a template for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification and flow-through hybridization technology using the HPV typing test kit (PCR + Membrane Hybridization Method) (Chaozhou Kaipu Biotechnology Co. Ltd., Catalog: 20143402188) and nucleic acid molecule rapid hybridization instrument (HHM-2, Chaozhou Kaipu Biotechnology Co. Ltd.) according to the manufacturer’s guidelines.This testing method used PCR to amplify HPV DNA. The PCR products were then applied to a low-density gene chip, and flow-hybridization technology was used to detect hybridization between the amplified products and type-specific probe membranes; thereby, a total of 27 different HPV genotypes were detected.According to the HPV classification framework of IARC, HPV types were classified into group 1 (carcinogenic to humans), group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans), group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans), and group 3 (non-oncogenic HPV or uncertain oncogenic significance). In this study, the HPV types of IARC Group 1/2A/2B were classified as HR-HPV. Meanwhile, the HPV types of IARC Group 3 were classified as low-risk/uncertain oncogenic significance HPV (LR-HPV). Here, we detected 17 HR-HPV types (HPV16, HPV18, HPV26, HPV31, HPV33, HPV35, HPV39, HPV45, HPV51, HPV52, HPV53, HPV56, HPV58, HPV59, HPV66, HPV68, HPV82) and 10 LR-HPV types (HPV6, HPV11, HPV40, HPV42, HPV43, HPV44, HPV55, HPV61, HPV81, HPV83) using HPV kit.2.4Quality control and judgment criteria(1) Limit of detection (LOD): The kit’s LOD is no higher than 5,000 copies per reaction.(2) Specificity: The detection results of HPV negative standard samples should all be negative. In addition, the detection results of HPV-positive standard samples or HR-HPV samples should not exhibit any cross-reactions. The cross-reactivity rate in the detection of LR-HPV samples should be less than 10%.(3) Quality control: Plasmid clones containing HPV DNA were used as the positive control samples. DNase-free H2O was used as the negative control sample. Each membrane has a biotin control point to detect the reaction between alkaline phosphatase and its substrate. In addition, the membrane contains an internal control point, which serves as an inner quality control template for DNA. If the internal control point is positive, the results are reliable.(4) Judgment criteria: This reagent is a qualitative detection reagent. The positive test result is a clear and visible blue-purple dot. Based on the arrangement of various HPV probes on the membrane strip, the HPV type can be determined by the positive point. If the internal control point and biotin point are positive while the other points are negative, the test result is judged negative. If one or more HPV genotyping points are positive, the sample is judged as single- or multiple HPV positive.Single genotype infection was defined as the infection of one HPV genotype among the 27 HPV types mentioned above; multiple infection is defined as the infection of ≥2 positive HPV types among the 27 HPV types mentioned above.2.5Statistical analysisStatistical analysis was performed using SPSS software 26.0 (IBM Corp., NY, USA). The prevalence of age-specific or HPV type-specific infection was reported with Wilson score 95% confidence intervals (CI). Odds ratios (ORs) were estimated by comparing the HPV prevalence across different age groups with ≥60-year age group as reference; 95% confidence intervals for ORs were calculated by Woolf’s logit method. Chi-square or Fisher’s exact test was applied for the comparison of prevalence in different age groups with ≥60-year age group. For comparison between multiple age groups, p-value was adjusted using Bonferroni method; p < 0.05/10 = 0.005 was considered statistically significant.Logistic regression analysis was performed with age and age squared (age2) as continuous variables to evaluate non-linear (quadratic) associations between the prevalence of HPV infection and age. HPV infection status (positive or negative) was included as the dependent variable, whereas age and age squared were included as independent variables. full_text_sections.abstract: IntroductionThis retrospective, single-center study aims to analyze the prevalence and genotype distribution of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection in women undergoing HPV testing at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China.MethodsA total of 13,492 females, 18–85 years, undergoing HPV testing at the physical examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou, China, were recruited. Cervical cast-off cells were collected for HPV testing by low-density gene chip and flow hybridization technology using HPV typing test kit. A total of 27 kinds of HPV types were detected using this method, including 17 kinds of high-risk HPV (HR-HPV) and 10 kinds of low-risk/uncertain oncogenic significance HPV (LR-HPV).ResultsThe overall HPV infection rate was 16.86% (2,275/13,492), with 12.59% (1,699/13,492) females detected as single HPV-type infection and 4.27% (576/13492) females detected as multiple HPV-type infection. Among all 27 detected HPV types, HPV52 exhibited the highest prevalence (3.58%, 483/13,492), followed by HPV53 (1.76%, 237/13,492) and HPV81 (1.71%, 231/13,492). The most common HPV coinfection pattern was HPV52 + HPV53 (12/2,275). Overall HPV prevalence showed a “two-peak” age-related distribution, with the first peak in the ≤29-year age group (19.69%) and the second peak in the ≥60-year age group (24.45%), respectively. It decreased in the 40- to 49-year age group (13.64%). The prevalence of single/multiple HPV and HR-HPV/LR-HPV infection also exhibited age-related trends similar to those described above. Binary logistic regression analysis revealed a non-linear relationship between HPV prevalence and age (p < 0.05).ConclusionOur study revealed the basic genotype- and age-specific distribution of HPV infection among females attending the physical examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou. These results emphasized that the specific population should strengthen regular HPV surveillance and improve awareness of vaccination, especially for the highly prevalent HPV types (HPV52,53,51). In addition, our findings provide valuable insights for the measurement of HPV prevention interventions.

No samples were excluded due to incomplete data or duplication, resulting in 13,492 final included participants.2.3HPV genotypingTo collect the cervical cast-off cells, a vaginal dilator was used to expose the cervix. Cervical mucus was removed with a cotton swab. The cervical brush was placed at the cervical opening and gently rotated clockwise for 3–5 times. Ltd., Catalog: 20143402188) and nucleic acid molecule rapid hybridization instrument (HHM-2, Chaozhou Kaipu Biotechnology Co. Ltd.) according to the manufacturer’s guidelines.This testing method used PCR to amplify HPV DNA. The PCR products were then applied to a low-density gene chip, and flow-hybridization technology was used to detect hybridization between the amplified products and type-specific probe membranes; thereby, a total of 27 different HPV genotypes were detected.According to the HPV classification framework of IARC, HPV types were classified into group 1 (carcinogenic to humans), group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans), group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans), and group 3 (non-oncogenic HPV or uncertain oncogenic significance). In this study, the HPV types of IARC Group 1/2A/2B were classified as HR-HPV. Meanwhile, the HPV types of IARC Group 3 were classified as low-risk/uncertain oncogenic significance HPV (LR-HPV). In addition, the detection results of HPV-positive standard samples or HR-HPV samples should not exhibit any cross-reactions. The cross-reactivity rate in the detection of LR-HPV samples should be less than 10%.(3) Quality control: Plasmid clones containing HPV DNA were used as the positive control samples. DNase-free H2O was used as the negative control sample. Each membrane has a biotin control point to detect the reaction between alkaline phosphatase and its substrate. In addition, the membrane contains an internal control point, which serves as an inner quality control template for DNA. If the internal control point is positive, the results are reliable.(4) Judgment criteria: This reagent is a qualitative detection reagent. The positive test result is a clear and visible blue-purple dot. Based on the arrangement of various HPV probes on the membrane strip, the HPV type can be determined by the positive point. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionIn this study, we investigated the age- and genotype-specific HPV prevalence among females attending the physical examination center at a hospital in Zhangzhou City, Fujian Province, China. Our research identified the predominant HPV types in Zhangzhou and the age-related distribution of HPV prevalence among all participants. Our research provides baseline HPV prevalence data in Zhangzhou, which contributes to the formulation of HPV preventive measures and emphasizes the importance of HPV surveillance, especially for the age groups with high HPV prevalence.Our data revealed that the overall HPV prevalence in Zhangzhou is 16.86%, which was similar to the overall HPV prevalence in Beijing (17.28%) (8) and the nation-wide research among Chinese women (17.70%) (6). The overall prevalence in our study was significantly lower than that reported in Fujian Province in 2017 (38.3%) (7) and higher than that reported in Zhejiang Province (15.29%) (9). These significant discrepancies may partly reflect the increasing HPV vaccination coverage and the improvement of social HPV-preventive awareness in Fujian Province in recent years. Other potential explanations for the discrepancies should also be considered, including discrepancies in study populations, sampling strategies, age-group distribution, laboratory detection assays, study time windows, cervical screening-seeking behaviors, and additional epidemiological determinants. However, vaccination status and other epidemiological factors were not available for individual participants in this study. Therefore, this hypothesis needs further investigation in the future. These observations suggest that HPV infection remains a public health challenge in some regions of China. In addition, regional disparities in HPV prevalence across China highlight the importance of effective public health measures for the prevention of HPV infection.We observed that the predominant HR-HPV types in Zhangzhou City were HPV52, HPV53, HPV51, HPV58, and HPV39, respectively. A previous study in Fujian Province reported that HPV16 (8.5%), HPV52 (7.9%), HPV58 (6.2%), and HPV53 (3.5%) accounted for over 60% of all HPV-positive cases (7). Another study in Zhejiang Province demonstrated that HPV-16, HPV-52, HPV-58, and HPV-18 were the predominant HPV types (9). In addition, HPV-52, HPV-16, and HPV-58 were predominant types in Guangzhou (10). Based on these studies, we found that the prevalence of HPV16 and HPV18 was comparatively low in Zhangzhou, which was inconsistent with the findings from other geographical regions of China. Therefore, these results indicate that HPV genotype distribution differs significantly across geographical regions, which may be attributable to regional differences in economic conditions or HPV vaccination programs.In China, the licensed 9-valent HPV vaccines provide predominant protection against the most prevalent HR-HPV genotypes, including HPV16, 18, 6, 11, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 (11, 12). In this study, we observed that the most prevalent HPV type, HPV-52, has been included in the licensed vaccine in China. However, other prevalent HR-HPV types, including HPV53 and HPV51, were not included in the licensed vaccines in China. In addition, the included types HPV16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 6, and 11 exhibited relatively low prevalence in Zhangzhou. These findings reflect only the genotype diversity of local individual HPV infection characteristics and do not indicate the inadequacy or ineffectiveness of the currently available HPV vaccine in China. Therefore, additional local HPV vaccination data need to be collected to further clarify the protective effectiveness of current HPV vaccines against HPV infection in Zhangzhou. In conclusion, these findings underscore the need to consider the relationship between the currently available HPV vaccine and the currently prevalent HPV types. Furthermore, it provides valuable insights for the development of next-generation HPV vaccines.In our study, we observed that the ≥60-year age group exhibited the highest HPV prevalence, implying that HPV infection still posed a substantial disease burden among older adult females. The females in the ≤29-year age group also showed an elevated HPV prevalence. Therefore, the HPV prevalence among females in Zhangzhou City seemed to exhibit a “two-peak” age-related distribution. Furthermore, logistic regression analysis also revealed a non-linear association between age and HPV infection. These observations were similar to previous research in Zhejiang Province and nation-wide research in China (6, 9). However, the correlation between age and infection rate was only limited to speculation, as a few factors, such as sexual activity (13), changing sexual partners, immune weakening, and vaccine coverage, may influence HPV infection (14–17), have not been taken into account in our research. In conclusion, our data underscore the need for regular HPV screening and surveillance among young and older adult females in Zhangzhou.Our research still has the following limitations: (1) We only provided basic and limited information about the study population, including age and testing results. Other important population characteristics, including marital status, residence/urban–rural status, previous cervical cancer screening, HPV vaccination status, and history of cervical lesions, may significantly influence HPV infection. Therefore, more detailed information about the study population needs to be collected. (2) The participants in this study are hospital-based, which may differ substantially from the general population. Therefore, our findings may not be applicable to the general population. (3) Our research is a single-center retrospective study. Therefore, these findings may not be generalized to a wider population in Zhangzhou. (4) Cytological and histopathological findings related to cervical lesions and clinical follow-up data were unavailable. Consequently, we could not identify CIN1/CIN2/CIN3 or invasive cervical cancer cases, and could not establish associations between specific HPV genotypes and cervical cancer based on the current data. The conclusions are limited to HPV prevalence and genotype distribution.In conclusion, this research investigated the prevalence and genotype distribution of HPV infection in females attending the physical examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou City, China. A non-linear distribution was observed between HPV prevalence and age, with older adult females (≥60 years old) exhibiting the highest HPV infection rate. In addition, HPV52, 53, and 51 were the highly prevalent HR-HPV types in Zhangzhou City. Our results implied that HR-HPV infection still poses a substantial disease burden among older adult females in Zhangzhou City and revealed the prevalent HR-HPV types in Zhangzhou City. This study emphasized the importance of HPV infection surveillance, especially among older adult females, and provided valuable insights into the preventive measures targeting predominant HR-HPV types in Zhangzhou City.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionCervical cancer ranks as the fourth most prevalent cancer among females across the world, contributing an estimated 660,000 newly diagnosed cases and 350,000 disease-related mortalities globally in 2022 (1). Cervical cancer ranked sixth in mortality among all female malignancies in China in 2022, with an estimated 150,700 new cervical cancer cases and 55,700 related deaths (2). Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) has been identified as a risk factor for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer. The World Health Organization proposed a 90–70–90 global strategy to accelerate the elimination of cervical cancer by 2030, which is to achieve HPV vaccination rates of ≥90% in women before the age of 15, efficient screening coverage rates of ≥70% in women before the age of 35 and 45, and treatment rates of ≥90% for diagnosed cervical lesions (3).Over 200 types of HPV have been identified. According to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) Working Group HPV classification framework, 12 HPV types, including HPV16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, and 59, have been classified as carcinogenic (IARC Group 1) to humans, other eight HPV types in this high-risk clade, including 26, 53, 66, 67, 68, 70, 73, and 82, were classified as probable/possible carcinogenic (IARC Group 2A and IARC Group 2B). In addition, HPV types 6, 11, 40, 42, 43, 44, 54, 61, 72, 81, and 89 were classified as non-oncogenic (IARC Group 3). Currently, the HPV vaccine is still the most effective strategy to prevent HPV infection and cervical cancer. In addition, routine HPV screening, especially HR-HPV screening, is strongly recommended, which can contribute to the prevention of cervical cancer (4, 5).Previously, a nationwide study in China revealed that the overall HPV prevalence of Chinese females was at a relatively high level (17.70%), with high- and low-risk types being 13.12 and 4.58%, respectively (6). Several studies have demonstrated that HPV prevalence among women and the distribution of predominant HPV genotypes exhibit distinct geographical disparities and genotypic diversity. A study in Fujian Province demonstrated that HR-HPV infections were mainly attributed to HPV16, HPV52, HPV58, and HPV53 types (7). Zhangzhou City is located in southeastern China, Fujian Province. However, the prevalence and infection patterns of HPV among females in Zhangzhou City have not been reported yet. Therefore, it is necessary to obtain the local baseline data of HPV prevalence in Zhangzhou City, which will contribute to the prevention of HPV infection and the implementation of the HPV vaccination program.In this study, we aim to investigate the local genotype-specific prevalence of HPV infection and analyze the age-related trends of HPV infection among females undergoing HPV testing in a physical examination center of a hospital in Zhangzhou City. 2.1Ethics statementThe study involving humans was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhangzhou Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University (Ethics approval number: 2026LWB202) on 4 June 2026. The study was conducted in accordance with the local legislation and institutional requirements. Written informed consent for participants was not required from the participants or the participants’ legal guardians/next of kin because this is a retrospective study, and all the participants’ results were retrospectively collected. 2.3HPV genotypingTo collect the cervical cast-off cells, a vaginal dilator was used to expose the cervix. Cervical mucus was removed with a cotton swab. The cervical brush was placed at the cervical opening and gently rotated clockwise for 3–5 times. The cervical brush was slowly removed and placed into a sample tube containing cell preservation solution. The brush head was left in the sample tube, and the bottle cap was tightened. The sample tubes were labeled with number and date and then transported to the laboratory for immediate DNA extraction or stored at 2–8 °C for no more than 2 weeks.To extract the HPV DNA, 0.5–1.0 mL of cell preservation solution containing cervical cast-off cells was centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 1 min, and the supernatant was discarded. Then HPV DNA was extracted using cell lysis buffer (Kaipu Biotechnology, China, Catalog: 20150019) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Then, 1 μL of extracted DNA sample was served as a template for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification and flow-through hybridization technology using the HPV typing test kit (PCR + Membrane Hybridization Method) (Chaozhou Kaipu Biotechnology Co. Ltd., Catalog: 20143402188) and nucleic acid molecule rapid hybridization instrument (HHM-2, Chaozhou Kaipu Biotechnology Co. Ltd.) according to the manufacturer’s guidelines.This testing method used PCR to amplify HPV DNA. The PCR products were then applied to a low-density gene chip, and flow-hybridization technology was used to detect hybridization between the amplified products and type-specific probe membranes; thereby, a total of 27 different HPV genotypes were detected.According to the HPV classification framework of IARC, HPV types were classified into group 1 (carcinogenic to humans), group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans), group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans), and group 3 (non-oncogenic HPV or uncertain oncogenic significance). In this study, the HPV types of IARC Group 1/2A/2B were classified as HR-HPV. Meanwhile, the HPV types of IARC Group 3 were classified as low-risk/uncertain oncogenic significance HPV (LR-HPV). Here, we detected 17 HR-HPV types (HPV16, HPV18, HPV26, HPV31, HPV33, HPV35, HPV39, HPV45, HPV51, HPV52, HPV53, HPV56, HPV58, HPV59, HPV66, HPV68, HPV82) and 10 LR-HPV types (HPV6, HPV11, HPV40, HPV42, HPV43, HPV44, HPV55, HPV61, HPV81, HPV83) using HPV kit. 2.4Quality control and judgment criteria(1) Limit of detection (LOD): The kit’s LOD is no higher than 5,000 copies per reaction.(2) Specificity: The detection results of HPV negative standard samples should all be negative. In addition, the detection results of HPV-positive standard samples or HR-HPV samples should not exhibit any cross-reactions. The cross-reactivity rate in the detection of LR-HPV samples should be less than 10%.(3) Quality control: Plasmid clones containing HPV DNA were used as the positive control samples. DNase-free H2O was used as the negative control sample. Each membrane has a biotin control point to detect the reaction between alkaline phosphatase and its substrate. In addition, the membrane contains an internal control point, which serves as an inner quality control template for DNA. If the internal control point is positive, the results are reliable.(4) Judgment criteria: This reagent is a qualitative detection reagent. The positive test result is a clear and visible blue-purple dot. Based on the arrangement of various HPV probes on the membrane strip, the HPV type can be determined by the positive point. If the internal control point and biotin point are positive while the other points are negative, the test result is judged negative. If one or more HPV genotyping points are positive, the sample is judged as single- or multiple HPV positive.Single genotype infection was defined as the infection of one HPV genotype among the 27 HPV types mentioned above; multiple infection is defined as the infection of ≥2 positive HPV types among the 27 HPV types mentioned above. 2.5Statistical analysisStatistical analysis was performed using SPSS software 26.0 (IBM Corp., NY, USA). Odds ratios (ORs) were estimated by comparing the HPV prevalence across different age groups with ≥60-year age group as reference; 95% confidence intervals for ORs were calculated by Woolf’s logit method. papers.title_original: Prevalence and genotype distribution of human papillomavirus infection among women undergoing HPV testing at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China: a retrospective study

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the prevalence and genotype distribution of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection among women undergoing HPV testing at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China, to provide insights into the epidemiological patterns of HPV in this population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective, single-center study was conducted at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China, involving 13,492 females aged 18–85 years who underwent HPV testing. Male participants were excluded, leaving 13,492 females in the study population.
analysis.methods: DNA samples were extracted and used as templates for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification, followed by flow-through hybridization technology using an HPV typing test kit. Logistic regression analysis was performed with age and age squared as continuous variables to assess non-linear associations between HPV prevalence and age. The Bonferroni method was used to adjust p-values for multiple comparisons.
analysis.main_results: The overall HPV infection rate was 16.86% (2,275/13,492), with 12.59% (1,699/13,492) being single-type infections and 4.27% (576/13,492) being multiple-type infections. HPV52 had the highest prevalence at 3.58% (483/13,492), followed by HPV53 (1.76%) and HPV81 (1.71%). The prevalence showed a "two-peak" age-related distribution, with peaks in the ≤29-year and ≥60-year age groups, and a decrease in the 40- to 49-year age group.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study revealed the age-specific and genotype-specific distribution of HPV infection in females attending a hospital in Zhangzhou, highlighting the need for targeted surveillance and awareness of vaccination for highly prevalent HPV types.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings can inform public health strategies for HPV surveillance and vaccination programs, particularly emphasizing the importance of monitoring and managing the most prevalent HPV types in this population.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its single-center design and retrospective nature, which may affect generalizability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational approach and potential for confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective study analyzed the prevalence and genotype distribution of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection among 13,492 females aged 18–85 years undergoing HPV testing at a hospital in Zhangzhou, China. The overall HPV infection rate was 16.86%, with HPV52 being the most prevalent type. The prevalence showed a "two-peak" age-related distribution, peaking in the ≤29-year and ≥60-year age groups, and decreasing in the 40–49-year age group. The study also identified common co-infection patterns, such as HPV52 + HPV53. These findings highlight the need for targeted HPV surveillance and vaccination efforts, especially for the most prevalent types. The study's limitations include its single-center design and retrospective nature, which may limit generalizability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational approach and potential for confounding factors.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 中国漳州一家医院进行了一项回顾性单中心研究,纳入了 13,492 名 18-85 岁女性,她们接受了 HPV 检测。男性参与者被排除在外,研究人群中只剩下 13,492 名女性。
elements_zh.methods: 提取 DNA 样本并用作聚合酶链式反应 (PCR) 扩增的模板,然后使用 HPV 分型检测试剂盒进行流通杂交技术。以年龄和年龄平方作为连续变量进行逻辑回归分析,以评估 HPV 患病率 与年龄之间的非线性关联。Bonferroni 方法用于调整多重比较的 p 值。

elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为 HPV 监测 和 疫苗接种 计划的公共卫生策略提供信息,特别强调监测和管理该人群中最流行的 HPV 类型的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其单中心设计和回顾性而受到限制,这可能会影响普遍性。由于观察方法和潜在的混杂因素,证据的强度中等。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在调查在中国漳州一家医院接受 HPV 检测的女性中的 患病率 和 人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 感染的基因型分布,以深入了解该人群中 HPV 的流行病学模式。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 中国漳州一家医院进行了一项回顾性单中心研究,纳入了 13,492 名 18-85 岁女性,她们接受了 HPV 检测。男性参与者被排除在外,研究人群中只剩下 13,492 名女性。
analysis_zh.methods: 提取 DNA 样本并用作聚合酶链式反应 (PCR) 扩增的模板,然后使用 HPV 分型检测试剂盒进行流通杂交技术。以年龄和年龄平方作为连续变量进行逻辑回归分析,以评估 HPV 患病率 与年龄之间的非线性关联。Bonferroni 方法用于调整多重比较的 p 值。
analysis_zh.main_results: HPV总体感染率为16.86%(2,275/13,492),其中单一型别感染率为12.59%(1,699/13,492),多重型别感染率为4.27%(576/13,492)。HPV52 的 患病率 最高,为 3.58% (483/13,492),其次是 HPV53 (1.76%) 和 HPV81 (1.71%)。患病率呈现出与年龄相关的“双峰”分布,峰值出现在≤29岁和≥60岁年龄组,下降出现在40至49岁年龄组。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究揭示了漳州一家医院就诊的女性中 HPV 感染的年龄特异性和基因型特异性分布,强调了有针对性的 监测 的必要性以及对 疫苗接种 对高流行 HPV 类型的认识。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为 HPV 监测 和 疫苗接种 计划的公共卫生策略提供信息,特别强调监测和管理该人群中最流行的 HPV 类型的重要性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其单中心设计和回顾性而受到限制,这可能会影响普遍性。由于观察方法和潜在的混杂因素,证据的强度中等。

papers.full_text: AbstractIntroductionThe cervicovaginal microbiome is a proposed modifier of HPV-associated cervical disease, yet its relationship with viral type heterogeneity, cytological grade, and community state type (CST) remains incompletely understood.MethodsThis cross-sectional study characterized cervicovaginal microbiome composition and functional potential across HPV infection status, viral type categories (No HPV, HPV High Risk, HPV16, HPV18, HPV Other), cervical cytological grades, and CSTs in 311 non-pregnant women using whole-genome shotgun metagenomic sequencing, integrated diversity analyses, MaAsLin2 differential abundance testing, and HUMAnN 3.0 functional pathway profiling.ResultsHPV-positive samples showed increased bacterial species richness, and a reciprocal Lactobacillus-to-Gardnerella dominance shift compared to HPV-negative samples. HPV Other showed the highest bacterial species richness and distinct taxonomic and predicted functional associations, including higher inferred abundance of siderophore- and lipopolysaccharide-biosynthesis pathways; however, overall species-level community composition did not differ significantly across HPV type groups. CST I and CST II exhibited compositional stability regardless of HPV status, while CST IV showed pronounced Lactobacillus depletion in HPV-positive women. LSIL was associated with lower Fannyhessea vaginae and Alloscardovia omnicolens abundance and higher Phocaeicola vulgatus abundance relative to NILM.DiscussionThese findings indicate that oncogenic potential and dysbiosis severity are not aligned, and that CST type modifies HPV–microbiome interactions.Keywords: cervical dysbiosis, cervicovaginal microbiome, community state type, human papillomavirus, shotgun metagenomics 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study design and populationThis cross-sectional study was conducted at the National Research Center for Mother and Child Health, a tertiary academic medical center in Astana, Kazakhstan. Non-pregnant women aged 18–46 years with regular menstrual cycles and an intact cervix were recruited from the outpatient gynecology clinic. Participants were excluded for major chronic or immunocompromising conditions, acute inflammation, recent antibiotic/probiotic/immunosuppressive therapy, smoking, intrauterine device use, prior HPV vaccination, or recent invasive gynecological procedures. Samples with incomplete metadata, insufficient sequencing data, or missing CST classification were excluded from the relevant analyses. A subset of the HPV-negative, NILM (normal cytology) participants characterized here (n = 92) was previously reported as a dedicated multi-kingdom baseline cohort in Rakhmankulova et al. (2026), which used the same BioProject accession (PRJNA1337009) to describe bacterial, viral, fungal, and archaeal community structure in HPV-negative women prior to HPV-positive comparison. The present study extends those baseline findings by incorporating HPV-positive comparator groups (HPV16, HPV18, HPV Other, HPV High Risk), cervical cytological grade stratification, and CST-based differential abundance and functional pathway analyses not covered in the earlier report.2.2.Sample collection, DNA extraction and sequencingCervical samples were stored at −80 °C until processing. Total genomic DNA was extracted using the ZymoBIOMICS DNA Miniprep Kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Sterile nuclease-free water was included as a negative extraction control, and the ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Community Standard was used as a positive control. DNA samples were required to contain at least 1.0 μg total DNA, with good integrity and no visible impurities. DNA concentration was measured using a microplate reader with a broad-range DNA assay, and DNA integrity was assessed by agarose gel electrophoresis.Raw paired-end sequencing reads were processed using fastp for adapter trimming and quality filtering. Read pairs were discarded when adapter contamination was detected, when more than 5 bp contained ambiguous nucleotides, or when more than 40% of bases were of low quality. Sliding-window trimming was performed using a 4-bp window and a Q15 threshold. The mean numbers of raw and clean reads were 48.5 million and 47.9 million reads per sample, respectively. Mean Q20/Q30 values were 98.2%/93.8% for raw reads and 99.0%/95.3% for clean reads.Human-read depletion was performed by alignment against the human GRCh38 reference genome using Bowtie2 v2.4.4. In the original pipeline, read pairs failing concordant alignment to the human reference were retained using the --un-conc-gz option while preserving paired-read structure for downstream metagenomic classification. Residual host content after depletion was evaluated using Kraken2 v2.1.3. On average, 92.1% of reads in the Bowtie2-retained fraction were subsequently classified as Homo sapiens, indicating substantial residual host sequence after this permissive depletion step. Approximately 7.9% of reads in the retained fraction were not classified as human and comprised microbial and unclassified reads available for downstream taxonomic classification.Taxonomic classification was performed using Kraken2 v2.1.3 against the PlusPFP Kraken2/Bracken database. Bracken v3.0 was subsequently used to refine genus- and species-level abundance estimates. Functional profiling was performed using HUMAnN 3.0 with UniRef90 protein annotations and MetaCyc pathway reconstruction. No predefined minimum non-host sequencing-depth threshold was applied in the original pipeline. Because effective bacterial sequencing depth varied substantially among samples, classified bacterial depth was quantified directly from the unnormalized Kraken2/Bracken bacterial count table and was explicitly evaluated in subsequent depth-corrected and sensitivity analyses. Classified bacterial sequencing depth was defined as the total number of reads assigned to the bacterial domain (d:Bacteria) in the unnormalized Kraken2/Bracken count table.2.3.GroupingsSamples were analyzed according to four main clinical and microbiome grouping variables: HPV status, HPV type group, cytology/histology grade, and bacterial community state type (CST). HPV status was assessed using the RealBest DNA HPV High Carcinogenic Risk Genotype real-time PCR kit (Cat. No. C8899; Vector-Best), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The assay detects the following high-risk HPV genotypes: 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, and 59. A sample was considered positive when at least one HPV genotype produced a cycle-threshold value of Ct ≤35. Samples without detection of any target genotype were classified as negative for the high-risk HPV types included in the assay. Whole-genome shotgun sequencing data were also screened for HPV sequences to identify genotypes not included in the PCR panel. The standard Reference sequence databases were used. Samples positive by either PCR or WGS were classified as HPV-positive. For descriptive analyses, HPV16 and HPV18 were retained as separate categories, other oncogenic genotypes were classified as HPV High Risk, and detected genotypes outside the predefined high-risk list were classified as HPV Other. The HPV Other group comprised samples in which WGS screening identified only genotypes classified as low-risk or non-carcinogenic by IARC (HPV6b, 7, 11, 26, 30, 32, 34, 53, 54, 71, 85, 90, 144, 156, and 166). A small number of HPV Other samples additionally showed trace-level WGS reads mapping to the high-risk genotypes HPV16, HPV31, or HPV35; because these reads represented less than 5% of the relative HPV sequence abundance within the sample, well below the threshold used to call a genotype present, these samples were retained in the HPV Other group rather than reclassified as HPV16, HPV High Risk, or HPV-positive for the corresponding high-risk type. Cytology/histology grade was categorized as NILM, ASC-US, LSIL, and ASC-H. CSTs were assigned manually from species-level relative abundance profiles following the five-community framework of Ravel et al. (2011). The dominant taxon was defined as the CST-associated bacterial species with the highest relative abundance within each sample. Samples were classified as CST I, CST II, CST III, or CST V when Lactobacillus crispatus, L. gasseri, L. iners, or L. jensenii, respectively, showed the highest relative abundance. Samples lacking dominance by these Lactobacillus species and characterized by predominance of anaerobic bacteria were assigned to CST IV. No fixed abundance threshold was used.2.4.Statistical and bioinformatic analysisBacterial alpha- and beta-diversity analyses were performed using species-level bacterial relative-abundance features only. Observed richness was defined as the number of detected bacterial species per sample; Shannon diversity and Pielou evenness were calculated from the same species-level matrix.Samples with zero total microbial abundance were excluded before diversity analysis. Because alpha-diversity and pathway-abundance measures were not assumed to follow a normal distribution, non-parametric tests were used for group comparisons. Differences across more than two groups were assessed using the Kruskal-Wallis test, whereas two-group and stratified HPV-positive versus HPV-negative comparisons were assessed using the Mann-Whitney U test.Beta diversity was calculated using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and visualized by principal coordinates analysis. Differences in overall community composition were tested using PERMANOVA with 999 permutations. Pseudo-F statistics, permutation p-values, and pseudo-R2 values were reported, with R2 interpreted as the proportion of total variation in the distance matrix attributable to the grouping variable. PERMDISP with 999 permutations was performed to assess homogeneity of within-group multivariate dispersion and to determine whether PERMANOVA findings could be influenced by differences in dispersion rather than group-centroid separation.Because observed richness is sensitive to sequencing depth, we performed a depth-corrected sensitivity analysis using exact rarefaction of terminal species-level bacterial counts. Species counts summed exactly to total classified bacterial counts for each sample. All 311 samples were rarefied without replacement to 357,456 bacterial reads per sample, corresponding to the minimum classified bacterial depth. Rarefaction was repeated independently 100 times to assess sensitivity to stochastic subsampling. We additionally evaluated the association of observed richness with HPV status using linear regression adjusted for log10-transformed classified bacterial depth.Species-level differential abundance was evaluated using MaAsLin2 in R. Two abundance datasets were used according to the primary predictor. CST-associated analyses were performed using a taxonomically collapsed species table to reduce artificial inflation from strain- and isolate-level labels. Assignments corresponding to Gardnerella vaginalis strains and reference isolates were aggregated into a single G. vaginalis feature, whereas the remaining unresolved Gardnerella assignments were combined as Gardnerella unspecified. Strain-like Lactobacillus assignments were aggregated to the corresponding species-level labels. HPV type group- and cytological grade-associated analyses were performed using the uncollapsed species table to retain finer species-, strain-, and isolate-level resolution. Taxon names were standardized for formatting, and only exact duplicate labels generated by formatting standardization were aggregated. No biological consolidation of Gardnerella, Lactobacillus, or other taxa was applied in the HPV type group and Grade models. Predefined implausible assignments, including Clostridium tetani, were excluded from both datasets. Taxon filtering was performed independently for the collapsed and uncollapsed datasets after matching participants with complete model covariates. Taxa were retained when detected in at least 10% of samples and when their mean relative abundance was at least 0.05%. Samples with zero total bacterial abundance or incomplete model covariates were excluded from the corresponding analysis. Because the input tables contained relative-abundance percentages, no additional normalization was applied within MaAsLin2. Relative abundances were log-transformed, and linear models were fitted without predictor standardization. Each model included HPV type group, CST group, cytological grade, age, number of deliveries, bacterial sequencing depth, and marital status as fixed effects. Age and number of deliveries were entered as mean-centered continuous covariates. Bacterial sequencing depth was calculated from the unnormalized Kraken2/Bracken bacterial count table, transformed as log10(depth + 1), and mean-centered. Marital status was modelled as a categorical variable comprising married, not married, and divorced/widowed categories. No HPV, CST I, NILM, and married status were used as the respective reference categories. Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied, and q-values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. MaAsLin2 coefficients represent the direction and magnitude of association with log-transformed relative abundance relative to the relevant reference category while holding the remaining model variables constant. For visualization, up to six species with the lowest adjusted q-values for each primary predictor were displayed as boxplots. The boxplots show raw relative-abundance distributions, whereas the reported coefficients and q-values were obtained from the adjusted models. Coefficient heatmaps included all significant taxa up to a maximum of 50 features. Heatmap colors represent unscaled MaAsLin2 coefficients; rows were hierarchically clustered, whereas comparison columns were retained in predefined order.To evaluate the robustness of differential-abundance results, MaAsLin2 analyses were additionally repeated after exclusion of samples below the 25th percentile of classified bacterial depth (3,108,006 reads). This retained 226 of 302 complete-case participants. The same feature matrices and model specifications as in the primary analyses were used, and taxa were not re-filtered after exclusion so that removal of low-depth samples was the only analytical change.Categorical variables were compared using Pearson’s chi-squared test when expected cell counts were adequate. Fisher’s exact test was used for sparse contingency tables. For larger-than-2 × 2 tables where exact computation was impractical, Fisher’s exact test with Monte Carlo simulation was applied.An additional exploratory HPV-positive versus HPV-negative taxonomic comparison was performed using Welch’s two-sample t-test, which does not assume equal group variances, together with Cohen’s d as a standardized effect-size measure. Before differential testing, the same predefined taxonomic exclusion filter used in the main bacterial analyses was applied to remove implausible environmental, animal-associated, and likely misclassified assignments at both genus and species levels. Taxa absent from both HPV groups were excluded. Positive Cohen’s d values indicated higher abundance in HPV-positive samples, whereas negative values indicated higher abundance in HPV-negative samples. Taxa meeting the exploratory thresholds of p < 0.05 and |Cohen’s d> 0.25 were included in the cladogram and effect-size plot. This analysis was considered exploratory, and nominal p-values were used for feature selection.All microbiome, functional, and network analyses were performed in Python v3.12 using NumPy (v2.0.1) (Harris et al., 2020), SciPy (v1.15.1) (Virtanen et al., 2020), Pandas (The pandas development team, 2026), statsmodels (v0.14.4), scikit-learn (v1.6.1), Matplotlib (v3.10.0) (Hunter, 2007), seaborn (v0.13.2) (Waskom, 2021) and in R using MaAsLin2, ggplot2, pheatmap, dplyr, tidyr, and related packages. Demographic and baseline clinical characteristics were analyzed using Stata v18 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). 2.1.Study design and populationThis cross-sectional study was conducted at the National Research Center for Mother and Child Health, a tertiary academic medical center in Astana, Kazakhstan. The present study extends those baseline findings by incorporating HPV-positive comparator groups (HPV16, HPV18, HPV Other, HPV High Risk), cervical cytological grade stratification, and CST-based differential abundance and functional pathway analyses not covered in the earlier report. The assay detects the following high-risk HPV genotypes: 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, and 59. A sample was considered positive when at least one HPV genotype produced a cycle-threshold value of Ct ≤35. Samples without detection of any target genotype were classified as negative for the high-risk HPV types included in the assay. Whole-genome shotgun sequencing data were also screened for HPV sequences to identify genotypes not included in the PCR panel. The standard Reference sequence databases were used. Samples positive by either PCR or WGS were classified as HPV-positive. For descriptive analyses, HPV16 and HPV18 were retained as separate categories, other oncogenic genotypes were classified as HPV High Risk, and detected genotypes outside the predefined high-risk list were classified as HPV Other. Cytology/histology grade was categorized as NILM, ASC-US, LSIL, and ASC-H. CSTs were assigned manually from species-level relative abundance profiles following the five-community framework of Ravel et al. (2011). The dominant taxon was defined as the CST-associated bacterial species with the highest relative abundance within each sample. Samples were classified as CST I, CST II, CST III, or CST V when Lactobacillus crispatus, L. gasseri, L. iners, or L. jensenii, respectively, showed the highest relative abundance. full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.Clinical and demographic characteristics of the study populationA total of 311 non-pregnant women were included in the study. Of these, 148 (47.6%) were HPV-positive and 163 (52.4%) were HPV-negative. By HPV type group, 163 participants (52.4%) had no HPV infection, 64 (20.6%) were classified as HPV High Risk, 43 (13.8%) as HPV16, 34 (10.9%) as HPV Other (low-risk types), and 7 (2.3%) as HPV18. The mean age of participants was 34.5 ± 6.3 years and differed significantly across HPV type groups (p = 0.002), with HPV16 (31.4 ± 5.3 years) and HPV18 (30.4 ± 6.1 years) groups being younger compared to No HPV (35.3 ± 6.1 years) and HPV Other (35.3 ± 6.7 years) groups. Body mass index (mean 23.5 ± 4.3 kg/m2) and age at menarche (mean 13.4 ± 1.4 years) did not differ significantly across groups (p = 0.41 and p = 0.35, respectively). Because the HPV18 group comprised only 7 participants (2.3% of the cohort), demographic and clinical contrasts involving this group, including the younger age and lower parity noted above, are based on a small subgroup and should be regarded as descriptive and exploratory rather than definitive. Cytological grade distribution differed significantly across HPV type groups (p < 0.001). Overall, NILM was the most prevalent grade (142 women, 45.7%), followed by LSIL (79, 25.4%), ASC-US (73, 23.5%), and ASC-H (10, 3.2%). Among No HPV participants, NILM predominated (61.3%), whereas LSIL was the most common grade in HPV High Risk (43.8%) and HPV16 (55.8%) groups. The HPV Other group showed the highest proportion of NILM (67.6%). ASC-H was most prevalent in the HPV16 group (11.6%) and was rare in No HPV (0.6%). Community state type (CST) distribution did not differ significantly across HPV type groups (p = 0.074). CST IV was the most common overall (140 participants, 45.0%), followed by CST III (70, 22.5%), CST I (67, 21.5%), CST II (25, 8.0%), and CST V (9, 2.9%). The HPV Other and HPV16 groups had the highest proportions of CST IV (61.8% and 62.8%, respectively), while CST I was most prevalent in HPV High Risk (26.6%).Regarding demographic and reproductive characteristics, the majority of participants identified as Kazakh (91.3%), with no significant difference in ethnicity across groups (p = 0.93). Most participants held a bachelor’s degree (69.8%), and educational level did not differ across HPV groups (p = 0.52). Marital status differed significantly (p = 0.008): married women comprised 65.6% of the total cohort and were most prevalent in the No HPV group (74.8%), while the proportions of unmarried and divorced/widowed women were higher among HPV-positive groups, particularly HPV18 (57.1% unmarried) and HPV Other (26.5% unmarried). The mean number of deliveries differed significantly across groups (p = 0.005), being lowest in the HPV18 group (0.5 ± 0.8) and highest in the No HPV group (1.9 ± 1.4). Mean cycle length also differed modestly across groups (p = 0.025), with HPV Other showing the longest mean cycle (34.3 ± 18.8 days) compared with HPV High Risk (28.8 ± 2.1 days). Menstrual cycle regularity (92.6% regular overall), menstrual phase at sampling, and days since last menstrual period did not differ significantly across groups (p = 0.69, p = 0.89, and p = 0.98, respectively). full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionIn this study, we characterized cervicovaginal microbiome composition and predicted functional potential in relation to HPV status, HPV type group, cytological grade, and community state type. The HPV-negative NILM subset of the present cohort overlaps with the multi-kingdom baseline cohort described in Rakhmankulova et al. (2026); the CST distribution and Lactobacillus-dominance patterns observed here for HPV-negative women are consistent with that earlier report, supporting the internal consistency of CST assignment across the two analyses and reinforcing the present study’s characterization of HPV-positive comparator groups against this baseline. HPV-positive samples showed increased bacterial species richness, whereas Shannon diversity and Pielou evenness were not significantly different between HPV-positive and HPV-negative groups. HPV-positive samples were also enriched in phylogenetically diverse anaerobic taxa and depleted in several health-associated bacterial lineages. These findings are consistent with previous studies reporting Lactobacillus depletion and enrichment of anaerobic bacteria in HPV-positive women (Lee et al., 2013; Brotman et al., 2014; Audirac-Chalifour et al., 2016; Łaniewski et al., 2018). At the genus level, the lower relative abundance of Lactobacillus and higher abundance of Gardnerella were consistent with a shift toward a dysbiosis-associated community profile. This pattern is also consistent with meta-analyses linking bacterial vaginosis and Lactobacillus-depleted communities with HPV infection (Gillet et al., 2011; Brusselaers et al., 2019). However, the direction and mechanistic basis of this association remains debated. Dysbiosis may facilitate HPV persistence through altered mucosal immunity and reduced colonization resistance, whereas HPV-associated epithelial or inflammatory changes may themselves disrupt microbiome homeostasis (Aldunate et al., 2015; Mitra et al., 2015; Hearps et al., 2017; Shannon et al., 2017). Species-level Bray-Curtis community composition did not differ significantly by HPV status, suggesting that the principal HPV-associated diversity signal was an increase in the number of detected species rather than broad restructuring of overall community composition.HPV Other showed the highest observed species richness, but species-level Bray-Curtis differences across HPV type groups did not reach statistical significance. This pattern differed from the expectation that greater oncogenic risk would necessarily correspond to greater microbiome alteration. However, HPV Other comprised a heterogeneous collection of genotypes, and the observed differences may reflect genotype composition, infection duration, age, reproductive characteristics, behavioral factors, or baseline microbial ecology. In the final covariate-adjusted model, HPV type group was associated with only four species. Suicoccus acidiformans and Globicatella sp. PHS GS PNBC 21–1553 were associated with HPV Other, whereas Enterococcus faecalis and Alloscardovia omnicolens were associated with HPV High Risk. The narrower set of significant taxa after adjustment suggests that some variation observed in preliminary analyses was explained by CST, grade, age, number of deliveries, sequencing depth, or marital status. Because several of these species were abundant only in subsets of participants, they should not be interpreted as stable HPV-specific biomarkers without external validation. The cross-sectional design cannot determine whether bacterial differences preceded HPV acquisition, followed infection, or reflected common underlying determinants.Shotgun metagenomic functional profiling further suggested that HPV type-specific microbiome differences extended beyond taxonomic composition to differences in predicted microbial functional capacity. The HPV Other group showed higher inferred abundance of pathways annotated to siderophore-group nonribosomal peptide biosynthesis, drug metabolism involving other enzymes, lipoic acid metabolism, lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, porphyrin metabolism, glycan degradation, streptomycin biosynthesis, flavonoid biosynthesis, and stilbenoid-related pathways. These findings indicate differences in the genetic potential for secondary-metabolite biosynthesis, lipid-associated processes, and complex carbohydrate degradation; however, they do not demonstrate that these pathways were transcriptionally active or that the corresponding metabolites were produced in vivo. Some pathways were relatively higher in HPV-negative samples, although their biological interpretation in the cervicovaginal microbiome remains uncertain. The pathway patterns were broadly consistent with the higher species richness and the taxonomic patterns observed in the HPV Other group, but they do not establish that these communities were metabolically more active or that the predicted products influenced HPV persistence or epithelial function. Metatranscriptomic and metabolomic validation will be required to determine whether these predicted pathways are expressed and whether their products are biologically relevant in vivo.High-risk HPV-mediated carcinogenesis is primarily driven by viral oncogene activity, which may help explain why oncogenic HPV types were not necessarily associated with the most pronounced microbiome disruption (Zur Hausen, 2002; Doorbar et al., 2012). Conversely, the association of HPV Other with higher species richness and selected taxonomic/functional patterns may reflect differences in viral persistence, host susceptibility, or local ecological conditions rather than greater transforming potential. This pattern may reflect distinct ecological strategies: high-risk HPV types may be adapted to establish persistent infection in health-associated microbiomes where intact colonization resistance would otherwise facilitate viral clearance (Hearps et al., 2017), whereas one possibility is that different HPV categories may be associated with distinct local ecological contexts with compromised colonization resistance and altered local immunity (Molijn et al., 2005; Godoy-Vitorino et al., 2018). Alternatively, dysbiosis may impair immune-mediated clearance of low-risk types that would otherwise be rapidly eliminated, allowing their persistence without malignant transformation. This interpretation is biologically plausible because anaerobe-rich cervicovaginal communities have been associated with altered cytokine and interferon responses that may influence viral persistence across HPV types (Torcia, 2019; Mitra et al., 2020), which could theoretically facilitate viral persistence across HPV types regardless of oncogenic potential. The differing patterns observed for HPV16 and HPV18 further suggest that microbiome associations may vary among individual oncogenic genotypes (Anahtar et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2015). However, the HPV18 group included only seven participants, and its apparent microbiome pattern may therefore be strongly influenced by individual observations and should be interpreted as exploratory. Few studies have directly compared taxonomic and predicted functional profiles across HPV risk categories, because most previous investigations have focused on HPV-positive versus HPV-negative comparisons. Such binary comparisons may obscure heterogeneity among HPV genotypes and risk groups (Piyathilake et al., 2016; Mitra et al., 2017; Usyk et al., 2020), potentially obscuring important heterogeneity in HPV-microbiome associations. Rather than dysbiosis uniformly driving progression, our data suggest that HPV types differ in their associated microbiome states and metabolic activities.CST-stratified analysis indicated that HPV-associated microbiome differences depended on the baseline community state. CST I and CST II remained predominantly Lactobacillus-dominated regardless of HPV status, suggesting greater ecological stability of these community configurations (Boris and Barbés, 2000; Tachedjian et al., 2017…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionsThis study demonstrates that HPV infection, HPV type group, cytological grade, and community state type are associated with distinct cervicovaginal microbiome patterns. HPV-positive women showed greater bacterial species richness and shifts in dominant bacterial taxa, whereas Shannon diversity, Pielou evenness, and overall species-level Bray–Curtis composition did not differ significantly by HPV status. CST analyses confirmed the expected separation between Lactobacillus-dominant and anaerobe-rich communities. Predicted functional differences were also observed across HPV groups, but these findings represent microbial potential rather than measured activity. Overall, the results support a complex relationship between HPV and the cervicovaginal microbiome, while the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality or disease progression.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionHuman papillomavirus (HPV) infection remains the primary etiological factor in cervical carcinogenesis, with high-risk HPV types responsible for virtually all cervical cancer cases worldwide (Walboomers et al., 1999; Okunade, 2020). However, the transition from transient HPV infection to persistent infection and subsequent progression to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and invasive carcinoma occurs in only a fraction of infected individuals, suggesting that host factors beyond viral oncogenicity play critical roles in disease pathogenesis (Schiffman and Wentzensen, 2013). The cervicovaginal microbiome has emerged as a potential modifier of HPV-associated disease risk, with accumulating evidence indicating that bacterial community composition influences viral persistence, immune responses, and epithelial transformation (Mitra et al., 2016; Kyrgiou et al., 2017; Łaniewski et al., 2020).The cervicovaginal microbiome exhibits distinct community state types (CSTs), primarily classified by dominant Lactobacillus species or absence thereof (Ravel et al., 2011). Lactobacillus-dominant communities, particularly those dominated by L. crispatus (CST I), are associated with vaginal health through production of lactic acid, hydrogen peroxide, and bacteriocins that maintain acidic pH and inhibit pathogen colonization (O’Hanlon et al., 2013; Petrova et al., 2015; Amabebe and Anumba, 2018). Conversely, polymicrobial communities depleted of Lactobacillus and enriched in anaerobic bacteria (CST IV), characteristic of bacterial vaginosis, associate with increased susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections, including HPV, and adverse reproductive outcomes (Ma et al., 2012; Borgdorff et al., 2014). However, the specific interactions between HPV infection, viral type heterogeneity, cervical cytological changes, and microbiome composition remain incompletely characterized.Important knowledge gaps remain regarding whether HPV–microbiome associations differ by viral type group, whether different HPV categories are associated with distinct bacterial profiles, and how cervicovaginal microbiome composition differs across cytological grades. Furthermore, the context-dependency of HPV-microbiome interactions across different baseline CST configurations requires systematic investigation. elements_zh.main_results: 与 HPV 阴性样本相比,HPV 阳性样本显示细菌种类丰富度增加,并且乳杆菌向加德纳菌的优势相互转变。HPV 其他样本具有最高的细菌物种丰富度和独特的分类学和功能关联,包括推断的铁载体和脂多糖生物合成途径丰度更高。CST IV 在 HPV 阳性女性中表现出明显的乳酸菌消耗。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,致癌潜力和生态失调的严重程度并不一致,并且 CST 类型改变了 HPV 与微生物组的相互作用,凸显了微生物组组成和 HPV 感染结果之间的复杂关系。

papers.title: Host chromatin architecture in HPV-driven cervical cancer: molecular mechanisms and therapeutic resistance
papers.abstract: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) is the principal etiologic driver of cervical cancer. However, HPV status and E6/E7-mediated disruption of the p53/RB axis do not fully explain why HPV-associated lesions differ in persistence, malignant progression, therapeutic response, and relapse. This review examines how host chromatin architecture and related transcriptional programs may contribute to the stabilization of malignant cell states following HPV-mediated checkpoint disruption. We discuss evidence linking HPV persistence and integration to epigenetic permissiveness, three-dimensional genome organization, enhancer-promoter rewiring, cohesin dynamics, and WAPL-associated chromatin regulation. Particular attention is given to how these mechanisms may influence MYC/E2F-centered proliferative output and cooperate with context-dependent signaling and tumor microenvironmental adaptation to contribute to treatment tolerance and resistant malignant states. We also consider how chromatin-informed biomarkers, public datasets, perturbation-guided prioritization, authenticated cervical cancer cell lines, organoids, and patient-derived models can be used to evaluate therapeutically relevant vulnerabilities. By integrating viral oncogenesis with host genome regulation and adaptive resistance, this review proposes a conceptual and experimentally testable framework for stratifying HPV-driven cervical cancer and prioritizing candidate intervention nodes.

papers.title: HPV vaccine coverage among adults aged 27–45: Implications for oropharyngeal cancer prevention
papers.abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection contributes to rising incidence of HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer (OPC). expanded HPV vaccination to adults aged 27-45 y in 2018, COVID-19 caused preventive visits and routine immunizations to plunge. We analyzed 2019 and 2022 NHIS data among adults aged 27-45 (2019 n = 8,745; 2022 n = 7,303). The primary outcome was ever HPV vaccination (≥1 dose), regardless of age at first vaccination. We estimated age-adjusted, survey-weighted coverage and used multivariable logistic regression to estimate adjusted odds of vaccination by sociodemographic characteristics; secondary 2022 analyses assessed initiation between ages 27 and 45. Ever HPV vaccine uptake increased from 15.1% in 2019 to 20.7% in 2022 (difference 5.6 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.03-7.07). In both years, lower odds were observed with increasing age, men, non-Hispanic Asian adults, individuals with lower educational attainment, and those without a usual place for care. By 2022, lower income-to-poverty ratios and lack of insurance were associated with reduced odds, whereas LGB+ and unmarried adults had higher odds, and adults in the Northeast had higher odds than those in the South. Only 1.43% (95% CI, 1.07-1.80) initiated vaccination between ages 27 and 45 in 2022. Initiation was more common among females, LGB+ and non-Hispanic Asian adults, and unmarried adults, and less common among those with lower education and no usual place for care. The increase in lifetime HPV vaccine coverage likely reflects childhood and adolescent vaccination rather than initiation at ages 27-45, which remained uncommon, and persistent inequities highlight missed opportunities for equitable OPC prevention.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines HPV vaccine coverage among adults aged 27–45 and its implications for oropharyngeal cancer prevention. The study analyzed NHIS data from 2019 and 2022, finding that ever HPV vaccine uptake increased from 15.1% to 20.7% during this period. However, initiation of vaccination between ages 27 and 45 remained uncommon, with only 1.43% of adults in 2022 receiving their first dose in this age range. The findings highlight persistent inequities in vaccination rates, with lower odds observed among older adults, men, non-Hispanic Asian adults, individuals with lower educational attainment, and those without a usual place for care. The increase in coverage is likely due to childhood and adolescent vaccinations rather than adult initiation, underscoring missed opportunities for equitable prevention of HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer.

papers.title: Oncobiome relation with HPV and Gynecological cancer
papers.abstract: By now, it is well understood that the human body is inhabited by millions of tiny organisms that are alive and found in different parts of our body that called microbiota. Over the past decades, these tiny microorganisms have worked together like a smart network that links to human health, and any alterations or dysbiosis in this network lead to different disorders as well as cancer development. Hence, many preclinical and clinical studies have focused on clarifying the exact role of microflora in cancer development. One of these cancers is gynecological cancer, which is considered a major threat to health in the female population. In the case of gynecological malignancy, the presence and persistent infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) is also important. Persistent infection with HPV leads to alterations in the commensal population of microbiota in the vagina and even the gut, resulting in cancer progression. Therefore, we aimed to comprehensively review the current knowledge on the interaction between gut microbiota and vaginal microbiota in HPV acquisition, favoring gynecological cancer development.

papers.title: Neurological Complications of Oncogenic Viruses: Mechanisms, Clinical Manifestations, and Emerging Insights.
papers.abstract: Oncogenic viruses are widely recognized for their pivotal role in malignant transformation; however, their capacity to induce neurological disorders has received comparatively less attention. Increasing evidence indicates that several oncogenic viruses, including human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1), human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological complications involving both the central and peripheral nervous systems. These manifestations arise through diverse mechanisms, including direct viral neuroinvasion, persistent infection, immune-mediated tissue injury, chronic neuroinflammation, and disruption of neurovascular integrity. Moreover, virus-induced molecular alterations, such as oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, epigenetic remodelling, and aberrant cytokine signalling, contribute t neuronal dysfunction and disease progression. In this review, we critically examine the current understanding of the neurological complications associated with major oncogenic viruses by integrating evidence from molecular, experimental, and clinical studies. We first discuss the general mechanisms by which viral infections induce neurological injury, highlighting pathways shared among neurotropic and non-neurotropic viruses. We then summarise the neurological manifestations and virus-specific pathogenic mechanisms associated with each oncogenic virus, emphasising both common and distinct molecular pathways underlying neuropathogenesis. Finally, we address current diagnostic challenges, emerging biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies while identifying critical knowledge gaps that limit causal interpretation and clinical translation. A comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between oncogenic viruses, the immune system, and the nervous system will facilitate earlier diagnosis, improve patient management, and support the development of targeted therapeutic approaches for virus-associated neurological disorders.

papers.title_zh: 致癌病毒的神经并发症:机制、临床表现和新见解。
papers.source_body_en: Oncogenic viruses are widely recognized for their pivotal role in malignant transformation; however, their capacity to induce neurological disorders has received comparatively less attention. Increasing evidence indicates that several oncogenic viruses, including human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1), human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological complications involving both the central and peripheral nervous systems. These manifestations arise through diverse mechanisms, including direct viral neuroinvasion, persistent infection, immune-mediated tissue injury, chronic neuroinflammation, and disruption of neurovascular integrity. Moreover, virus-induced molecular alterations, such as oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, epigenetic remodelling, and aberrant cytokine signalling, contribute t neuronal dysfunction and disease progression. In this review, we critically examine the current understanding of the neurological complications associated with major oncogenic viruses by integrating evidence from molecular, experimental, and clinical studies. We first discuss the general mechanisms by which viral infections induce neurological injury, highlighting pathways shared among neurotropic and non-neurotropic viruses. We then summarise the neurological manifestations and virus-specific pathogenic mechanisms associated with each oncogenic virus, emphasising both common and distinct molecular pathways underlying neuropathogenesis. Finally, we address current diagnostic challenges, emerging biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies while identifying critical knowledge gaps that limit causal interpretation and clinical translation. A comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between oncogenic viruses, the immune system, and the nervous system will facilitate earlier diagnosis, improve patient management, and support the development of targeted therapeutic approaches for virus-associated neurological disorders.
papers.abstract_zh: 致癌病毒因其在恶性转化中的关键作用而被广泛认可。然而,它们引起神经系统疾病的能力相对较少受到关注。越来越多的证据表明,多种致癌病毒,包括人类 T 细胞白血病病毒 1 型 (HTLV-1)、人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV)、乙型肝炎病毒 (HBV)、丙型肝炎病毒 (HCV) 和卡波西肉瘤相关疱疹病毒 (KSHV),与涉及中枢和周围神经系统的广泛神经系统并发症有关。这些表现是通过多种机制产生的,包括直接病毒神经侵袭、持续感染、免疫介导的组织损伤、慢性神经炎症和神经血管完整性破坏。此外,病毒诱导的分子改变,如氧化应激、线粒体功能障碍、表观遗传重塑和异常的细胞因子信号传导,会导致神经元功能障碍和疾病进展。在这篇综述中,我们通过整合分子、实验和临床研究的证据,批判性地研究了目前对与主要致癌病毒相关的神经并发症的理解。我们首先讨论病毒感染引起神经损伤的一般机制,强调嗜神经病毒和非嗜神经病毒之间共享的途径。然后,我们总结了与每种致癌病毒相关的神经学表现和病毒特异性致病机制,强调神经发病机制中常见和独特的分子途径。最后,我们解决当前的诊断挑战、新兴生物标志物和治疗策略,同时确定限制因果解释和临床转化的关键知识差距。全面了解致癌病毒、免疫系统和神经系统之间复杂的相互作用将有助于早期 诊断,改善患者管理,并支持开发针对病毒相关神经系统疾病的靶向治疗方法。

papers.title: Optimising HPV Vaccination for Cervical Cancer Prevention in Women Living with HIV: A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis Across 13 African Countries
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Women living with HIV (WLHIV) have an increased risk of persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and cervical cancer. We evaluated the lifetime health impact and cost-effectiveness of HPV vaccination strategies targeting WLHIV across 13 African countries. Methods We developed an age-structured Markov model of HPV infection and cervical cancer in a closed cohort of 100,000 females, stratified by HIV status, and calibrated it separately for each country to age-specific cervical cancer incidence, cervical cancer mortality, and female HIV prevalence. Six HIV-targeted strategies were compared with routine two-dose vaccination at age 14 years. The strategies either provided a booster dose to previously vaccinated WLHIV or combined a booster for previously vaccinated WLHIV with a three-dose primary catch-up course for previously unvaccinated WLHIV. Interventions were delivered at ages 18 or 24 years under standard- and high-coverage assumptions. Outcomes included cervical cancer cases averted, cervical cancer deaths averted among WLHIV, discounted disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) averted, additional physical vaccine doses, and incremental costs from the health-system and vaccination-programme perspectives. Results All six strategies generated additional health gains relative to routine vaccination alone. Mean DALYs averted across countries ranged from 8.21 for booster vaccination at age 24 years to 81.36 for high-coverage combined booster and catch-up vaccination at age 24 years. Booster-only strategies produced the greatest health gains per additional physical vaccine dose, whereas the high-coverage combined strategy at age 24 years produced the largest average absolute health gain. However, the relative performance of vaccination at ages 18 and 24 years varied by strategy and country. From the health-system perspective, 68 of 78 country–strategy comparisons were more effective and less costly than routine vaccination after accounting for avoided cervical cancer treatment costs. From the vaccination-programme perspective, all strategies required additional expenditure. Conclusions HPV vaccination strategies targeting WLHIV generated additional health benefits beyond routine adolescent vaccination and were cost-saving in many country–strategy comparisons when avoided cervical cancer treatment costs were included. Booster-only strategies were the most dose-efficient, whereas combined booster and primary catch-up strategies produced larger absolute health gains. The relative performance of strategies delivered at ages 18 and 24 years was context dependent and should not be interpreted as evidence of a universal advantage of later vaccination. Given the limited direct evidence on the clinical effectiveness and duration of protection following HPV booster vaccination among WLHIV, the booster scenarios should be interpreted as exploratory.
