Methods We developed an age-structured Markov model of HPV infection and cervical cancer in a closed cohort of 100,000 females, stratified by HIV status, and calibrated it separately for each country to age-specific cervical cancer incidence, cervical cancer mortality, and female HIV prevalence. Six HIV-targeted strategies were compared with routine two-dose vaccination at age 14 years. The strategies either provided a booster dose to previously vaccinated WLHIV or combined a booster for previously vaccinated WLHIV with a three-dose primary catch-up course for previously unvaccinated WLHIV. Interventions were delivered at ages 18 or 24 years under standard- and high-coverage assumptions. Outcomes included cervical cancer cases averted, cervical cancer deaths averted among WLHIV, discounted disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) averted, additional physical vaccine doses, and incremental costs from the health-system and vaccination-programme perspectives. Mean DALYs averted across countries ranged from 8.21 for booster vaccination at age 24 years to 81.36 for high-coverage combined booster and catch-up vaccination at age 24 years. Booster-only strategies produced the greatest health gains per additional physical vaccine dose, whereas the high-coverage combined strategy at age 24 years produced the largest average absolute health gain. However, the relative performance of vaccination at ages 18 and 24 years varied by strategy and country. From the health-system perspective, 68 of 78 country-strategy comparisons were more effective and less costly than routine vaccination after accounting for avoided cervical cancer treatment costs. From the vaccination-programme perspective, all strategies required additional expenditure. Conclusions HPV vaccination strategies targeting WLHIV generated additional health benefits beyond routine adolescent vaccination and were cost-saving in many country-strategy comparisons when avoided cervical cancer treatment costs were included. Booster-only strategies were the most dose-efficient, whereas combined booster and primary catch-up strategies produced larger absolute health gains. The relative performance of strategies delivered at ages 18 and 24 years was context dependent and should not be interpreted as evidence of a universal advantage of later vaccination. Given the limited direct evidence on the clinical effectiveness and duration of protection following HPV booster vaccination among WLHIV, the booster scenarios should be interpreted as exploratory.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 感染艾滋病毒 (WLHIV) 的女性持续感染 人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 和 宫颈癌 的风险增加。本研究旨在评估 13 个非洲国家针对 WLHIV 的 HPV 疫苗接种 策略对终生健康的影响和成本效益。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究在 100,000 名女性的封闭 队列研究 中使用了 HPV 感染的年龄结构马尔可夫模型和 宫颈癌,按 HIV 状况进行分层,并针对每个国家将其分别校准为特定年龄的 宫颈癌 发病率、宫颈癌 死亡率 和女性 HIV 患病率。
elements_zh.methods: 使用特定年龄的 宫颈癌 发病率、宫颈癌 死亡率 和女性 HIV 患病率 数据对每个国家的模型进行校准。在标准覆盖率和高覆盖率假设下,干预措施是在 18 岁或 24 岁时实施的。
elements_zh.main_results: 在 14 岁时,将六种针对 HIV 的策略与常规两剂 疫苗接种 进行了比较。与单独的常规 疫苗接种 相比,所有六种策略都产生了额外的健康收益。各国避免的平均 DALY 范围从 24 岁时加强剂 疫苗接种 的 8.21 到 24 岁时高覆盖率联合加强剂和追赶 疫苗接种 的 81.36。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些策略要么为先前接种过的 WLHIV 提供加强剂量,要么为先前接种过的 WLHIV 提供加强剂量,并为先前未接种过疫苗的 WLHIV 提供三剂初级补补课程。单纯加强策略每增加 疫苗 物理剂量就能产生最大的健康收益,而高覆盖率联合策略在 24 岁时产生最大的平均绝对健康收益。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 针对 WLHIV 的 HPV 疫苗接种 策略产生了超出常规青少年 疫苗接种 的额外健康益处,并且在许多国家(当包括避免的 宫颈癌 治疗 成本时)可以节省成本。仅加强剂策略的剂量效率最高,而加强剂和初级追赶策略相结合可产生更大的绝对健康收益。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 鉴于关于 WLHIV 中 HPV 加强疫苗 疫苗接种 的临床有效性和保护持续时间的直接证据有限,加强疫苗方案应被解释为探索性的。18 岁和 24 岁时实施的策略的相对表现取决于具体情况,不应被解释为后来 疫苗接种 的普遍优势的证据。

papers.title_zh: 优化 HPV 疫苗接种 以预防感染艾滋病毒的女性:针对 13 个非洲国家的成本效益分析
papers.source_body_en: Abstract Background Women living with HIV (WLHIV) have an increased risk of persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and cervical cancer. We evaluated the lifetime health impact and cost-effectiveness of HPV vaccination strategies targeting WLHIV across 13 African countries. Methods We developed an age-structured Markov model of HPV infection and cervical cancer in a closed cohort of 100,000 females, stratified by HIV status, and calibrated it separately for each country to age-specific cervical cancer incidence, cervical cancer mortality, and female HIV prevalence. Six HIV-targeted strategies were compared with routine two-dose vaccination at age 14 years. The strategies either provided a booster dose to previously vaccinated WLHIV or combined a booster for previously vaccinated WLHIV with a three-dose primary catch-up course for previously unvaccinated WLHIV. Interventions were delivered at ages 18 or 24 years under standard- and high-coverage assumptions. Outcomes included cervical cancer cases averted, cervical cancer deaths averted among WLHIV, discounted disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) averted, additional physical vaccine doses, and incremental costs from the health-system and vaccination-programme perspectives. Results All six strategies generated additional health gains relative to routine vaccination alone. Mean DALYs averted across countries ranged from 8.21 for booster vaccination at age 24 years to 81.36 for high-coverage combined booster and catch-up vaccination at age 24 years. Booster-only strategies produced the greatest health gains per additional physical vaccine dose, whereas the high-coverage combined strategy at age 24 years produced the largest average absolute health gain. However, the relative performance of vaccination at ages 18 and 24 years varied by strategy and country. From the health-system perspective, 68 of 78 country–strategy comparisons were more effective and less costly than routine vaccination after accounting for avoided cervical cancer treatment costs. From the vaccination-programme perspective, all strategies required additional expenditure. Conclusions HPV vaccination strategies targeting WLHIV generated additional health benefits beyond routine adolescent vaccination and were cost-saving in many country–strategy comparisons when avoided cervical cancer treatment costs were included. Booster-only strategies were the most dose-efficient, whereas combined booster and primary catch-up strategies produced larger absolute health gains. The relative performance of strategies delivered at ages 18 and 24 years was context dependent and should not be interpreted as evidence of a universal advantage of later vaccination. Given the limited direct evidence on the clinical effectiveness and duration of protection following HPV booster vaccination among WLHIV, the booster scenarios should be interpreted as exploratory.

papers.title: Spatial organization of HPV-associated immune programs across tissue compartments in oropharyngeal cancer
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) is characterized by a distinct immune microenvironment; however, the biological significance of immune-related transcriptional programs may vary according to their spatial localization. We investigated the spatial organization of HPV-associated transcriptional programs across anatomically distinct tissue compartments in OPC. METHODS: An oropharynx-restricted The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) cohort comprising 77 tumors (51 HPV-positive and 26 HPV-negative) was analyzed using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA). Spatial transcriptomic profiling using GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiling was evaluated in lymphoid follicular regions (LFRs) and tumor tissue regions (TTRs) from six OPC patients (four HPV-positive and two HPV-negative), with the patient treated as the primary experimental unit. Tumor-free surrounding palatine tonsillar tissue (PTT) was analyzed in an independent microarray cohort comprising 23 HPV-positive and four HPV-negative cases. Eight prespecified immune- and metabolism-related transcriptional programs were evaluated, with additional exploratory cell-type deconvolution and overall survival analyses. RESULTS: In TCGA-OPSCC, all five immune-related programs were higher in HPV-positive tumors, and Stem-like, Tpex, B-cell activity, and T-cell activity remained significantly associated with HPV-positive status after adjustment for clinicopathological covariates and FDR correction. In paired GeoMx analyses, all five immune-related programs were higher in LFRs than in TTRs in all six patients, whereas Estrogen Response Early and Estrogen Response Late were higher in TTRs in all six patients (BH-FDR = 0.0357 for each program). Bile Acid Metabolism showed no consistent compartment-specific difference. HPV-associated differences within individual GeoMx compartments and HPV-by-compartment interactions were not statistically significant after FDR correction. In PTT, immune-related and metabolic programs showed directional HPV-associated differences, but none remained significant after FDR correction. Higher scores for several immune-related programs were associated with improved overall survival in univariable TCGA-OPSCC analyses, but these associations were attenuated after accounting for HPV status. CONCLUSIONS: HPV-associated immune transcriptional programs identified in bulk OPC show consistent spatial organization across lymphoid follicular and tumor tissue compartments. The most robust spatial feature was within-patient compartmentalization between LFRs and TTRs, whereas evidence for HPV-associated differences within individual spatial compartments was limited. These findings emphasize the importance of anatomical context when interpreting transcriptional programs in OPC.

analysis.methods: Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) was used to evaluate immune-related transcriptional programs in the TCGA-OPSCC cohort. analysis.main_results: In TCGA-OPSCC, all five immune-related programs were higher in HPV-positive tumors, and four remained significantly associated with HPV-positive status after adjustment for clinicopathological covariates and FDR correction. analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the spatial organization of HPV-associated immune transcriptional programs in oropharyngeal cancer (OPC). It finds that immune-related programs are consistently higher in HPV-positive tumors compared to HPV-negative ones, with significant associations remaining after statistical adjustments. Spatial transcriptomic profiling reveals that immune programs are more active in lymphoid follicular regions (LFRs) than in tumor tissue regions (TTRs) across all six patients, while estrogen response programs are more prevalent in TTRs. However, HPV-associated differences within individual compartments and interactions between HPV and compartments are not statistically significant after FDR correction. The study highlights the importance of anatomical context in interpreting transcriptional programs in OPC, which may have implications for targeted surveillance and treatment strategies. The findings are based on a TCGA-OPSCC cohort and independent microarray analyses, but the evidence for compartment-specific HPV differences is limited, suggesting the need for further research.

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) is characterized by a distinct immune microenvironment, but the biological significance of immune-related transcriptional programs may vary based on their spatial localization.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: A TCGA-OPSCC cohort comprising 77 tumors (51 HPV-positive and 26 HPV-negative) was analyzed, alongside spatial transcriptomic profiling in six OPC patients (four HPV-positive and two HPV-negative) and an independent microarray cohort of 23 HPV-positive and four HPV-negative cases of tumor-free palatine tonsillar tissue.
analysis_en.methods: Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) was used to evaluate immune-related transcriptional programs in the TCGA-OPSCC cohort. Spatial transcriptomic profiling using GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiling was conducted in lymphoid follicular regions (LFRs) and tumor tissue regions (TTRs) from six OPC patients, with patient as the primary experimental unit. Eight prespecified immune- and metabolism-related transcriptional programs were assessed, including cell-type deconvolution and overall survival analyses.
analysis_en.main_results: In TCGA-OPSCC, all five immune-related programs were higher in HPV-positive tumors, and four remained significantly associated with HPV-positive status after adjustment for clinicopathological covariates and FDR correction. In GeoMx analyses, all five immune-related programs were higher in LFRs than in TTRs in all six patients, whereas Estrogen Response Early and Estrogen Response Late were higher in TTRs (BH-FDR = 0.0357 for each program). Bile Acid Metabolism showed no consistent compartment-specific difference. HPV-associated differences within individual GeoMx compartments and HPV-by-compartment interactions were not statistically significant after FDR correction.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that HPV-associated immune transcriptional programs identified in bulk OPC show consistent spatial organization across lymphoid follicular and tumor tissue compartments, with the most robust spatial feature being within-patient compartmentalization between LFRs and TTRs.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings emphasize the importance of anatomical context when interpreting transcriptional programs in OPC, which may inform more precise surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for HPV-associated cancers.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence for HPV-associated differences within individual spatial compartments was limited, and HPV-associated differences within GeoMx compartments were not statistically significant after FDR correction, suggesting the need for further studies with larger sample sizes and more detailed spatial analyses.

papers.title_zh: 口咽癌组织区室中 HPV 相关免疫程序的空间组织
papers.source_body_en: BACKGROUND: Human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) is characterized by a distinct immune microenvironment; however, the biological significance of immune-related transcriptional programs may vary according to their spatial localization. We investigated the spatial organization of HPV-associated transcriptional programs across anatomically distinct tissue compartments in OPC. METHODS: An oropharynx-restricted The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) cohort comprising 77 tumors (51 HPV-positive and 26 HPV-negative) was analyzed using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA). Spatial transcriptomic profiling using GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiling was evaluated in lymphoid follicular regions (LFRs) and tumor tissue regions (TTRs) from six OPC patients (four HPV-positive and two HPV-negative), with the patient treated as the primary experimental unit. Tumor-free surrounding palatine tonsillar tissue (PTT) was analyzed in an independent microarray cohort comprising 23 HPV-positive and four HPV-negative cases. Eight prespecified immune- and metabolism-related transcriptional programs were evaluated, with additional exploratory cell-type deconvolution and overall survival analyses. RESULTS: In TCGA-OPSCC, all five immune-related programs were higher in HPV-positive tumors, and Stem-like, Tpex, B-cell activity, and T-cell activity remained significantly associated with HPV-positive status after adjustment for clinicopathological covariates and FDR correction. In paired GeoMx analyses, all five immune-related programs were higher in LFRs than in TTRs in all six patients, whereas Estrogen Response Early and Estrogen Response Late were higher in TTRs in all six patients (BH-FDR = 0.0357 for each program). Bile Acid Metabolism showed no consistent compartment-specific difference. HPV-associated differences within individual GeoMx compartments and HPV-by-compartment interactions were not statistically significant after FDR correction. In PTT, immune-related and metabolic programs showed directional HPV-associated differences, but none remained significant after FDR correction. Higher scores for several immune-related programs were associated with improved overall survival in univariable TCGA-OPSCC analyses, but these associations were attenuated after accounting for HPV status. CONCLUSIONS: HPV-associated immune transcriptional programs identified in bulk OPC show consistent spatial organization across lymphoid follicular and tumor tissue compartments. The most robust spatial feature was within-patient compartmentalization between LFRs and TTRs, whereas evidence for HPV-associated differences within individual spatial compartments was limited. These findings emphasize the importance of anatomical context when interpreting transcriptional programs in OPC.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景:人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 阳性口咽癌 (OPC) 的特点是独特的免疫微环境;然而,免疫相关转录程序的生物学意义可能因其空间定位而异。我们研究了 OPC 中解剖学上不同的组织区室中 HPV 相关转录程序的空间组织。方法:使用单样本基因集富集分析 (ssGSEA) 对包含 77 个肿瘤(51 个 HPV 阳性和 26 个 HPV 阴性)的口咽限制癌症 基因组 图谱 (TCGA)-口咽鳞状细胞癌 (OPSCC) 队列研究 进行分析。使用 GeoMx 数字空间分析对六名 OPC 患者(四名 HPV 阳性和两名 HPV 阴性)的淋巴滤泡区域 (LFR) 和肿瘤组织区域 (TTR) 进行空间转录组分析评估,该患者被视为主要实验单位。在独立微阵列 队列研究 中分析无肿瘤周围腭扁桃体组织 (PTT),其中包括 23 例 HPV 阳性病例和 4 例 HPV 阴性病例。评估了八个预先指定的免疫和代谢相关转录程序,并进行了额外的探索性细胞类型解卷积和总体生存分析。结果:在 TCGA-OPSCC 中,所有五个免疫相关项目在 HPV 阳性肿瘤中均较高,并且在调整临床病理协变量和 FDR 校正后,干细胞样、Tpex、B 细胞活性和 T 细胞活性仍然与 HPV 阳性状态显着相关。在配对 GeoMx 分析中,所有 6 名患者的所有 5 个免疫相关项目的 LFR 均高于 TTR,而所有 6 名患者的早期雌激素反应和晚期雌激素反应的 TTR 均较高(每个项目的 BH-FDR = 0.0357)。胆汁酸代谢没有表现出一致的隔室特异性差异。FDR 校正后,各个 GeoMx 区室中 HPV 相关的差异以及 HPV 与区室之间的相互作用没有统计学意义。在 PTT 中,免疫相关和代谢程序显示出与 HPV 相关的定向差异,但在 FDR 校正后没有任何显着差异。在单变量 TCGA-OPSCC 分析中,一些免疫相关项目的得分较高与总体生存率的提高相关,但在考虑 HPV 状态后,这些关联性减弱。结论:在大量 OPC 中鉴定出的 HPV 相关免疫转录程序在淋巴滤泡和肿瘤组织区室中显示出一致的空间组织。最稳健的空间特征是 LFR 和 TTR 之间的患者内部划分,而各个空间划分内 HPV 相关差异的证据有限。这些发现强调了解释 OPC 转录程序时解剖背景的重要性。

Researchers at the Affiliated Hospital of Putian University and the First Hospital of Putian City analyzed samples from 731 male outpatients treated between May 2023 and February 2026 and found that more than one in three was infected with at least one HPV genotype. The overall prevalence of 35.2 percent, reported in BMC Infectious Diseases, included single-genotype infections in 22.7 percent of patients and multiple-genotype infections in 12.5 percent, a pattern that underscores how frequently men harbor several viral types simultaneously. The technical approach behind these numbers is worth noting. Rather than relying on a single broad screening assay, the team used polymerase chain reaction amplification combined with flow-through hybridization, a method that allows simultaneous detection and identification of 21 distinct HPV genotypes. This matters because HPV is not one pathogen but a family of more than 200 related viruses, only some of which are classified as high-risk for cancer. Distinguishing which genotypes circulate in a given population is essential for predicting how well existing vaccines will perform and for designing regional screening programs that target the types actually present. The five most frequently detected genotypes among the men were HPV6, HPV52, HPV16, HPV51, and HPV42. This list mixes low-risk and high-risk types: HPV6 and HPV42 are classified as low-risk, typically associated with genital warts rather than malignancy, while HPV52, HPV16, and HPV51 belong to the high-risk category linked to anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers. HPV16 is the single most carcinogenic genotype worldwide and a dominant driver of HPV-positive cancers in both sexes. The fact that it ranks among the top types in these male outpatients reinforces why vaccination and, eventually, male screening remain central to cancer prevention efforts. Discover more Infections Find Vaccines vaccines vaccine Vaccine One of the study’s most striking findings is the overlap between the genotypes circulating in men and those previously reported in local women in the Putian region. The predominant types in the male cohort, including low-risk HPV6 and HPV42 and high-risk HPV52, HPV51, and HPV16, substantially mirror the genotype distribution described for females in the same area. Such concordance is consistent with sexual transmission within partner networks and suggests that vaccinating or screening only one sex leaves a persistent viral reservoir in the other. The authors argue that this overlap supports including men in HPV prevention strategies and may inform future evaluation of partner-oriented prevention approaches, in which couples are considered jointly rather than in isolation. Age emerged as a significant axis of variation. Prevalence was highest among patients older than 60 years, a pattern that contrasts with the classic bimodal age distribution often described in women, where infection peaks in young adulthood and again around midlife. In men, clearance of infection can be less efficient with age, and cumulative exposure over a lifetime may raise the probability of detectable infection in older age groups. The researchers also conducted sensitivity analyses using broader age categories, combining the 51-to-60 and over-60 groups, to confirm the robustness of the association between older age and high-risk HPV infection, indicating that the age signal was not an artifact of how the categories were drawn. Discover more Health health Support Pride Clinical diagnosis also shaped the picture. HPV prevalence varied significantly across the six diagnostic subgroups into which patients were stratified: warts, urinary tract infections, dermatitis, genital diseases, health check-ups, and others. The warts group showed the highest infection rate at 48.7 percent, dominated by HPV6 and HPV11, the two low-risk genotypes most classically responsible for condyloma acuminatum, or genital warts. That result is biologically coherent, since patients presenting with visible warts are, by definition, already expressing an HPV-driven lesion. More unexpected was the dermatitis group, which came in a close second at 46.5 percent and displayed remarkable genotype diversity, with HPV52, HPV16, HPV42, HPV51, and HPV59 all appearing among the detected types. The dermatitis finding carried enough statistical weight to survive multivariable regression analysis. After adjusting for other variables, dermatitis was identified as an independent risk factor for high-risk HPV infection, with the authors reporting an adjusted odds ratio and controlling for confounding using generalized variance inflation factors to check for collinearity among predictors. The biological interpretation is not settled from these data alone, but plausible mechanisms include disruption of the skin barrier providing an easier entry point for virions, local immune dysregulation reducing viral clearance, or inflammatory conditions serving as a marker for behaviors or exposures that also raise HPV risk. Whatever the direction of causality, the association suggests that dermatology clinics could represent an underused point of contact for HPV testing in men. Discover more Book a Checkup Check Symptoms infection Study Biology infections The vaccine analysis is where the study’s public health implications become most concrete. China’s regional vaccination programs have historically focused on girls and women, and the 9-valent HPV vaccine, which protects against genotypes 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58, is the broadest formulation in widespread use. Yet even against this nine-type panel, the researchers calculated that 33.5 percent of HPV-positive men in the cohort carried at least one genotype not covered by the vaccine, and the coverage gap was nearly identical, at 33.9 percent, among men carrying high-risk types. In other words, roughly one third of infections, including those with cancer-associated potential, would not be prevented by the current nonavalent vaccine, a gap driven by types such as HPV51 and HPV59 that fall outside the formulation. These coverage gaps do not diminish the case for vaccination, but they do complicate it. On one hand, the predominance of HPV6, HPV16, and HPV52 in the male cohort means the 9-valent vaccine would still address a majority of circulating infections, and HPV16 in particular is responsible for a disproportionate share of HPV-related cancers. On the other hand, the persistence of a substantial non-vaccine reservoir means that vaccination alone cannot eliminate transmission in this population, and the finding strengthens arguments for extending vaccination to boys and men, both to protect them directly against cancers and warts and to build herd protection that benefits unvaccinated partners. The study has limitations inherent to its design. It was retrospective and drew exclusively on male outpatients at a single hospital in Putian, a prefecture-level city in Fujian Province, so the 35.2 percent prevalence cannot be generalized to the general male population, which typically shows lower rates than clinic-based cohorts. Patients visiting dermatology or urology clinics are more likely to have conditions related to or coinciding with HPV infection than men sampled at random. The ethics committee of the First Hospital of Putian City approved the study and granted an exemption from individual informed consent, and the authors declare no competing interests. Even with those caveats, the work fills a genuine gap: no previous research on male HPV prevalence in Putian had been reported, and region-specific genotype data of this kind are scarce across much of China. The broader takeaway is that HPV epidemiology in men deserves the same granular, genotype-level attention that has long been applied to women. As vaccination programs expand and as oropharyngeal and anal cancers linked to HPV rise in many countries, understanding which types circulate in male populations, at which ages, and in association with which clinical conditions becomes essential for modeling transmission, forecasting vaccine impact, and deciding whether and when to introduce routine male screening. The Putian data, with their high prevalence, distinctive age gradient, dermatitis signal, and measurable vaccine gap, offer a template for the kind of local surveillance that global HPV control efforts will increasingly require. Researchers at the Affiliated Hospital of Putian University and the First Hospital of Putian City analyzed samples from 731 male outpatients treated between May 2023 and February 2026 and found that more than one in three was infected with at least one HPV genotype. The overall prevalence of 35.2 percent, reported in BMC Infectious Diseases, included single-genotype infections in 22.7 percent of patients and multiple-genotype infections in 12.5 percent, a pattern that underscores how frequently men harbor several viral types simultaneously. The technical approach behind these numbers is worth noting. Rather than relying on a single broad screening assay, the team used polymerase chain reaction amplification combined with flow-through hybridization, a method that allows simultaneous detection and identification of 21 distinct HPV genotypes. This matters because HPV is not one pathogen but a family of more than 200 related viruses, only some of which are classified as high-risk for cancer. Distinguishing which genotypes circulate in a given population is essential for predicting how well existing vaccines will perform and for designing regional screening programs that target the types actually present. The five most frequently detected genotypes among the men were HPV6, HPV52, HPV16, HPV51, and HPV42. This list mixes low-risk and high-risk types: HPV6 and HPV42 are classified as low-risk, typically associated with genital warts rather than malignancy, while HPV52, HPV16, and HPV51 belong to the high-risk category linked to anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers. HPV16 is the single most carcinogenic genotype worldwide and a dominant driver of HPV-positive cancers in both sexes. The fact that it ranks among the top types in these male outpatients reinforces why vaccination and, eventually, male screening remain central to cancer prevention efforts. Discover more Infections Find Vaccines vaccines vaccine Vaccine One of the study’s most striking findings is the overlap between the genotypes circulating in men and those previously reported in local women in the Putian region. The predominant types in the male cohort, including low-risk HPV6 and HPV42 and high-risk HPV52, HPV51, and HPV16, substantially mirror the genotype distribution described for females in the same area. Such concordance is consistent with sexual transmission within partner networks and suggests that vaccinating or screening only one sex leaves a persistent viral reservoir in the other. The authors argue that this overlap supports including men in HPV prevention strategies and may inform future evaluation of partner-oriented prevention approaches, in which couples are considered jointly rather than in isolation. Age emerged as a significant axis of variation. Prevalence was highest among patients older than 60 years, a pattern that contrasts with the classic bimodal age distribution often described in women, where infection peaks in young adulthood and again around midlife. In men, clearance of infection can be less efficient with age, and cumulative exposure over a lifetime may raise the probability of detectable infection in older age groups. The researchers also conducted sensitivity analyses using broader age categories, combining the 51-to-60 and over-60 groups, to confirm the robustness of the association between older age and high-risk HPV infection, indicating that the age signal was not an artifact of how the categories were drawn. Discover more Health health Support Pride Clinical diagnosis also shaped the picture. HPV prevalence varied significantly across the six diagnostic subgroups into which patients were stratified: warts, urinary tract infections, dermatitis, genital diseases, health check-ups, and others. The warts group showed the highest infection rate at 48.7 percent, dominated by HPV6 and HPV11, the two low-risk genotypes most classically responsible for condyloma acuminatum, or genital warts. That result is biologically coherent, since patients presenting with visible warts are, by definition, already expressing an HPV-driven lesion. More unexpected was the dermatitis group, which came in a close second at 46.5 percent and displayed remarkable genotype diversity, with HPV52, HPV16, HPV42, HPV51, and HPV59 all appearing among the detected types. The dermatitis finding carried enough statistical weight to survive multivariable regression analysis. After adjusting for other variables, dermatitis was identified as an independent risk factor for high-risk HPV infection, with the authors reporting an adjusted odds ratio and controlling for confounding using generalized variance inflation factors to check for collinearity among predictors. The biological interpretation is not settled from these data alone, but plausible mechanisms include disruption of the skin barrier providing an easier entry point for virions, local immune dysregulation reducing viral clearance, or inflammatory conditions serving as a marker for behaviors or exposures that also raise HPV risk. Whatever the direction of causality, the association suggests that dermatology clinics could represent an underused point of contact for HPV testing in men. Discover more Book a Checkup Check Symptoms infection Study Biology infections The vaccine analysis is where the study’s public health implications become most concrete. China’s regional vaccination programs have historically focused on girls and women, and the 9-valent HPV vaccine, which protects against genotypes 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58, is the broadest formulation in widespread use. Yet even against this nine-type panel, the researchers calculated that 33.5 percent of HPV-positive men in the cohort carried at least one genotype not covered by the vaccine, and the coverage gap was nearly identical, at 33.9 percent, among men carrying high-risk types. In other words, roughly one third of infections, including those with cancer-associated potential, would not be prevented by the current nonavalent vaccine, a gap driven by types such as HPV51 and HPV59 that fall outside the formulation. These coverage gaps do not diminish the case for vaccination, but they do complicate it. On one hand, the predominance of HPV6, HPV16, and HPV52 in the male cohort means the 9-valent vaccine would still address a majority of circulating infections, and HPV16 in particular is responsible for a disproportionate share of HPV-related cancers. On the other hand, the persistence of a substantial non-vaccine reservoir means that vaccination alone cannot eliminate transmission in this population, and the finding strengthens arguments for extending vaccination to boys and men, both to protect them directly against cancers and warts and to build herd protection that benefits unvaccinated partners. The study has limitations inherent to its design. It was retrospective and drew exclusively on male outpatients at a single hospital in Putian, a prefecture-level city in Fujian Province, so the 35.2 percent prevalence cannot be generalized to the general male population, which typically shows lower rates than clinic-based cohorts. Patients visiting dermatology or urology clinics are more likely to have conditions related to or coinciding with HPV infection than men sampled at random. The ethics committee of the First Hospital of Putian City approved the study and granted an exemption from individual informed consent, and the authors declare no competing interests. Even with those caveats, the work fills a genuine gap: no previous research on male HPV prevalence in Putian had been reported, and region-specific genotype data of this kind are scarce across much of China. The broader takeaway is that HPV epidemiology in men deserves the same granular, genotype-level attention that has long been applied to women. As vaccination programs expand and as oropharyngeal and anal cancers linked to HPV rise in many countries, understanding which types circulate in male populations, at which ages, and in association with which clinical conditions becomes essential for modeling transmission, forecasting vaccine impact, and deciding whether and when to introduce routine male screening. The Putian data, with their high prevalence, distinctive age gradient, dermatitis signal, and measurable vaccine gap, offer a template for the kind of local surveillance that global HPV control efforts will increasingly require. analysis.brief_en: A study conducted in coastal China, published on October 6, 2026, highlights the high prevalence of male HPV infections, with over one-third of 731 male outpatients infected with at least one HPV genotype. The research, reported in BMC Infectious Diseases, found that the most common genotypes among men were HPV6, HPV52, HPV16, HPV51, and HPV42, which include both low-risk and high-risk types. High-risk HPV types such as HPV16 are linked to cancers, and the study revealed that 33.5 percent of HPV-positive men carried genotypes not covered by the 9-valent vaccine, indicating a significant coverage gap. The study also noted that the prevalence of HPV infections in men was highest among those over 60 years old, suggesting that age-related factors may influence infection rates.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 9, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Silencing HPV16 Oncogenes E5 and E6 Emerges as a Promising Route Against Cervical Cancer by October 9, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Silencing HPV16 Oncogenes E5 and E6 Emerges as a Promising Route Against Cervical Cancer Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Cervical cancer remains one of the most significant global health challenges of our time, and its strongest molecular driver is well established: persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, above all genotype 16. A new narrative review published in Virology Journal by researchers at Tabriz University of Medical Sciences and collaborators takes a close look at two of the virus’s most consequential weapons, the oncoproteins E5 and E6, and surveys how modern gene-silencing technologies could be harnessed to neutralize them. The work, led by Zahra Zenderuh Ravanlo and corresponding author Hossein Bannazadeh Baghi, synthesizes the biological roles of these viral proteins in carcinogenesis and evaluates the preclinical evidence behind RNA interference and CRISPR/Cas-based strategies aimed at shutting them down. The logic behind targeting E5 and E6 rests on their central position in HPV-mediated malignant transformation. According to the review, these oncoproteins collectively promote cell proliferation, immune evasion, resistance to apoptosis, and genomic instability, the four pillars on which a virus-infected cell can progress toward cancer. E5 contributes to tumor progression by modulating growth factor signaling and promoting cell survival, effectively creating a cellular environment in which abnormal proliferation is favored. E6, by contrast, plays the more notorious role: it drives malignant transformation primarily by tagging the tumor suppressor p53 for degradation, thereby removing one of the cell’s most important safeguards against uncontrolled division and DNA damage. The significance of p53 degradation cannot be overstated. In normal cells, p53 acts as a guardian of the genome, halting the cell cycle when DNA damage is detected and triggering programmed cell death when the damage is irreparable. When HPV16 E6 orchestrates the destruction of p53, infected cells lose this critical checkpoint and accumulate mutations with impunity. Because this mechanism is virus-encoded rather than a mutation in the host genome itself, it presents an attractive therapeutic window: a treatment that silences E6 could, in principle, allow p53 function to be restored in tumor cells while leaving normal cells untouched. This selectivity is precisely what makes HPV oncogenes such compelling drug targets compared with conventional cytotoxic approaches. analysis.brief_en: A new narrative review published in Virology Journal by researchers at Tabriz University of Medical Sciences and collaborators explores the potential of silencing HPV16 oncogenes E5 and E6 as a promising therapeutic approach for cervical cancer. The study highlights the critical roles of these oncoproteins in promoting cell proliferation, immune evasion, resistance to apoptosis, and genomic instability, which are key drivers of HPV-mediated malignant transformation. The review evaluates preclinical evidence supporting RNA interference and CRISPR/Cas-based strategies to target these oncogenes, aiming to restore tumor suppressor functions and enhance the effectiveness of conventional therapies like chemotherapy and radiotherapy. While these methods show potential, challenges such as efficient delivery and minimizing off-target effects remain. The findings suggest that targeting viral oncogenes could offer a more specific and less toxic alternative to traditional cancer treatments, aligning with the broader movement toward precision oncology. However, the evidence does not report specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers, focusing instead on the biological mechanisms and therapeutic implications.

news.content_title: HPV vaccination linked to lower risk of pregnancy complications
news.content: The benefits of the HPV vaccine may extend beyond protection against cancer. In a study published in The BMJ, researchers at Karolinska Institutet found that women who had been vaccinated against HPV were less likely to experience several pregnancy and childbirth complications, particularly preterm birth. HPV (human papillomavirus) is the leading cause of cervical cancer. HPV infection and treatment of cervical cell changes have also been associated with an increased risk of certain pregnancy complications. A new study has investigated the link between the HPV vaccine and complications such as preterm birth, premature rupture of membranes, babies being small for their gestational age, stillbirth, and neonatal mortality. The study is based on Swedish registers and covers 624,713 pregnancies among first-time mothers aged 16 to 35 between 2006 and 2023. 92,620 of these women had received the quadrivalent HPV vaccine prior to becoming pregnant, providing protection against four common types of HPV. Stronger link when vaccinated at a younger age Women who had been vaccinated before pregnancy consistently had a lower risk of the studied complications, particularly preterm birth. Compared with unvaccinated women, they were around five per cent less likely to give birth prematurely and around 15 per cent less likely to give birth very prematurely. "We also observed that the associations were stronger among women who had been vaccinated before the age of 17," says Zhongsong Zhang, doctoral student at the Department of Medical Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Karolinska Institutet. "This is consistent with previous findings that the HPV vaccine provides the best protection against HPV-related disease when administered at a younger age." A large register-based study Although the researchers took into account several factors that could have influenced the results, as this was an observational study, it was not possible to conclude that the lower risk was caused by HPV vaccination. Nevertheless, the study covered a large number of women from the Swedish population over a long period of time. "Even a relatively small reduction in the risk of preterm birth can be significant at a population level, given that HPV vaccination is administered to millions of young people worldwide," says Jiayao Lei, assistant professor at the same department at Karolinska Institutet. "Our results suggest that the benefits of HPV vaccination may extend beyond cancer prevention to include the reduction of complications that can arise during pregnancy and childbirth." The study was carried out in collaboration with researchers at the University of Gothenburg, Sahlgrenska University Hospital and the Norwegian Institute of Public Health. Funding for the research came from the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish Research Council for Health, Working Life and Welfare, the Swedish Cancer Society, Karolinska Institutet and ALF grants, among others. Source: Journal reference

news.content_title: A 3-year-old child developed genital warts on her face; doctors say it was due to sharing a towel.
news.content: A 3-year-old child developed genital warts on her face; doctors say it was due to sharing a towel. The family panicked when genital warts appeared on the boy's face; after a thorough examination, doctors determined that the boy contracted the disease through the family's habit of sharing towels. ZNews • 08/10/2026 This clinical case was shared by Gu Fangyu, a renowned urologist in Taiwan ( China ). The patient, only 3 or 4 years old, had developed pointed warts – commonly known as genital warts – on their face. After tracing the source of infection, the cause was determined to be the habit of sharing towels within the family. The boy's grandfather contracted HPV after visiting a red-light district. Because the family shared towels, the virus spread to his grandson. The grandmother was furious when she learned the cause of the incident. news.content_title: HPV vaccination may protect against adverse pregnancy outcomes
news.content: Having received the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine before pregnancy is associated with a lower risk of major pregnancy complications including preterm birth, with the greater reduction in risk seen among women vaccinated at an earlier age, finds a large Swedish study published by The BMJ today. The findings suggest that the benefits of HPV vaccination may extend beyond cancer prevention to the reduction of adverse pregnancy outcomes, say the researchers. HPV is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections. The quadrivalent HPV vaccine targets four types of HPV, including two (HPV types 16 and 18) that are responsible for about 70% of all cervical cancers. Growing evidence indicates that HPV infection, and the methods used to treat cervical lesions caused by HPV, are linked to an increased risk of pregnancy complications, including preterm birth, so preventing HPV holds potential benefits. To explore this further, researchers in Sweden used data from nationwide Swedish registers to evaluate the association between quadrivalent HPV vaccination before pregnancy and subsequent risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Their findings are based on 624,713 singleton, first-time births among women aged 16-35 years in Sweden between 2006 and 2023, of whom 92,620 (15%) had received quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy. Cases were women with at least one adverse pregnancy outcome, including preterm birth (before 37 weeks), very preterm birth (28 to 31 weeks), preterm and/or prelabor rupture of membranes, delivering a small or severely small baby, stillbirth, or newborn death. Each case was matched with up to 10 control women of the same age and year of conception and a range of other potentially influential factors were taken into account including self-reported cigarette smoking and body mass index at first antenatal visit, maternal diagnoses and assisted reproduction, mother's country of birth, family income and education level. After accounting for these factors, quadrivalent HPV vaccination was associated with lower odds of all included adverse pregnancy outcomes, compared with no vaccination. Statistically significant associations were seen for preterm and very preterm birth, spontaneous preterm birth, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, and delivering a severely small baby. Risk reduction was generally more pronounced among women vaccinated before age 17. This is an observational study so no firm conclusions can be drawn about cause and effect, and the authors acknowledge incomplete information on spontaneous abortions, and limited investigation of the underlying clinical pathways. Nor can they rule out the possibility that other unmeasured factors may have affected their results. However, they say this large study based on high quality data with long follow-up in a real world setting minimized bias and misclassification, enabling assessment of both common and rare adverse pregnancy outcomes. And results were similar after further analyses, suggesting that they are robust. As such, they say: "Together with previous research showing the safety of human papillomavirus vaccination during pregnancy, our results suggest that human papillomavirus vaccination is not only safe with respect to pregnancy outcomes but may also confer additional benefits by reducing the risk of adverse events." "Collectively, this evidence supports the global strategy for human papillomavirus vaccination and its continued implementation in routine immunization programs," they add. Source: Journal reference

analysis.brief_en: A large Swedish study published in The BMJ on October 7, 2026, found that HPV vaccination before pregnancy is associated with a lower risk of major pregnancy complications, including preterm birth. The research, based on data from 624,713 singleton, first-time births among women aged 16-35 years in Sweden between 2006 and 2023, revealed that 15% of the participants had received quadrivalent HPV vaccination prior to pregnancy. The findings suggest that HPV vaccination may offer additional benefits beyond cancer prevention by reducing the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. The study highlights that the risk reduction was more significant among women vaccinated before age 17. However, the researchers emphasize that this observational study cannot establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship, and they acknowledge limitations such as incomplete data on spontaneous abortions and unmeasured factors that could influence the results. Despite these uncertainties, the study's high-quality data and long follow-up period help minimize bias, supporting the safety and potential benefits of HPV vaccination during pregnancy.

The research, based on data from 624,713 singleton, first-time births among women aged 16-35 years in Sweden between 2006 and 2023, revealed that 15% of the participants had received quadrivalent HPV vaccination prior to pregnancy. The findings suggest that HPV vaccination may offer additional benefits beyond cancer prevention by reducing the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. The study highlights that the risk reduction was more significant among women vaccinated before age 17. However, the researchers emphasize that this observational study cannot establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship, and they acknowledge limitations such as incomplete data on spontaneous abortions and unmeasured factors that could influence the results. Despite these uncertainties, the study's high-quality data and long follow-up period help minimize bias, supporting the safety and potential benefits of HPV vaccination during pregnancy.

news.content_zh: 2026 年 10 月 7 日在《BMJ》上发表的一项瑞典大型研究发现,怀孕前感染 HPV 疫苗接种 与降低早产等主要妊娠并发症的风险相关。该研究基于 2006 年至 2023 年间瑞典 624,713 名 16-35 岁女性首次生育的​​单胎数据,结果显示,15% 的参与者在怀孕前接种了四价 HPV 疫苗接种。研究结果表明,HPV 疫苗接种 可能通过降低不良妊娠结局的风险,提供除癌症预防之外的其他益处。该研究强调,17 岁之前接种疫苗的女性风险降低更为显着。然而,研究人员强调,这项观察性研究无法建立明确的因果关系,他们承认自然流产数据不完整以及可能影响结果的未测量因素等局限性。尽管存在这些不确定性,该研究的高质量数据和长期随访有助于最大限度地减少偏差,支持妊娠期间 HPV 疫苗接种 的安全性和潜在益处。

analysis.time: The article was published on 2026-10-08. The date of the underlying research or sample collection is not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: The study examined 45 salivary‐gland tumour (SGT) samples (66.67 % benign, 33.34 % malignant). No specific geographic location of the sample collection or patient population is reported.
analysis.event: A research article in Scientific Reports investigated the methylation status of the DAPK gene in SGT tissues and its association with HPV16/18 and p16 protein expression. The investigation was reported by the journal and summarized by the news site; the findings are presented as exploratory and not yet confirmed.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Among the 45 SGT samples, HPV16 L1 positivity was 68 %, HPV16/18 E6 positivity 88 %, and p16 protein expression 77 %. No cases of disease transmission, deaths, or broader public‐health impact were reported. The study suggests a possible link between DAPK methylation and tumour type, but the biological significance remains uncertain.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The authors describe the results as preliminary and note methodological limitations, recommending further larger‐scale studies with PCR‐based HPV typing and functional validation. No public‐health interventions or official response actions are indicated.

analysis.brief_en: A Scientific Reports study examined 45 salivary‐gland tumour specimens to assess DAPK gene methylation and its relationship with HPV16/18 and p16 expression. The cohort comprised roughly two‐thirds benign and one‐third malignant tumours. HPV16 L1 was detected in 68 % of samples, HPV16/18 E6 in 88 %, and p16 protein in 77 %, with higher expression rates observed in benign lesions. While DAPK methylation correlated with tumour type, no direct association with HPV markers was confirmed. The authors caution that the findings are exploratory, limited by sample size and reliance on immunohistochemistry without molecular HPV typing, and call for larger, PCR‐based investigations to clarify these relationships. No public‐health actions or outbreak implications were reported.
analysis.summary_en: A Scientific Reports study examined 45 salivary‐gland tumour specimens to assess DAPK gene methylation and its relationship with HPV16/18 and p16 expression. The cohort comprised roughly two‐thirds benign and one‐third malignant tumours. HPV16 L1 was detected in 68 % of samples, HPV16/18 E6 in 88 %, and p16 protein in 77 %, with higher expression rates observed in benign lesions. While DAPK methylation correlated with tumour type, no direct association with HPV markers was confirmed. The authors caution that the findings are exploratory, limited by sample size and reliance on immunohistochemistry without molecular HPV typing, and call for larger, PCR‐based investigations to clarify these relationships. No public‐health actions or outbreak implications were reported.

Home News National New Delhi News HPV vaccine linked to lower risk of pregnancy complications: Study In Short Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common sexually transmitted infection. Persistent, high-risk infections can cause cervical cancer, among other types The Hans India Created On: 9 Oct 2026 1:17 AM ISTComment Share : X HPV vaccine linked to lower risk of pregnancy complications: Study A− Font size A+ Select Hans India Now FOLLOW ON Google News New Delhi: Getting vaccinated against HPV before pregnancy could be related with a lower risk of major pregnancy complications including preterm birth, suggesting that benefits of the HPV vaccine may extend beyond cancer prevention, according to Swedish research. Findings published in the British Medical Journal (BMJ) show that the greatest benefits in risk reduction were seen among women immunised at an earlier age. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common sexually transmitted infection. Persistent, high-risk infections can cause cervical cancer, among other types. Researchers, including those at Sweden’s Karolinska Institutet, said a growing evidence indicates that HPV infection, and the methods used to treat cervical lesions caused by HPV, are linked to an increased risk of pregnancy complications, including preterm birth, and therefore, preventing HPV holds potential benefits. A 2025 study from Aberdeen in the UK, published in the European Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, analysed 9,200 women with a pregnancy recorded between 2006 and 2020. It found that while there was no difference in rates of spontaneous preterm birth according to HPV vaccination status, other outcomes, including preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, pre-eclampsia and antepartum haemorrhage, may be significantly reduced in women immunised against HPV. The team used data from nationwide Swedish registers to look at 624,713 single-child, first-time births among women aged 16-35 years between 2006 and 2023, of whom 92,620 (15 per cent) had received a quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy. The quadrivalent HPV vaccine targets four types of HPV, including two (HPV types 16 and 18) that are responsible for about 70 per cent of all cervical cancers. Adverse pregnancy outcomes that were looked at included preterm birth (before 37 weeks), very preterm birth (28 to 31 weeks), preterm and prelabour rupture of membranes, delivering a small or severely small baby, stillbirth, or newborn death. analysis_en.location_and_population: The study analyzed data from nationwide Swedish registers and included 624,713 single-child, first-time births among women aged 16-35 years in Sweden.
analysis_en.event: A study published in the British Medical Journal (BMJ) found that HPV vaccination before pregnancy may reduce the risk of certain pregnancy complications, such as preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, pre-eclampsia, and antepartum haemorrhage. The study was reported by The Hans India.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: The study found that women immunized against HPV before pregnancy had a significantly reduced risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, including preterm birth, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, pre-eclampsia, and antepartum haemorrhage. The risk reduction was most pronounced among those vaccinated at an earlier age.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is a published research finding, and the results are based on data analysis from Swedish registers. The findings suggest potential benefits of HPV vaccination beyond cancer prevention, but further investigation or clinical validation may be needed.

news.title_zh: 研究显示 HPV 疫苗 与降低妊娠并发症风险有关
news.source_body_en: A study published in the British Medical Journal (BMJ) found that HPV vaccination before pregnancy may reduce the risk of certain pregnancy complications, such as preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, pre-eclampsia, and antepartum haemorrhage. The research, conducted by Swedish scientists, analyzed data from nationwide Swedish registers covering 624,713 single-child, first-time births among women aged 16-35 years between 2006 and 2023. The findings indicate that women immunized against HPV at an earlier age experienced the greatest risk reduction. The study highlights the potential benefits of HPV vaccination beyond cancer prevention, suggesting it may improve pregnancy outcomes. However, the results are based on observational data and may require further clinical validation to confirm their implications for public health.

Today, it is one of the most preventable cancers through human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and routine cervical cancer screening. The HPV vaccine also protects boys and girls against other HPV-related cancers that can develop later in life. Yet thousands of women and men in the United States are still diagnosed with HPV-related cancers each year, and thousands more lose their lives to diseases that, in many cases, can be prevented or detected early. That reality represents both a challenge and an opportunity. The Role of HPV Vaccination Nearly all cervical cancers are caused by persistent infection with certain types of HPV, a common virus that most people will encounter at some point in their lives. The HPV vaccine - known by its brand name Gardasil - protects against aggressive HPV types responsible for most cervical cancers and several other cancers as well. HPV vaccination provides safe, effective, and long-lasting protection for both boys and girls. HPV can cause cancers in women and men, including cervical, throat, anal and penile cancers. HPV is responsible for an estimated 60-70% of oropharyngeal cancers in the United States, and these cancers occur far more often in men than women. Vaccinating all children at the recommended age helps protect them from HPV-related cancers later in life. With more than 135 million doses distributed in the United States, the HPV vaccine has a reassuring safety record that's backed by over 15 years of monitoring and research. And the data show it works: HPV infections, genital warts, and cervical pre-cancers (abnormal cells on the cervix that can lead to cancer) have dropped since the vaccine was introduced in the United States. Infections with HPV types that cause most HPV cancers and genital warts have dropped 88% among teen girls and 81% among young adult women. And among vaccinated women, the percentage of cervical pre-cancers caused by the HPV types most often linked to cervical cancer has dropped by 40%. Since the introduction of Gardasil, healthcare professionals have viewed HPV vaccination as one of the most promising cancer prevention tools available. Today, we are beginning to see the impact of that investment. Research published this year by the American Cancer Society found that cervical cancer incidence among women ages 20 to 31 declined 27% nationally in the years following HPV vaccine introduction, with states that achieved higher vaccination rates generally experiencing larger declines. Higher vaccination coverage was associated with greater reductions in cervical cancer risk. Even more striking, new observational research published in The Lancet found that in England, where HPV vaccination rates have been high, no cervical cancer deaths occurred among women ages 20 to 24 between 2020 and 2024, compared with more than 23 expected deaths based on historical trends. Researchers concluded that high HPV vaccination coverage was associated with substantial reductions in cervical cancer mortality. "The HPV vaccine is recommended beginning in adolescence because it is most effective before exposure to the virus," said Dr. Gourdine, SVP and Chief Medical Officer for CVS Caremark®, a trained pediatrician and public health leader. "When your child is 11 or 12 years old, it can feel uncomfortable to think about care connected to their future sexual activity-but this is one of the best tools we have to prevent cervical cancer, as well as other HPV-related cancers that can affect both women and men." Screening Remains Essential Vaccination is only one part of the prevention story. Routine cervical cancer screening remains one of the most effective ways to identify precancerous changes before they become cancer or to detect cancer at an earlier, more treatable stage. The Pap test and HPV test can identify abnormalities long before symptoms appear, creating opportunities for timely intervention and better outcomes. However, screening rates remain a concern. Data from the Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion show that cervical cancer screening rates have been declining for years and have not fully recovered to pre-pandemic levels. This trend is especially concerning because regular screening continues to be a cornerstone of cervical cancer prevention. "Cervical cancer screening remains essential, even for people who have received the HPV vaccine," said Dr. Joanne Armstrong, VP and Chief Medical Officer, Women's Health and Genomics, CVS Health®. "Following recommended screening guidelines can help identify precancerous changes before they become cancer, when treatment may be most effective." Prevention Works Best When We Use Every Tool Available Too often, conversations about cervical cancer focus only after a diagnosis. Yet some of the most important actions happen years earlier through preventive care. Vaccination helps reduce the risk of HPV infection. Screening helps detect abnormalities early. Together, these tools create a powerful opportunity to reduce the burden of cervical cancer and improve long-term health outcomes. As physicians, we see firsthand the value of prevention. We also recognize that navigating healthcare decisions can sometimes feel overwhelming. But cervical cancer prevention offers a rare example of a public health success story already within our reach. The science is clear: preventive care saves lives. By staying up to date on recommended vaccinations and routine screenings, patients can take meaningful steps to protect their health and reduce their risk of cervical cancer. While no prevention strategy is perfect, cervical cancer demonstrates what is possible when medical innovation, preventive care, and patient action come together. It is one of the clearest examples in modern medicine that the best cancer treatment may be preventing cancer from developing in the first place. Today, it is one of the most preventable cancers through human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and routine cervical cancer screening. The HPV vaccine also protects boys and girls against other HPV-related cancers that can develop later in life. Yet thousands of women and men in the United States are still diagnosed with HPV-related cancers each year, and thousands more lose their lives to diseases that, in many cases, can be prevented or detected early. That reality represents both a challenge and an opportunity. The Role of HPV Vaccination Nearly all cervical cancers are caused by persistent infection with certain types of HPV, a common virus that most people will encounter at some point in their lives. The HPV vaccine - known by its brand name Gardasil - protects against aggressive HPV types responsible for most cervical cancers and several other cancers as well. HPV vaccination provides safe, effective, and long-lasting protection for both boys and girls. HPV can cause cancers in women and men, including cervical, throat, anal and penile cancers. HPV is responsible for an estimated 60-70% of oropharyngeal cancers in the United States, and these cancers occur far more often in men than women. Vaccinating all children at the recommended age helps protect them from HPV-related cancers later in life. With more than 135 million doses distributed in the United States, the HPV vaccine has a reassuring safety record that's backed by over 15 years of monitoring and research. And the data show it works: HPV infections, genital warts, and cervical pre-cancers (abnormal cells on the cervix that can lead to cancer) have dropped since the vaccine was introduced in the United States. Infections with HPV types that cause most HPV cancers and genital warts have dropped 88% among teen girls and 81% among young adult women. And among vaccinated women, the percentage of cervical pre-cancers caused by the HPV types most often linked to cervical cancer has dropped by 40%. Since the introduction of Gardasil, healthcare professionals have viewed HPV vaccination as one of the most promising cancer prevention tools available. Today, we are beginning to see the impact of that investment. Research published this year by the American Cancer Society found that cervical cancer incidence among women ages 20 to 31 declined 27% nationally in the years following HPV vaccine introduction, with states that achieved higher vaccination rates generally experiencing larger declines. Higher vaccination coverage was associated with greater reductions in cervical cancer risk. Even more striking, new observational research published in The Lancet found that in England, where HPV vaccination rates have been high, no cervical cancer deaths occurred among women ages 20 to 24 between 2020 and 2024, compared with more than 23 expected deaths based on historical trends. Researchers concluded that high HPV vaccination coverage was associated with substantial reductions in cervical cancer mortality. "The HPV vaccine is recommended beginning in adolescence because it is most effective before exposure to the virus," said Dr. Gourdine, SVP and Chief Medical Officer for CVS Caremark®, a trained pediatrician and public health leader. "When your child is 11 or 12 years old, it can feel uncomfortable to think about care connected to their future sexual activity-but this is one of the best tools we have to prevent cervical cancer, as well as other HPV-related cancers that can affect both women and men." Screening Remains Essential Vaccination is only one part of the prevention story. Routine cervical cancer screening remains one of the most effective ways to identify precancerous changes before they become cancer or to detect cancer at an earlier, more treatable stage. The Pap test and HPV test can identify abnormalities long before symptoms appear, creating opportunities for timely intervention and better outcomes. However, screening rates remain a concern. Data from the Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion show that cervical cancer screening rates have been declining for years and have not fully recovered to pre-pandemic levels. This trend is especially concerning because regular screening continues to be a cornerstone of cervical cancer prevention. "Cervical cancer screening remains essential, even for people who have received the HPV vaccine," said Dr. Joanne Armstrong, VP and Chief Medical Officer, Women's Health and Genomics, CVS Health®. "Following recommended screening guidelines can help identify precancerous changes before they become cancer, when treatment may be most effective." Prevention Works Best When We Use Every Tool Available Too often, conversations about cervical cancer focus only after a diagnosis. Yet some of the most important actions happen years earlier through preventive care. Vaccination helps reduce the risk of HPV infection. Screening helps detect abnormalities early. Together, these tools create a powerful opportunity to reduce the burden of cervical cancer and improve long-term health outcomes. As physicians, we see firsthand the value of prevention. We also recognize that navigating healthcare decisions can sometimes feel overwhelming. But cervical cancer prevention offers a rare example of a public health success story already within our reach. The science is clear: preventive care saves lives. By staying up to date on recommended vaccinations and routine screenings, patients can take meaningful steps to protect their health and reduce their risk of cervical cancer. While no prevention strategy is perfect, cervical cancer demonstrates what is possible when medical innovation, preventive care, and patient action come together. It is one of the clearest examples in modern medicine that the best cancer treatment may be preventing cancer from developing in the first place. news.content: cec gyanesh kumarelection commissionflydubai incidentrahul gandhi ❯ E हिं অ বাং ગુ ಕ മ म ଓ ਪੰ த తె ار ❯ National English हिंदी उत्तर प्रदेशउत्तराखंडछत्तीसगढ़झारखंडदिल्लीबिहारमध्य प्रदेशराजस्थानहरियाणाहिमाचल प्रदेश অসমীয়া বাংলা ગુજરાતી ಕನ್ನಡ മലയാളം मराठी ଓଡିଆ ਪੰਜਾਬੀ தமிழ் తెలుగు ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్తెలంగాణ اردو Live NATIONAL WORLD SPORTS ENTERTAINMENT OPINION PHOTOS HEALTH STATE BUSINESS More Live ETV Bharat / health Pune-based Lab Launches HPV Self-Sampling Kit To Make Cervical Cancer Testing More Accessible For some women, awkward, embarrassment, privacy concerns or limited access to healthcare facilities can become barriers to undergoing HPV testing. HPV16 was the most frequently detected genotype of the Human Papillomavirus in the study published in Frontiers in Medical Technology (Getty Images) By ETV Bharat Health Team Published : October 6, 2026 at 12:05 PM IST 4 Min Read In an effort to make cervical cancer screening more accessible to women, Pune-based Greenarray Labs has launched CerviSens, a vaginal self-sampling kit that allows women to collect their own sample for Human Papillomavirus (HPV) testing, without requiring a speculum examination at the time of sample collection. Cervical cancer is largely preventable through HPV vaccination, regular screening and timely treatment. However, screening continues to remain a challenge for many women. Conventional sample collection generally requires a visit to a healthcare facility, a trained healthcare professional and a pelvic examination using a speculum. Why Self-Sampling? For some women, awkward, embarrassment, privacy concerns or limited access to healthcare facilities can become barriers to undergoing screening. CerviSens has been developed to simplify the sample collection process by allowing women to collect a vaginal sample themselves in privacy. The collected sample is subsequently tested in a laboratory for high-risk HPV, which is associated with the majority of cervical cancer cases. The self-sampling approach has also undergone clinical validation. A study published in the international journal Frontiers in Medical Technology in September 2025 evaluated 203 paired self-collected and clinician-collected samples. The study reported very good agreement between the two collection methods. Using clinician-collected samples as the reference standard, CerviSens self-collected samples showed 98.0% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity for HPV detection. Dr. Sanjay Gupte, Founder, Greenarray Labs, said, “Cervical cancer is one of the cancers where screening can make a significant difference, yet many women still do not undergo regular screening. One of the reasons is that the conventional process of sample collection may be uncomfortable or difficult to access for some women. Self-sampling provides another way for women to participate in screening while maintaining their privacy and comfort. The important next step is ensuring that women who test positive are appropriately counselled and connected to further clinical evaluation and care.” Beyond making sample collection simpler, Greenarray Labs has also been studying the different high-risk HPV genotypes found among women across India. Its wider HPV testing programme has analysed more than 20,000 clinical samples, including a five-year multicentric study of 12,373 samples from Maharashtra, Karnataka, Odisha and Itanagar in Arunachal Pradesh. How Prevalent Is HPV In India? The multicentric study found that 2.6% of the samples were positive for high-risk HPV, with approximately 63% of positive cases seen among women aged 31-50 years. HPV16 was the most frequently detected genotype, followed by HPV31, HPV33 and HPV18. The data also showed geographical variation. High-risk HPV positivity was recorded at 2.4% in Maharashtra, 3.6% in Karnataka, 3.1% in Odisha and 6.5% in Itanagar. Another finding was the presence of more than one high-risk HPV type in some women. Among HPV-positive samples, 34.5% showed co-infection with two or more high-risk HPV genotypes. The commonly observed combinations included HPV16 with HPV66, HPV33 with HPV58, and HPV18 with HPV33. Dr. Preeti Helkar, Chief Genomic Scientist, Greenarray Labs, said, “HPV16 and HPV18 are widely recognised as important high-risk types, but they are not the only high-risk HPV genotypes that we encounter. Our data also showed infections involving other high-risk types as well as women carrying more than one genotype. Looking at individual genotypes gives us a more detailed understanding of HPV patterns across different populations and can contribute to surveillance as well as appropriate clinical follow-up.” HPV DNA testing associated with the programme identifies 14 high-risk HPV genotypes: HPV16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66 and 68. While several HPV tests separately identify HPV16 and HPV18 and report other high-risk types together, individual genotyping can provide additional information on genotype distribution, persistence and co-infections. Nitin Gupte, CEO, Greenarray Labs, said, “For screening to reach more women, it has to become easier to access and simpler to participate in. Self-sampling can help reduce some of the practical barriers associated with conventional sample collection, particularly for women who may otherwise postpone screening. Our focus is on combining easier sample collection with validated laboratory testing and ensuring that screening ultimately leads to appropriate medical follow-up wherever required.” The World Health Organization’s cervical cancer elimination strategy focuses on HPV vaccination, screening and timely treatment. Making screening easier to access, particularly for women who remain outside routine screening programmes, could play an important role in increasing participation and identifying high-risk HPV infections that require further clinical evaluation. analysis.brief_en: On October 6, 2026, Pune-based Greenarray Labs launched CerviSens, a self-sampling kit for Human Papillomavirus (HPV) testing, designed to make cervical cancer screening more accessible. The kit allows women to collect their own vaginal samples in privacy, eliminating the need for a speculum examination. This initiative aims to address barriers such as embarrassment, privacy concerns, and limited access to healthcare facilities. The self-sampling method has been clinically validated, showing 98.0% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity for HPV detection. A multicentric study of 12,373 samples from Maharashtra, Karnataka, Odisha, and Itanagar in Arunachal Pradesh found that 2.6% of samples were positive for high-risk HPV, with 63% of these cases among women aged 31-50 years. Additionally, 34.5% of HPV-positive samples showed co-infection with two or more high-risk genotypes, including combinations like HPV16 with HPV66, HPV33 with HPV58, and HPV18 with HPV33. The lab emphasizes the importance of combining easier sample collection with validated laboratory testing and ensuring appropriate medical follow-up for those testing positive. The World Health Organization’s strategy for cervical cancer elimination includes HPV vaccination, screening, and timely treatment, highlighting the significance of such initiatives in increasing screening participation and identifying high-risk infections.

news.title_zh: 浦那实验室推出 HPV 自采样套件,使 宫颈癌 检测更容易进行 - ETV Bharat
news.source_body_en: On October 6, 2026, Pune-based Greenarray Labs launched CerviSens, a self-sampling kit for Human Papillomavirus (HPV) testing, designed to make cervical cancer screening more accessible. The kit allows women to collect their own vaginal samples in privacy, eliminating the need for a speculum examination. This initiative aims to address barriers such as embarrassment, privacy concerns, and limited access to healthcare facilities. The self-sampling method has been clinically validated, showing 98.0% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity for HPV detection. A multicentric study of 12,373 samples from Maharashtra, Karnataka, Odisha, and Itanagar in Arunachal Pradesh found that 2.6% of samples were positive for high-risk HPV, with 63% of these cases among women aged 31-50 years. Additionally, 34.5% of HPV-positive samples showed co-infection with two or more high-risk genotypes, including combinations like HPV16 with HPV66, HPV33 with HPV58, and HPV18 with HPV33. The lab emphasizes the importance of combining easier sample collection with validated laboratory testing and ensuring appropriate medical follow-up for those testing positive. The World Health Organization’s strategy for cervical cancer elimination includes HPV vaccination, screening, and timely treatment, highlighting the significance of such initiatives in increasing screening participation and identifying high-risk infections.
