Despite advances in vaccination against human papillomavirus and improvements in screening, many patients are diagnosed at stages where treatment options narrow and outcomes deteriorate. A new study published in Reproductive Sciences by Cong Xu, Guangming Wang and colleagues at Dali University and collaborating hospitals in China now adds a fresh dimension to the search for better prognostic tools. The team has built a gene-based risk model centered on telomeres, the protective caps at the ends of chromosomes, and shown that it can stratify cervical cancer patients by survival with striking statistical confidence. Telomeres are repetitive DNA-protein structures that shield chromosome ends from degradation and from being mistaken for broken DNA. Each time a cell divides, its telomeres shorten a little, and when they become critically short, the cell normally enters senescence, a state of permanent growth arrest. This mechanism, first described in the classic experiments of Hayflick and Moorhead in 1961, acts as a natural brake on uncontrolled proliferation. Cancer cells, however, frequently subvert it, reactivating telomere-maintaining machinery such as telomerase or alternative lengthening of telomeres to divide indefinitely. Understanding how telomere biology goes awry in cervical cancer, where viral oncoproteins from HPV already disable key tumor suppressor pathways like p53, has remained an open and uncertain question. To address this, the researchers assembled a comprehensive catalog of telomere-associated genes from the TelNet database and cross-referenced it with expression data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, using the TCGA-CESC cervical cancer cohort. Within that dataset they identified 327 telomere-related genes that were differentially expressed between tumor and healthy tissue. They then intersected this list with genes linked to cellular aging, narrowing the field to 31 overlapping genes that sit at the crossroads of telomere maintenance and senescence. Functional enrichment analysis of these genes revealed that they are concentrated in processes central to cancer biology: the cell cycle, DNA replication, and DNA repair. The enrichment results carry biological weight. Several of the overlapping genes participate in homologous recombination, the high-fidelity pathway cells use to repair double-strand DNA breaks, while others are implicated in cellular senescence programs and even in pathways activated by Human T-cell leukemia virus 1 infection, a hint of shared vulnerabilities between retroviral and papillomaviral oncogenesis. The authors note that dysfunction in these genes could disturb the balance between cellular synthesis and apoptosis, the programmed death of damaged cells, thereby accelerating tumor progression. This fits with earlier findings that telomeric DNA damage is particularly difficult to repair and can lock cells into a persistent DNA damage response, fueling inflammation and genomic instability in the tumor microenvironment. The methodological core of the study is a classic bioinformatic pipeline executed with care. The team first applied univariate Cox regression to screen the 31 genes for associations with overall survival, then used Lasso regression, a technique that shrinks coefficients to avoid overfitting, to select the most informative subset, and finally refined the model with multivariate Cox regression. The resulting telomere-related gene risk score assigns each patient a numerical value based on the expression pattern of the selected genes. When the TCGA cohort was split by this score, patients in the high-risk group showed significantly poorer outcomes, with the difference reaching a p-value below 0.001, a threshold that indicates the result is very unlikely to have arisen by chance. Importantly, the risk score held up as an independent prognostic factor, meaning it predicted survival even after accounting for established clinical variables. That independence matters because existing prognostic markers for cervical cancer, such as stage, grade, and lymph node status, leave considerable uncertainty in individual cases. A molecular signature rooted in telomere and senescence biology could complement these measures, helping clinicians identify patients whose tumors behave more aggressively than their clinical profile alone suggests. The authors also suggest that patient subgroups defined by the signature may respond differently to specific therapies, opening the door to more tailored treatment selection. The study goes beyond prognosis to touch on therapeutic implications. Because telomere maintenance mechanisms are increasingly recognized as actionable targets, with recent reviews in Nature Reviews Cancer cataloging telomere-specific therapies in development, a gene signature that captures telomere dysfunction could help identify which patients are most likely to benefit from such approaches. The researchers also analyzed drug sensitivity patterns associated with the risk score, and point to the tumor immune microenvironment as a relevant axis, given the known roles of macrophages, neutrophils, and regulatory T cells in HPV-related cancers. If validated, the model could assist in selecting suitable drugs for individual patients rather than applying one-size-fits-all regimens. The scientific context here is rich. HPV oncoproteins E6 and E7, encoded by high-risk viral types 16 and 18, promote the degradation of p53 and disable the retinoblastoma pathway, effectively dismantling the checkpoints that would normally force telomere-shortened cells into senescence. This creates a permissive environment in which telomere biology becomes decisive: cells that escape senescence and maintain their telomeres can achieve the replicative immortality that defines cancer. Prior work has shown that telomere shortening inactivates cell cycle checkpoints in liver carcinogenesis, and that telomere length dynamics shape the evolution of cancer genome architecture. The present study extends this logic to cervical cancer in a systematic, genome-wide fashion. As with any computational study built on public databases, caveats apply. The model was derived and tested within the TCGA cohort, and independent external validation in additional patient cohorts, ideally with prospective sample collection, will be needed before it can inform clinical decisions. The authors note that the datasets used are publicly available, and the study received ethics approval from the First Affiliated Hospital of Dali University. The work was supported by the Science and Technology Department of Yunnan Province and by key construction disciplines at the First Affiliated Hospital of Dali University. The declared absence of commercial conflicts of interest strengthens the case that the findings reflect genuine scientific inquiry rather than commercial positioning. Nevertheless, the study represents a meaningful step in translating telomere biology from bench curiosity to bedside tool. It demonstrates that the intersection of telomere maintenance and cellular senescence is not merely a background process in cervical cancer but a measurable, quantifiable axis of tumor behavior with prognostic power. As telomere-targeted therapies mature and immunotherapy reshapes the treatment landscape for gynecologic cancers, gene signatures of this kind could become the compass that guides clinicians through an expanding arsenal of options. For a disease that kills hundreds of thousands of women each year, mostly in settings with limited access to advanced screening, a robust molecular prognostic model offers a path toward smarter, more personalized care. SHOW MORE HPV vaccination before pregnancy was linked to lower odds of preterm birth in a Swedish study of 624,713 births. Advertisement Quadrivalent human papillomavirus (qHPV) vaccination before pregnancy was associated with lower odds of preterm birth and several other adverse pregnancy outcomes, with stronger associations among women vaccinated at younger ages, according to a nationwide Swedish registry study published October 7, 2026, in BMJ. Preterm birth is one of the leading global causes of newborn mortality and a major contributor to medical and social impairment in adulthood, yet effective prevention and treatment options remain limited. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV is the primary cause of cervical precancer and cancer, and emerging evidence has linked HPV infection to adverse pregnancy outcomes, including preterm birth. Excisional cervical treatments, commonly performed for HPV-related high-grade lesions and early-stage cervical cancer, have also been shown to increase the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Because these lesions and treatments often occur during reproductive years, the investigators noted that HPV may be an important and potentially preventable contributor to preterm birth. Evaluating HPV vaccination and pregnancy outcomes Earlier data from Denmark, Australia, Finland, and Scotland suggested HPV vaccination before pregnancy may be associated with reduced risk of some adverse pregnancy outcomes. However, those studies often lacked nationwide data with individual-level linkage for detailed confounder control and frequently examined outcomes in isolation, the study authors noted. To address these gaps, they used population-based Swedish registers to analyze 624,713 singleton births among nulliparous women aged 16 to 35 years between 2006 and 2023. Of these women, 92,620 (14.8%) had received qHPV vaccination before pregnancy. Sweden introduced its first HPV vaccine in 2006, began offering subsidized vaccination to girls aged 13 to 17 years in 2007, and launched a free school-based program for girls aged 10 to 12 years in 2012, alongside catch-up vaccination for girls born from 1993 to 1998. Primary outcomes were preterm birth before 37 weeks, including its subtypes, and spontaneous preterm birth. Secondary outcomes included preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (PPROM), prelabor rupture of membranes, small for gestational age (SGA) infant below the 10th percentile, severe SGA infant below the 3rd percentile, stillbirth, and neonatal mortality. Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs), and effect modification by age at vaccination was assessed. Which adverse pregnancy outcomes were lower after qHPV vaccination? After adjustment for confounders, qHPV vaccination was associated with lower odds of all included adverse pregnancy outcomes. Statistically significant associations were observed for: Preterm birth (aOR, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.91-0.99) Very preterm birth at 28 to 31 weeks (aOR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.75-0.97) Spontaneous preterm birth (aOR, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.91-0.99), PPROM (aOR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.87-1.00) Severe SGA infant (aOR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.87-0.97) Risk reductions were generally more pronounced among women vaccinated at younger ages, in line with prior evidence that HPV vaccination offers stronger protection against infection, precancer, and cancer when given earlier. What do the findings mean for HPV vaccination programs? A large share of HPV vaccine doses worldwide are delivered to school-aged girls through routine programs, and the investigators noted that even modest reproductive benefits could translate into substantial population-level health gains. According to the authors, the findings extend the benefits of HPV vaccination beyond cancer prevention and further strengthen its clinical and public health value. Reference: Zhang Z, Ploner A, Sengpiel V, et al. Quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy and pregnancy outcomes: nationwide, population based case-control study. BMJ. supplementary_news.content: Swedish mothers who had been vaccinated against the human papillomavirus (HPV) have fewer complications during pregnancy, a new study has found, especially lower rates of preterm birth. The researchers acknowledge their methodology can’t prove vaccination caused the better pregnancy outcomes, but argue that the evidence points that way. Vaccination helping births All vaccinations today attract vocal opposition and conspiracy theories, but twenty years ago, when the Gardasil and Cervarix vaccines were introduced, that wasn’t true for the fight against most diseases. Nevertheless, the two vaccines designed to protect against cervical cancer set off a storm of controversy. Because HPV is primarily a sexually transmitted disease, opponents claimed that saving young people from cancer would “be a license to be promiscuous”. SPONSORED CONTENT - Strengthening human papillomavirus vaccination programs through multi-country peer learning: lessons... Christopher Morgan, Cancer Biology & Medicine, 2025 - Human papillomavirus vaccination willingness under resource inequities: momentary intervention effec... Yuxi Liu, Cancer Biology & Medicine, 2025 - Progress toward cervical cancer elimination: global disparities and China’s contributions Partha Basu, Cancer Biology & Medicine, 2025 Opponents tried to mask their opposition with unsupported medical claims, including saying that the vaccines would affect fertility later in life. Now it appears that claim was true, but in the exact opposite way that they meant – vaccination as a teenager may boost the chances of having a healthy baby years later. Scandinavian researchers used data on all first-time births in Sweden between 2006 and 2023 where the mother was aged 16 to 35. After excluding twins and triplets, mothers who migrated to Sweden after the age of 9, and a few other rare cases, they were left with a sample size of 624,713 births. Of these, 14.8 percent of the mothers had received the Gardasil vaccine against four strains of HPV before becoming pregnant. The team then looked at cases where at least one complication was reported during or soon after pregnancy, ranging from babies being born pre-term, to stillbirth or the baby dying in the first few days. The team concluded that vaccination was associated with lower risk of most, and probably all, of the adverse outcomes they studied. Moreover, in a rebuttal to those who have argued that HPV vaccination should only be given to adults, the risk reduction was usually greatest for those vaccinated before they turned 17. At 5 to 15 percent, the reduction in risk was modest, but the fall was statistically significant for most cases. Stillbirths were also lower when the mother had been vaccinated, but did not quite meet statistical significance. Since the study was observational, rather than a controlled trial, it is possible that the vaccinated mothers had some other differences that protected them compared to those who had not been vaccinated. However, the team randomly matched each adverse pregnancy with ten controls from their sample that matched for other potentially influential factors such as age, smoking, and education level. The association between vaccination and lower risk still held up after this. Multiple benefits from a one vaccine The connection may seem surprising, but there was a reason the researchers went looking for it. Even when HPV does not lead to cancer, there is evidence that the cervical lesions it can produce, and the methods used to treat them, may increase the chances of preterm births, and the health effects that follow. Several previous studies raised the possibility that vaccination might be protective, but were not large enough to be convincing. “Together with previous research showing the safety of human papillomavirus vaccination during pregnancy, our results suggest that human papillomavirus vaccination is not only safe with respect to pregnancy outcomes but may also confer additional benefits by reducing the risk of adverse events,” the authors write. Even before the vaccine’s effectiveness as a shield against cancer was showing up on a population-wide basis, research showed the vaccine was causing a dramatic fall in painful and embarrassing genital warts where vaccination was common. We now know that the vaccines have almost eliminated cervical cancer in certain populations, and there is evidence it is also greatly reducing several rarer cancers in both men and women. Predictably, the claimed harmful impact on fertility never showed up, but it looks likely thousands of mothers were spared the pain of losing a child. Even larger numbers of children did not have to go through life with the risks associated with premature birth. “Collectively, this evidence supports the global strategy for human papillomavirus vaccination and its continued implementation in routine immunization programs,” the authors write. The study is open access in the British Medical Journal

The nurse nurturing vaccine confidence in an Uzbek mountain exclave

In Shahimardan, nurse Nilyufar Tursunova says patient explanation of immunisation science is all nervous parents really need.

  • 6 October 2026
  • by Umida Maniyazova

At a glance

  • Nilyufar Tursunova looks after the 896 children of Shahimardan, a mountain exclave of Uzbekistan.
  • Despite the fact that Shahimardan’s unique geography means that a referral to any larger health centre means crossing an international border twice, she says logistics don’t hamper vaccine uptake in the locality – at least not since her clinic received a reliable vaccine fridge back in 2018.
  • Instead, her major challenge is communicating vaccines well in a climate of anxiety. Her approach is simple: trust the facts to do the talking. “When a mother understands what the vaccine protects her child from, she no longer needs to be persuaded. She makes the decision herself.”

“Despite the fact that we are located in an exclave, we have never had difficulties with the delivery of vaccines or with vaccinating children,” says nurse Nilyufar Tursunova of Shahimardan with deserved pride.

Shahimardan is part of Uzbekistan, but totally surrounded by Kyrgyzstan, which means that even a routine journey to a larger medical centre involves crossing an international border. That used to pose some problems for reliable vaccine supply, she concedes, but since her clinic got its own vaccine refrigerator back in 2018, the 896 children in her care have never needed to go without.

When a mother understands what the vaccine protects her child from, she no longer needs to be persuaded. She makes the decision herself.

- Nilyufar Tursunova

And that’s even though Shahimardan’s diplomatic reality is not its only geographic challenge. The village lies 1550 m above sea level, ringed by peaks of up to 2,800 m. The rivers Oq-Su and Kok-Su rush along steep valleys; houses seem to cling to the slopes. In the past, when getting kids vaccinated meant going door-to-door, that meant health workers like Tursunova either catching a lift with local residents on old “IZH” motorcycles, Soviet-era bikes fitted with sidecars, or walking house to house along mountain paths. Still, today, vaccine logistics in Shahimardan tick over with little stress or variation.

Instead, what most requires Tursunova’s vigilance is the challenge of effectively communicating vaccination. “If you properly explain to parents how vital vaccination is for the child’s healthy development, they understand,” she says.

She estimates that 80% of parents here make sure their children receive their vaccines on time. That means that there are still some who are unduly anxious.

Gently does it

One trigger phrase for the vaccine-worried, Tursunova says, is “live vaccine”. Mothers worry that live vaccines – such as the highly effective and extremely safe live-attenuated measles vaccine – are more liable to provoke fevers and other side-effects than inactivated, or ‘killed’ vaccines.

It’s untrue, but could still put parents off immunising their children. That would be dangerous. In 2025, the European Regional Verification Commission concluded that measles transmission had been re-established in Uzbekistan, making continued large-scale vaccination and surveillance all the more important.

Have you read?

  • The furthest ‘last mile’: how vaccines reach children in Uzbekistan’s most remote areas
  • New vaccines make big impact in rural Uzbekistan

Still, Tursunova doesn’t respond with pressure. She speaks in a quiet, even voice, soft and unhurried. Eight years of working with children seem to have scrubbed all the sharpness and hurry from her delivery. If it calms down her paediatric patients, it also seems to reach their parents. Once they know what to expect, their concerns usually ease, she says.

Tursunova explains what “live-attenuated” really means: that the vaccine uses a weakened, safe form of the virus to stimulate a healthy immune response. But the technical explanation is only part of the task. The way it is communicated matters just as much, she insists.

Her faith in kind, respectful conversation has also shaped how Shahimardan has responded to the arrival of unfamiliar vaccines.

Shock of the new

New vaccines can raise parents’ internal alarm systems. “When we first received the HPV vaccine and started vaccinating girls, there were, of course, some difficulties,” she says. “Not all parents understood what kind of vaccine it was.”

In 2019 the human papillomavirus, or HPV, vaccine made its first entrance to Uzbekistan’s vaccine portfolio. The fact that the vaccine, which protects adolescent girls against developing cervical cancer in the future, was being recommended for a different target group than most of the vaccines parents were used to opened the door to anxieties.

But over the years, Tursunova says attitudes and knowledge levels have shifted. “Now mothers come themselves and ask: isn’t it time for my daughter to get the vaccine?” At least some of that change appears to be down to Tursunova.

For Sayora, the mother of ten-year-old Gulbahor and three younger children, moving to Shahimardan dissolved her resistance to HPV vaccination.

When the family lived in Margilan city, about 55 km from Shahimardan, Sayora said neighbours and acquaintances had warned her off having her daughter vaccinated. “People around us used to say that the HPV vaccine could cause infertility and other problems. Many neighbours and acquaintances tried to convince me not to give it to my daughter. I listened to them because I didn’t know enough about the vaccine myself.”

When her family relocated to Shahimardan, she found herself part of a small, close-knit community with a high degree of confidence in the vaccine, and a high degree of confidence in the counsel of Tursunova.

“When Nilyufar explained to me what diseases the HPV vaccine protects against, I agreed. Of course I wanted my daughter to have that protection. Gulbahor received the vaccine here in Shahimardan.”

“I understood that what I had heard before was just talk – there was no scientific evidence behind those claims,” she added. “I realised that I had been wrong.”

A relationship of trust

In a remote community like Shahimardan, the relationship between the health system and families can be especially important.

The clinic serves a relatively small population. Parents return to the same health workers with questions, concerns and sometimes information they have heard from neighbours or relatives.

It helps that the local community is proud of their health centre’s competence and reliability. When mountain storms knock the village’s power out, the clinic’s lights – and crucially, its vaccine fridge – stay on. A solar energy system makes sure of that. According to Tursunova, even some clinics in Uzbekistan’s capital cannot boast such a system.

Tursunova, meantime, is quite as dependable. She has worked with the local children for eight years in steady, dependable service of a simple goal: parents should not leave the clinic having simply followed an instruction. They should leave understanding why they made that choice for their child.

“When a mother understands what the vaccine protects her child from, she no longer needs to be persuaded. She makes the decision herself.”

Dermatology Volume 13 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1949400 Case Report: Successful treatment of verruciform acanthotic vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia with 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy YQ Yitao Qian WZ Wenjing Zha JS Jie Shen KL Ke Li SC Szeman Cheung Yiwu Yu JH Jianhua Huang TL Ting Lyu Fei Miao HW Hongwei Wang +2 more Lei Shi * Department of Dermatology, Shanghai Key Laboratory of Clinical Geriatric Medicine, and Shanghai Institute of Geriatric Medicine, Huadong Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai, China Article metrics View details 340 Views 23 Downloads Abstract Verruciform acanthotic vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (vaVIN) is a rare, human papillomavirus (HPV)-independent, p53 wild-type intraepithelial precursor of the vulva, and standardized therapies for this disease are currently lacking. We report the case of a 68-year-old woman who presented with a 2-year history of multiple warty papules and vulvar pruritus and was diagnosed with vaVIN on the basis of histopathology (verruciform acanthosis with compact orthokeratosis, hypogranulosis, and superficial keratinocyte pallor with minimal cytologic atypia) and immunohistochemistry (HPV negativity, a p53 wild-type pattern, and non-block p16 expression) analyses. She underwent 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy (ALA-PDT) and achieved complete clinical remission, with no recurrence during the follow-up period. To our knowledge, reports on the use of photodynamic therapy for vaVIN are scarce. This case suggests that ALA-PDT may be a promising alternative treatment option for vaVIN. Introduction Verruciform acanthotic vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (vaVIN) is an uncommon, human papillomavirus (HPV)-independent verruciform intraepithelial disease of the vulva characterized by acanthotic and/or verruciform architecture, altered squamous differentiation, minimal cytologic atypia, wild-type p53 expression, and negative or patchy p16 staining (1). Clinically, vaVIN presents as solitary plaques or exophytic warty lesions. Despite typically subtle cytologic atypia, vaVIN is a precursor of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (VSCC) with a reported 10-year progression risk of approximately 28%; moreover, morphologic or molecular overlap with verrucous carcinoma suggests a spectrum in a subset of patients (2). Because of its rarity and deceptively subtle histology, vaVIN is often underrecognized, and high-quality therapeutic evidence remains limited. Current management is largely extrapolated and not standardized; complete excision is still commonly recommended. However, postoperative recurrence rates can reach up to 44%, necessitating long-term surveillance and highlighting the urgent need to explore alternative therapeutic strategies. Here, we report a case of successful treatment of vaVIN with 5-aminolevulinic acid–based photodynamic therapy (ALA-PDT), suggesting its therapeutic potential as an alternative for vulvar precursors and cancers. Case presentation A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 2-year history of vulvar pruritus. A physical examination revealed a whitish plaque adjacent to the labium majus, with multiple verrucous, papillomatous papules on its surface, accompanied by scaling and peripheral hyperpigmentation (Figure 1A). The initial differential diagnoses included condyloma acuminatum and vulvar lichen sclerosus. Further history taking revealed that the patient was otherwise healthy, with no relevant sexual exposure or a family history of the disease. Given the markedly different therapeutic implications of these diagnoses, a biopsy of the verrucous lesion was performed. Histopathological results revealed a marked verruciform acanthosis of the epidermis with exophytic papillomatosis, compact orthokeratosis with focal parakeratosis, attenuation of the granular layer, and cytoplasmic pallor of keratinocytes in the superficial spinous layer. No significant nuclear atypia was identified, and there was a minimal lymphocytic infiltrate in the superficial dermis (Figures 2A,B). The result of immunohistochemical staining for HPV was negative (Figures 2C,D). A further immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated a wild-type p53 staining pattern confined predominantly to the basal layer and non-block-type p16 positivity (Figures 2E–H). Collectively, these clinicopathological and immunohistochemical findings supported a diagnosis of vaVIN. Figure 1 (A) Exophytic verruciform papules emerging within a localized white atrophic plaque adjacent to the labia majora. (B) After four treatment sessions, the papules had diminished, leaving a residual white patch. (C) Following all nine treatment sessions, both the white patch and papules had resolved, and the previously affected area became clear and smooth. Figure 2 Histopathology and immunohistochemistry analyses. (A, 4×; B, 20×) Representative hematoxylin–eosin (H&E) staining images showing verruciform acanthosis with hypogranulosis and no significant atypia. (C, 4×; D, 20×) The result of a HPV immunohistochemistry test was negative. (E, 4×; F, 20×) p53 immunohistochemistry showed predominantly basal nuclear positivity (wild-type pattern). (G, 4×; H, 20×) p16 immunohistochemistry exhibited patchy, non-block positivity. Given that the patient strongly declined surgery and preferred a tissue-sparing approach, ALA-PDT was selected as a conservative treatment. The treatment regimen was based on previously reported ALA-PDT protocols for vulvar squamous neoplasia, including VSCC and HPV-associated high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSILs). The initial two sessions of ALA-PDT were performed once weekly, followed by seven sessions at 2-week intervals. During each session, ALA hydrochloride topical powder (118 mg/bottle, Fudan-Zhangjiang Bio-Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) was used to prepare 20% ALA cream and was applied to the lesion under occlusion for 3 h, followed by irradiation with 635-nm red light at an irradiance of 80 mW/cm2 and a fluence of 144 J/cm2. Pain was assessed during illumination using a numerical rating scale (NRS; 0–10). A modified painless PDT was available as an alternative if the pain became intolerable. However, all NRS scores remained below 6, and the patient considered the pain tolerable; therefore, the patient did not require treatment interruption or conversion to the modified painless PDT protocol. Her vulvar pruritus reduced substantially during treatment, accompanied by progressive flattening and regression of the verrucous papules (Figure 1B). After nine treatment sessions, complete clinical resolution of both the papules and the underlying plaque was achieved, with restoration of a smooth, nearly normal-appearing skin surface (Figure 1C). No clinical recurrence was observed during 9 months of initial post-treatment follow-up, and in the most recent remote follow-up (3 years after treatment), assessment of patient-provided photographs showed no evident clinical recurrence. The patient remained symptom-free and reported marked satisfaction with the treatment outcome and improvement in her quality of life. Discussion VaVIN shares morphologic features with several benign vulvar dermatoses and with other VSCC precursors, making careful clinicopathologic evaluation essential. Benign entities such as lichen simplex chronicus, psoriasis, and pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia typically present as diffuse, lichenoid flat plaques rather than as exophytic warty papules and lack the combination of superficial keratinocyte cytoplasmic pallor and hypogranulosis seen in vaVIN. Condyloma acuminatum is another common mimic. It is an exophytic verrucous lesion with koilocytosis and generally preserved basal maturation and is HPV-positive, thereby helping distinguish it from vaVIN. Among malignant precursors, the VSCC spectrum comprises HSIL and HPV-independent lesions, with the latter subdivided by TP53 status into differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (dVIN; usually TP53-mutant) and vaVIN (TP53 wild type). These conditions can be distinguished by their morphology and immunophenotype: HSIL (especially Bowenoid papulosis and warty/basaloid variants) shows full-thickness atypia with block-type p16 positivity, and dVIN features basal or parabasal atypia with aberrant p53 staining (basal or diffuse overexpression, complete null pattern, or cytoplasmic staining). In contrast, vaVIN is HPV-negative, exhibits a p53 wild-type pattern (either scattered, heterogeneous nuclear staining in basal/parabasal layers or a mid-epithelial strong pattern with basal sparing), and shows p16 negativity or only patchy, non-block positivity (2, 3). By analogy with related vulvar precancers and VSCC, ALA-PDT can be a rational therapeutic option for vaVIN (4, 5). Mechanistically, proliferating lesional keratinocytes preferentially accumulate protoporphyrin IX after ALA application, and subsequent red-light activation generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) that directly ablate these lesional cells. Beyond cytotoxicity, PDT orchestrates robust innate and adaptive immunity: neutrophils are rapidly recruited and activated (adhesion molecule upregulation and complement engagement); macrophages are stimulated by damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) such as Hsp70, leading to proinflammatory cytokine release; and enhanced expression of MHC-I and NKG2D ligands augments natural killer (NK) cell activity and CD4+/CD8+ T-cell–mediated cytotoxicity (6). These molecular and immunological mechanisms may underlie the clinical efficacy of PDT. Pain during illumination is the main adverse effect of ALA-PDT. To reduce treatment-related pain, we previously developed a modified painless PDT, which significantly reduced pain, while maintaining clinical efficacy in the treatment of condyloma acuminatum and acne (7, 8). However, given the premalignant nature of vaVIN and the potential uncertainty regarding efficacy associated with a shortened ALA incubation period, we adopted conventional ALA-PDT parameters in the present case as a cautious approach, with the modified painless protocol reserved for intolerable pain. Further studies are needed to determine the efficacy, safety, and optimal ALA-PDT parameters for vaVIN. This study has several limitations. First, only a single patient was reported. To further establish ALA-PDT as an alternative treatment for vaVIN, its efficacy and safety must be evaluated in larger case series and well-designed clinical studies. Second, although no evident clinical recurrence was identified during the initial in-person follow-up or subsequent remote follow-up, histological clearance could not be confirmed because the patient declined a post-treatment biopsy. Vulvar precancerous lesions such as vaVIN carry a potential risk for recurrence and progression. Therefore, patients require long-term, regular clinical surveillance, with prompt biopsy of any persistent, recurrent, or suspicious lesion. Conclusion In summary, this patient case suggests that ALA-PDT may be a feasible tissue-sparing option for carefully selected patients with vaVIN. Further studies are warranted to confirm its efficacy and elucidate the underlying mechanisms. Don't Waste Your Money Team Contests America 250 Events LifestyleHealth and Fitness Actions Facebook Tweet Email Millions of cancer cases may be prevented by fighting infections Prev Next Photo by: CI Photos/Shutterstock Gene Therapy for Cancer Treatment Concept Cancer therapy with T-cell and pipette By: Kelly Broderick Posted 4:37 PM, Oct 06, 2026 and last updated 4:40 PM, Oct 06, 2026 A new study published in The Lancet Oncology estimates that 2.3 million cancer cases worldwide in 2024 were attributable to infections. That's roughly 1 in every 8 cancer cases. Researchers found that the infections linked to the largest number of cancer cases are ones that can often be prevented, screened for, treated, or managed. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE "This recent Lancet data is a profound reminder that a significant portion of our global cancer burden is fundamentally preventable," said David Greenberg, M.D., medical director of hematology oncology at Hackensack Meridian Jersey Shore University Medical Center and a hematologist-oncologist at Ocean University Medical Center. RELATED STORY | Most women know breast cancer risks, yet they're not acting on them "We have historically siloed infectious diseases and oncology, but they are deeply intertwined. By shifting our focus toward aggressive infection control, we can literally vaccinate and treat our way out of millions of future cancer diagnoses." One example is H. pylori, or Helicobacter pylori, a common bacterial infection that can lead to stomach cancer and has also been linked to an increased risk of colorectal cancer. The infection can spread through saliva or contaminated food and water. It is treatable with antibiotics and medications that reduce stomach acid. Researchers estimated that 760,000 cancer cases worldwide were attributable to H. pylori, making it the leading infection-related cause of cancer in the study. Infectious disease specialist Alex Lazo-Vasquez, M.D., added that hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections can go unnoticed for decades before eventually leading to liver cancer. HPV is another major contributor. The virus can cause several cancers, including cervical cancer in women and penile cancer in men. "Fortunately, we have the tools to protect ourselves. Hepatitis B and HPV are vaccine-preventable, and hepatitis C is now curable with a short course of antiviral medication," Lazo-Vasquez said. "Unfortunately, we are still losing lives to cancers that could potentially be prevented because we are not prioritizing early viral screening and vaccination." A new study from Senegal, published in PLOS Global Public Health, offers a quantitative explanation for one of the most stubborn barriers: stigma. Researchers led by Fatou Bintou Seck and colleagues found that women who reported higher levels of cervical cancer–related stigma were significantly less likely to have ever been screened for the disease, a finding that could reshape how screening programs are designed in West Africa and beyond. The research team conducted a quantitative descriptive and analytical cross-sectional study in two of Senegal’s regions, Dakar and Kédougou, a pairing that is geographically and socially striking. Dakar is the country’s densely populated coastal capital, home to major hospitals and clinics, while Kédougou is a remote southeastern region near the Guinean border, where health infrastructure is thinner and travel to facilities can be arduous. By studying both settings, the investigators aimed to capture how stigma operates across very different social and logistical landscapes within a single nation. The study population consisted of women aged 25 to 69, the age range in which cervical cancer screening is generally recommended because it spans the decades when infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, the causative agent of nearly all cervical cancers, is most likely to progress to precancerous lesions and, if untreated, invasive cancer. Participants were recruited through a two-stage cluster sampling methodology, a design in which larger units such as neighborhoods or villages are selected first and individual households or respondents are sampled within them. This approach is well suited to community-based surveys in settings where complete population registries are unavailable. Discover more Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Cancer cancer From the sample, 287 women had complete data on their screening status. The numbers were sobering: only 15.7 percent reported having undergone one or more cervical cancer screenings in the past. The mean age of participants was 36.23 years, and the majority, 68.6 percent, were married and living in monogamous households. In other words, even in the capital region, where screening services physically exist, fewer than one in six women had ever taken advantage of them. That gap between availability and uptake is precisely the puzzle the study set out to solve. The methodological heart of the paper is a newly constructed stigma index, developed specifically for this Senegalese context. Rather than relying on instruments imported wholesale from other settings, the researchers built a composite measure whose items covered several domains previously shown to be powerful predictors of stigma in the health psychology literature. These domains typically encompass anticipated stigma, such as fear of being judged by health workers or neighbors; internalized shame associated with a cancer in a reproductive organ; and perceived social isolation or blame directed at women with the disease. By scoring responses across these dimensions, the team produced a single, quantifiable stigma value for each participant, allowing stigma to enter statistical models as a measurable exposure rather than a vague narrative concept. The analysis was performed with R version 4.5.0, and the investigators used logistic regression with a significance threshold of 5 percent to test whether stigma scores predicted screening behavior. Logistic regression is the standard tool for modeling binary outcomes, in this case whether a woman had ever been screened or not, and it yields an odds ratio that expresses how a one-unit change in the predictor shifts the odds of the outcome. Crucially, the researchers adjusted their models for age, marital status, and education level, three factors that could plausibly confound the relationship between stigma and screening by independently influencing both attitudes and health care use. The result was clear and statistically robust. After adjustment, higher stigma scores were associated with lower odds of screening, with an odds ratio of 0.58 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.38 to 0.83, and a p-value of 0.006. In practical terms, women with higher stigma were roughly 42 percent less likely to have been screened than women with lower stigma, holding age, marital status, and education constant. Because the entire confidence interval lies below 1, the association is unlikely to be a statistical fluke, although as with any cross-sectional study, causality cannot be definitively established. It remains possible that women who avoid screening also develop more stigmatizing attitudes, or that unmeasured factors influence both. Discover more Health Study Biology Biology Health research findings Electronic health records Why would stigma suppress screening so powerfully? The biology of cervical cancer offers a clue. Screening typically involves a pelvic examination and, in many low-resource programs, visual inspection of the cervix with acetic acid or HPV testing of a self-collected or clinician-collected sample. The intimate nature of the procedure, combined with the fact that cervical cancer is linked to a sexually transmitted virus, can make women fear that seeking screening will invite accusations of promiscuity, suspicion from husbands, or gossip in the community. A diagnosis of precancerous lesions, even though it is highly treatable, may be perceived socially as a mark of shame. Stigma thus transforms a routine preventive visit into a perceived social risk, and many women rationally choose to avoid it. The Senegalese findings arrive against a global backdrop of urgency. The World Health Organization has launched a global strategy to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem, built on three pillars: vaccination against HPV, screening with high-coverage targets, and prompt treatment of detected lesions. Countries are asked to screen a large proportion of eligible women at regular intervals. Yet uptake in much of sub-Saharan Africa remains far below those targets, and studies like this one demonstrate that building clinics and training providers, while essential, is not sufficient. Psychological and social barriers can throttle demand even when supply exists, which is why the authors argue that a better understanding of stigma is needed to adapt anti-cancer strategies to the realities of the communities they serve. The study’s authors point to patient navigation as a promising response. Navigation programs assign trained personnel, often community members themselves, to guide women through the screening pathway: explaining the procedure, addressing fears, arranging appointments and transport, and following up on results. By inserting a trusted intermediary between the woman and the health system, navigation can dismantle the stigma barrier along with logistical obstacles such as distance, cost, and long waiting times. The stigma index developed in this study is presented as a novel, adaptable tool that can be used in future research, including the evaluation of whether stigma actually declines after a navigation intervention is implemented. If subsequent trials confirm that reducing stigma raises screening rates, Senegal’s experience could offer a template for other countries racing toward the elimination goal: measure the stigma, then design programs that dissolve it. supplementary_news.content_title: Clinicopathological Analysis of 1,000 Cases of Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma With Special Emphasis on Histological Variants and p16 Expression
supplementary_news.content: Abstract Background: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) remains a major clinical and pathological concern in India. Its presentation varies by anatomical site and histological pattern, and recognizing uncommon variants, along with the appropriate interpretation of p16 expression, may provide useful diagnostic information. Objective: This study aimed to describe the demographic and clinicopathological profile of 1,000 HNSCC cases, with particular attention to histological variants, cervical lymph node involvement, and p16 expression. Materials and methods: This retrospective observational study included 1,000 histologically confirmed HNSCC cases diagnosed at a tertiary-care teaching hospital between January 2023 and December 2024. Age, sex, tumor site, histological grade, nodal status, histological variants, recurrence, and second primary malignancies were reviewed. p16 immunohistochemistry was performed in 109 cases with suitable tissue, including 50 conventional SCCs and 59 histological variants. Strong, diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic staining in more than 70% of tumor cells was considered positive. Results: The cohort included 832 men and 168 women, with most patients aged 51-70 years. The oral tongue was the most frequent individual site (24.7%), while supraglottic and glottic tumors together accounted for 29.4% of cases. Well-differentiated SCC was the predominant grade (71.0%). Cervical lymph node metastasis was present in 147 patients (14.7%), with the highest within-grade frequency in moderately differentiated SCC (20.4%); the association between histological grade and nodal metastasis was significant (χ2 = 9.89, p = 0.007). Of the 59 histological variants, 32 (54.2%) were p16 positive, with papillary SCC accounting for most positive cases. Of the 50 conventional SCCs, 20 (40.0%) showed p16 positivity. Twenty-five patients had second primary malignancies, and 16 had recurrence. Conclusions: This large single-center series demonstrates the clinicopathological diversity of HNSCC in an Indian tertiary-care setting. Histological variant recognition and assessment of nodal involvement remain important components of pathological evaluation. p16 immunohistochemistry may provide useful supplementary information in selected cases, but its expression should be interpreted as a surrogate marker rather than definitive evidence of HPV-driven disease without molecular confirmation. Introduction Head and neck cancers remain an important cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide. According to GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates from the International Agency for Research on Cancer, cancers of the lip and oral cavity accounted for 389,846 new cases and 188,438 deaths globally. During the same period, laryngeal cancer accounted for 189,191 new cases and 103,359 deaths, while approximately 120,434 cases of nasopharyngeal cancer and 86,257 cases of hypopharyngeal cancer were reported worldwide [1]. The burden is particularly relevant to India, where lip and oral cavity cancer was the most frequently diagnosed cancer among men in 2022, with an estimated 107,812 new cases [1]. More than 90% of malignant tumors arising from the mucosal surfaces of the oral cavity, pharynx, and larynx are squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) [2]. Despite improvements in surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic treatment, late presentation, locoregional recurrence, and second primary malignancies continue to influence the clinical course of head and neck SCC (HNSCC) [3]. The distribution and etiological profile of HNSCC vary considerably across geographical regions. In South and Southeast Asia, including India, tobacco smoking, smokeless tobacco, use of areca nut and betel quid, and alcohol consumption are well-established contributors to the high burden of oral and other head and neck cancers [4,5]. These exposures are particularly relevant as background epidemiological factors in the Indian population, although they were not the primary focus of the present clinicopathological analysis. In contrast, the incidence of HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC has increased substantially in several Western populations, with HPV-16 accounting for most HPV-driven tumors at this site [6]. HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma is now recognized as a biologically distinct disease with differences in treatment response and prognosis compared with conventional tobacco-related HNSCC [7]. Clinical presentation varies by anatomical site and disease extent. Patients may present with a persistent oral ulcer, dysphagia, change in voice, throat discomfort, or cervical lymphadenopathy, and some tumors are first diagnosed at an advanced stage [8]. Histopathological examination therefore remains central to diagnosis and tumor characterization. Although conventional SCC forms the largest group, HNSCC includes several less common histological variants with distinctive microscopic appearances and, in some instances, different biological behavior and prognostic implications [9]. Correct recognition of these variants is consequently important during routine pathological evaluation. Assessment of HPV-related disease has also become increasingly relevant, particularly in oropharyngeal SCC. p16 immunohistochemistry is widely used as a practical surrogate marker of HPV-associated carcinogenesis; however, p16 overexpression does not by itself establish the presence of transcriptionally active HPV, especially in tumors arising outside the oropharynx. Its findings should therefore be interpreted together with tumor site, morphology, and, where clinically required, HPV-specific molecular testing [10]. This distinction is particularly important when examining p16 expression across different anatomical sites and uncommon histological variants. Large single-center series describing the clinicopathological spectrum of HNSCC, including histological variants and p16 findings, remain relatively limited in India. This study aimed to describe the demographic and clinicopathological spectrum of 1,000 HNSCC cases, with particular attention to histological variants and p16 expression. Materials & Methods Study design and setting This retrospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Pathology, Government ENT Hospital, Osmania Medical College, Hyderabad, India. The study included patients with histologically confirmed HNSCC diagnosed between January 2023 and December 2024. The unit of analysis was the individual patient with histologically confirmed HNSCC. The study primarily described the demographic and clinicopathological profile of HNSCC, with additional evaluation of histological variants, cervical lymph node involvement, and p16 immunohistochemical expression. Ethical approval The Institutional Ethics Committee and Biomedical and Health Research Committee of Osmania Medical College approved the study protocol (approval number: IEC/OMC/M.NO (18)/P-192, dated June 8, 2026). As this was a retrospective study, the analysis was based on previously diagnosed cases, existing clinical records, pathology reports, and archived pathological material. The study required no additional investigations, treatment procedures, specimen collection, or direct patient contact. All identifying information was removed before analysis, and patient confidentiality was maintained throughout. In accordance with the approved retrospective study protocol, separate study-specific informed consent was not applicable. Case identification and eligibility criteria A census-based sampling approach was used rather than calculating a predetermined sample size. All consecutive histologically confirmed HNSCC cases diagnosed during the two-year study period were screened for eligibility. A total of 1,000 cases satisfying the study criteria were included in the final analysis. Eligible cases comprised primary SCCs arising from the oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, and other included mucosal head and neck sites. Cases were excluded when the available material was inadequate for histopathological assessment, paraffin blocks were poorly preserved, or essential clinical or pathological information required for the analysis was unavailable. Each patient was assigned to one primary anatomical site for analysis. Recurrent tumors and second primary malignancies were identified from the available clinical and pathology records and recorded separately. These events were described as additional clinical outcomes and were not counted as new independent primary cases within the principal 1,000-case analysis. Data collection and variable definitions Clinical and pathological information was retrieved from hospital case records, pathology requisition forms, archived histopathology reports, and available laboratory records. Variables included age, sex, primary anatomical site, histological grade, histological variant, cervical lymph node status, recurrence, second primary malignancy, and p16 immunohistochemical expression when tested. Age was grouped into predefined categories for descriptive analysis. Anatomical sites were coded as mutually exclusive categories so that each patient contributed to only one primary-site group. Histological grade was classified as well differentiated, moderately differentiated, or poorly differentiated. For the principal statistical analysis, cervical lymph node status was recorded from available clinical and pathological documentation as either nodal involvement present or absent. Some records included information on tobacco use, smokeless tobacco, alcohol consumption, areca nut, and related exposures, but these data were not recorded consistently across the cohort. Reliable definitions of duration, dose, frequency, and combined exposure could therefore not be applied consistently. Consequently, we excluded risk-factor variables from the quantitative analysis rather than treating them as complete exposure data. Cases with missing information for variables essential to inclusion were excluded during case selection. For variables available only in defined subsets, such as p16 immunohistochemistry, analyses were restricted to cases with recorded results. No statistical imputation of missing values was performed. Histopathological review and analysis Archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue blocks and corresponding histological sections were reviewed. Sections of approximately 3-5 μm thickness were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and examined by light microscopy. Conventional SCC was diagnosed on the basis of standard squamous differentiation and was categorized as well differentiated, moderately differentiated, or poorly differentiated according to established histomorphological criteria. Tumors were also reviewed for recognized histological variants using the applicable World Health Organization classification criteria for head and neck tumors. The histological variants in this series included papillary SCC, verrucous carcinoma, basaloid SCC, spindle cell/sarcomatoid carcinoma, acantholytic SCC, non-keratinizing SCC, and non-keratinizing undifferentiated carcinoma of nasopharyngeal type. Variant classification was based on the characteristic microscopic architecture and cytomorphological features identified on H&E-stained sections. Ascertainment of cervical lymph node status Cervical lymph node involvement was determined from the clinical and pathological information available in the medical record and pathology documentation. For the principal analysis examining the relationship between histological grade and nodal spread, lymph node metastasis was coded as a binary outcome: present or absent. When information on the side or distribution of nodal involvement was available, we retained these findings for descriptive assessment. Selection of cases for p16 immunohistochemistry p16 immunohistochemistry was performed in a defined subset of 109 cases from the main 1,000-case cohort. This group comprised 59 histological variant cases and 50 conventional SCC cases. The 109 cases were not selected because they were already known to be p16-positive, nor were they randomly sampled from the entire cohort. Selection was based on histological morphology and the availability of adequate, well-preserved formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue suitable for immunohistochemical staining. Histological variant cases were included when sufficient tissue was available for p16 assessment. The conventional SCC subset included 40 well-differentiated, eight moderately differentiated, and two poorly differentiated tumors selected from archived cases with suitable tissue. The remaining cases in the overall cohort were not tested because p16 immunohistochemistry was not routinely performed in every HNSCC case during the study period, and appropriate archived tissue was not uniformly available. The p16-tested group should therefore be regarded as an availability-based pathological subset rather than a random or population-representative sample. p16 immunohistochemistry Immunohistochemical staining for p16 was performed on selected formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections using a commercially available monoclonal antibody against p16 (Biogenex) and an avidin-biotin-based detection method. Appropriate positive and negative controls were included with each staining run. Stained sections were evaluated for both nuclear and cytoplasmic immunoreactivity. A case was considered p16 positive when strong, diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic staining involved more than 70% of tumor cells. Cases showing absent, focal, weak, or patchy staining below this threshold were classified as negative. Because HPV-specific molecular testing, such as HPV DNA testing, RNA in situ hybridization, or E6/E7 mRNA analysis, was not performed, p16 immunoreactivity was interpreted as a surrogate marker rather than direct confirmation of HPV-driven carcinogenesis. This distinction was particularly relevant for tumors arising outside the oropharynx. Statistical analysis Data were entered into Excel (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA, USA) and analyzed using SPSS Statistics version 25.0 (IBM Corp. Released 2017. IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 25.0. Armonk, NY). Descriptive statistics were used for the principal clinicopathological variables. Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages, while age was presented using predefined age categories. Associations between categorical variables were assessed using the Pearson chi-square test when expected cell frequencies were adequate. Fisher’s exact test was used when sparse cell counts made the chi-square approximation inappropriate. All statistical tests were two-sided, and a p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. For the analysis of histological grade and cervical lymph node metastasis, lymph node metastasis was defined as the outcome variable, while histological grade was the exposure variable. Well-differentiated SCC served as the reference category. Unadjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated for comparisons involving moderately differentiated and poorly differentiated SCC. No multivariable regression model was performed. Results Age and sex distribution Among the 1,000 patients with HNSCC, 832 were men and 168 were women, giving a male-to-female ratio of approximately 4.9:1. The largest proportion of patients was in the 51-60-year age group (29.0%), followed by 61-70 years (22.6%) and 41-50 years (22.0%). Patients aged 31-40 years accounted for 14.0% of the cohort, while 6.0% were aged 21-30 years and 6.4% were older than 70 years. Overall, most cases occurred between 41 and 70 years of age, with a clear male predominance across the age groups. Anatomical site distribution Table 1 shows the anatomical distribution of the 1,000 HNSCC cases. The oral tongue was the most frequently involved individual site, accounting for 247 cases (24.7%). This was followed by the supraglottis (162 cases; 16.2%), buccal mucosa (159 cases; 15.9%), and glottis (132 cases; 13.2%). Hypopharyngeal tumors accounted for 110 cases (11.0%). Less frequently involved sites were the alveolus/gingiva (6.4%), oropharynx (5.9%), floor of mouth (3.5%), and nasopharynx (3.2%). When grouped by region, oral cavity tumors formed the largest category, while supraglottic and glottic tumors together represented 29.4% of the cohort. Histological grade and cervical lymph node metastasis Of the 1,000 HNSCC cases, 710 (71.0%) were well differentiated, 245 (24.5%) were moderately differentiated, and 45 (4.5%) were poorly differentiated. Cervical lymph node metastasis was identified in 147 patients, corresponding to an overall nodal metastasis rate of 14.7%. The proportion of patients with nodal metastasis differed significantly across histological grades (χ2 = 9.89, df = 2, p = 0.007). Lymph node involvement was present in 94 of 710 well-differentiated tumors (13.2%), 50 of 245 moderately differentiated tumors (20.4%), and three of 45 poorly differentiated tumors (6.7%). Using well-differentiated SCC as the reference category, moderately differentiated SCC was associated with higher odds of cervical lymph node metastasis (OR = 1.68, 95% CI 1.15-2.45; p = 0.007). Poorly differentiated SCC showed lower observed odds of nodal involvement (OR = 0.47, 95% CI 0.14-1.54), but this difference was not statistically significant (Fisher’s exact p = 0.255) (Table 2). The finding in the poorly differentiated group should be interpreted cautiously because only three patients in this category had nodal metastasis. p16 expression in 59 histological variant cases A total of 59 histological variant cases were evaluated by p16 immunohistochemistry. Of these, 32 (54.2%) were p16 positive and 27 (45.8%) were negative. Papillary SCC was the largest subgroup, comprising 32 cases, of which 28 (87.5%) showed p16 positivity. supplementary_news.content_title: Reduced-Dose Radiation Cuts Patient-Reported Toxicity in HPV-Related Oropharyngeal Cancer
supplementary_news.content: Your Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More Video Events Specialties Topics RegisterLog In Medscape Medical NewsMedBrief Medbrief Reduced-Dose Radiation Cuts Patient-Reported Toxicity in HPV-Related Oropharyngeal Cancer October 05, 2026 0 TOPLINE Among patients with human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) who had a complete response to induction chemotherapy, those who received reduced-dose intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) reported significantly less difficulty swallowing and less voice impairment than those who received standard-dose IMRT, per the phase 2 E1308 trial. Disease-specific patient-reported outcome (PRO) tools detected these differences more reliably than general quality-of-life measures. A historical comparison with the earlier E2399 trial supported similar reductions in toxicity with IMRT vs three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy (3DRT). METHODOLOGY A phase 2 trial, E2399, showed that HPV-positive oropharynx cancer responds well to chemoradiation, raising the possibility of reducing treatment intensity without compromising cure rates. Because high-dose radiation drives most acute and long-term toxicity, the follow-up E1308 trial tested whether a response to induction chemotherapy could guide the use of lower-dose IMRT. This prospective phase 2 trial (ECOG-ACRIN E1308) evaluated reduced-dose IMRT of 54 Gy against standard-dose IMRT of 69.3 Gy in patients with HPV-associated OPSCC who achieved a complete clinical response to induction chemotherapy. A total of 80 patients were treated in E1308; 62 of 80 (78%) achieved a complete response to induction chemotherapy with paclitaxel, cisplatin, and cetuximab and received 54 Gy, while the remainder received 69.3 Gy. Fifty-one patients who remained progression-free at 12 months (42 patients who received 54 Gy and nine patients who received 69.3 Gy) were evaluated for PROs. Researchers assessed disease-specific symptom burden using the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Head & Neck (FACT-HN) and the Vanderbilt Head and Neck Symptom Survey Version 2 (VHNSSv2) and general quality of life using the Katz Index of Independence in Activities of Daily Living (ADL), Brief Fatigue Index (BFI), Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL), Baecke physical activity scale, and Community Health Activities Model Program for Seniors (CHAMPS) questionnaire. All measures were administered at baseline and at 6, 12, 24, and 30 months post-treatment. Toxicity outcomes in E1308 were compared historically with those of 69 patients treated in the earlier E2399 trial who received induction chemotherapy followed by 3DRT at 70 Gy over 7 weeks with concurrent weekly paclitaxel. TAKEAWAY At 6 months, VHNSSv2 scores indicated that reduced-dose IMRT eased swallowing of solids (P = .011) and liquids (P = .004), voice impairment (P = .026), dry mouth (P = .02), and neck/shoulder movement limitations (P = .03) compared with standard-dose IMRT. FACT-HN scores indicated that the reduced-dose IMRT group had less difficulty eating solid foods at 6 months (P = .054) and better voice strength and quality (P = .038) than the standard-dose group. Comparing reduced-dose IMRT (54 Gy) in E1308 with 3DRT (70 Gy) in E2399, FACT-HN scores showed that IMRT was associated with better ability to eat solid food at 12 months (P = .0103) and greater ability to eat preferred foods (P = .0067). Additionally, patients who received 3DRT had higher rates of grade ≥ 3 oral mucositis (58% vs 29%; P = .0003), dysphagia (39% vs 15%; P = .001), and esophagitis (8% vs 0%; P = .023) than those who received reduced-dose IMRT. General quality-of-life tools — CHAMPS, Katz ADL, BFI, IADL, and Baecke — did not detect significant reductions in toxicity or differences in function or fatigue between the dose groups. IN PRACTICE "Our data from the first prospective study of radiation dose reduction in treatment responsive HPV-associated oropharynx cancer demonstrate a statistically significantly less worsening of swallowing dysfunction and voice impairment for patients treated with reduced-dose IMRT based on disease-specific VHNSSv2 and FACT-HN instruments at 6 months post-treatment. This supports our initial hypothesis that reducing radiation dose and duration will reduce chronic symptom burden and has spawned a plethora of additional deintensification paradigms in ongoing clinical trials," the authors concluded. SOURCE The study, led by Anthony J. Cmelak, MD, Vanderbilt University/Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville, Tennessee, was published online in JCO Oncology Advances. LIMITATIONS Small standard-dose cohorts and declining PRO completion at later time points limited statistical power. Comparisons were not randomized, with E2399 including both HPV-positive and HPV-negative patients, introducing heterogeneity. Historical 3DRT-vs-IMRT comparisons also reflected inherent technical differences between the two radiation approaches beyond dose alone. DISCLOSURES This study was supported by the ECOG-ACRIN Cancer Research Group and grants from the National Cancer Institute of the National Institutes of Health. Several authors reported consulting, research funding, employment, leadership, or ownership ties to pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies, including Merck, AstraZeneca, Regeneron, Takeda, and others. Full disclosures are noted in the original article. This article was created using several editorial tools, including AI, as part of the process. Human editors reviewed this content before publication. 0 Comments Commenting is limited to medical professionals. To comment please . Please see our Commenting Guide for further information. We reserve the right to remove posts at our sole discretion. Pregnancy HPV Vaccine May Have Benefits Beyond Cancer Protection You can still access 2 more articles for free. - HPV vaccination may reduce pregnancy complications - Women vaccinated against HPV had lower risks of preterm birth, early rupture of the amniotic sac and having a very small baby - Women vaccinated before age 17 showed stronger benefits THURSDAY, Oct. 8, 2026 (HealthDay News) — The HPV vaccine is best known for protecting against cervical cancer. But, it may have another major benefit: reducing the risk of serious pregnancy complications. A team led by Zhongsong Zhang, of the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, conducted a large study that looked at more than 624,000 first-time births. About 93,000 of the women had been vaccinated against human papillomavirus, HPV — a common, sexually transmitted infection that can cause precancerous and cancerous changes. Those who were vaccinated had lower odds of several complications, including preterm and very preterm birth, the amniotic sac rupturing too early, and having a severely small baby. The link was generally stronger among women vaccinated before age 17. They had about 10% lower odds of preterm birth and 11% lower odds of spontaneous preterm birth. Researchers said vaccination may help by preventing HPV infection and reducing the need for procedures to remove abnormal cervical tissue. These procedures have been linked to a higher risk of preterm birth. Because this was an observational study, it can't prove cause and effect. But researchers say the study's large size, high-quality data and long follow-up strengthen the findings. "Our results suggest that human papillomavirus vaccination is not only safe with respect to pregnancy outcomes but may also confer additional benefits by reducing the risk of adverse events," they said in a news release. The findings were published Oct. 7 in The BMJ. More information The Cleveland Clinic has more on the human papillomavirus. SOURCE: HealthDay TV, Oct. 8, 2026 The HPV vaccine may not only protect against cervical cancer but also reduce the risk of serious pregnancy complications, especially when given at a younger age. www.healthday.com
