supplementary_news.content_title: Cancer screening in LGBTQIA populations
supplementary_news.content: Advertising Volume 55, Issue 10, October 2026 Cancer screening in LGBTQIA+ populations Matthew J Ruhl Background Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer/questioning, intersex and asexual/aromantic (LGBTQIA+, the plus referring to other sexuality and gender diverse groups) peoples in Australia experience lower levels of cancer screening and preventive activities when compared with the general population. This is especially the case for transgender and gender diverse (TGD) peoples, who experience additional barriers to access and discrimination above the rest of LGBTQIA+ peoples. Objective This article seeks to enhance cancer screening engagement among LGBTQIA+ individuals by addressing underscreening within these populations and offering strategies for improvement within primary care, including specific examples relevant to TGD peoples. Discussion Enhanced, individualised patient assessment, education and practitioner recommendations for cancer screening and prevention – supported by practitioner upskilling, LGBTQIA+ inclusivity training and the development of safer healthcare environments – may increase participation in screening programs, ultimately leading to earlier detection and better cancer outcomes. Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer/questioning, intersex, asexual/aromantic and other sexuality and gender diverse (LGBTQIA+) populations (noting some peoples are not well included in the literature and may not feel well aligned with the acronym, such as intersex peoples) experience healthcare differently to the wider population, with heteronormativity, minority stress, discrimination, uncertainties in finding safe spaces and practitioners, and other systemic and individual barriers, all influenced by intersectionality.1,2 Intersectionality is a term coined to describe the multiple overlapping and multiplying oppressions faced by many individuals,3 which might, for example, include gender, sexuality, ethnicity, disability and so on, and may further contribute to screening barriers. For transgender and gender diverse (TGD) peoples, there is insufficient evidence as yet to determine the effect of gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT) on long-term cancer risks.4–6 Many guidelines, including those regarding cancer screening and prevention, are based on large population studies that either do not include or do not acknowledge LGBTQIA+ individuals, making clear guidance for these peoples difficult.6 Many cancer registries do not specifically consider TGD peoples, which also limits their applicability.7 As a result, most guidance is extrapolated on the basis of known risk factors and, for TGD peoples, which organs or tissues they possess.5,6 Uptake of cancer screening is influenced by practitioner recommendation;8 this is specifically seen in TGD patients.9 Consideration of individual patient barriers, including patient education and test acceptability, may improve uptake. Some discomforts may be negotiated by prior preparation (eg cervical screening in transgender people with a cervix, discussed below) or prior communication (eg a call or letter to a provider), potentially improving the likelihood of patient engagement. Aim This paper aims to provide an overview of LGBTQIA+ populations’ engagement with, and uptake of, current cancer screening programs in Australia, with discussion of screening programs and what this means for TGD patients, including barriers to screening, and practice modifications to improve screening. Overarching principles Recognising each patient as an individual when determining appropriate preventive and screening activities is essential. This is also the foundation to building rapport, delivering tailored education, promoting positive healthcare behaviours and addressing potential barriers to accessing healthcare. LGBTQIA+-specific educational materials should be provided, where available.10 Use of appropriate and preferred anatomical terms for individual patients is also recommended, such as chest tissue rather than breast tissue.10,11 Practitioner flexibility, to adapt and work collaboratively with each patient, is therefore ideal. Organ- and tissue-specific screening is currently recommended; for example, if a patient has a cervix, then application of population-based screening recommendations for cervical cancer should be recommended.5 Some risk factors may influence additional specific screening or cancer vigilance, such as medication and meningiomas.12 Table 1 briefly summarises the recommendations for LGBTQIA+ cancer screening. National cancer screening programs Australia has four national screening programs, as follows.13–16 Breast cancer Breast cancer affects TGD peoples less often than cisgender females but more often than cisgender males, potentially because of TGD peoples’ lower lifetime exposure to oestrogen and progesterone when compared with cisgender females.6,17,18 Of people aged 50–74 years who live in Victoria and are eligible for breast screening, 22.6% of LGBTQI+ peoples have never had a mammogram, compared with 10.4% of the non-LGBTQI+ population.19 It was found that 60% of transgender women, 52% of transgender men and 42% of gender diverse people had ‘little concern’ for developing breast cancer, which may indicate a need for increased patient education.20 Other international breast screen programs, such as in Canada, show lower screening rates for TGD peoples than for the general population.21 Many patients will be happy to engage with screening; hence, it should not be assumed there is a barrier. Clinician recommendation and/or a reminder may be all that is needed. Screening recommendations should consider age at which GAHT was commenced, duration of GAHT and whether the patient has had ‘top surgery’ (such as mastectomy, acknowledging ‘mastectomy’ is a term rarely used in the TGD community), though broadly, cisgender recommendations for screening apply.17,18 State-based guidance is described in Table 2. Screening via private referral is also possible if required. Patients should be counselled that they may be questioned about their GAHT as it increases breast tissue density, which may make interpretation difficult.17 Cervical cancer Only 38.9% of eligible TGD peoples in Australia have been screened for cervical cancer.22 Many transgender men have never had a cervical screening test (CST),20,23 and nearly 9 out of 20 TGD people with a cervix have never had a CST recommended by a health professional.23 Dysphoria from CST collection may be a significant barrier for some patients,23 though many patients will be comfortable to proceed and may simply benefit from a routine reminder. The human papillomavirus (HPV) is the causative agent for most cervical cancer within LGBTQIA+ populations as for within the broader population.17,24 HPV vaccination should be encouraged within the usual schedule on the National Immunisation Program, or recommended if not previously accessed,18 and CST offered per the National Cervical Screening Program Guideline (the Guideline).15 The Guideline comments on some of the barriers to a CST and recommends asking patients about anatomy terms (eg some patients may prefer terms other than vagina and cervix, such as front hole, though many will find anatomical terms acceptable) and includes a link to letter templates that describe many of the techniques that can be considered to increase patient comfort during a CST.15 A fact sheet is also available.25 Topics include self-collection (where appropriate), self-insertion of the speculum and use of the smallest speculum, and patient preferences regarding positioning, environment and discussion during the test.15 The Guideline also guides clinicians to further national information and resources on engaging LGBTQI+ peoples in cervical screening.26 Given the test can be physically uncomfortable because of atrophy, patients presumed female at birth (PFAB) taking masculinising GAHT may be offered intravaginal oestrogen beforehand if needed, which decreases the discomfort from atrophy and increases result quality, similar to postmenopausal cisgender women.27 Not all patients will require this, especially if self-collecting, but suitable options include an oestradiol 10 microgram pessary or an application of estriol 0.1% cream daily for 2 weeks prior to the test, ceasing 1–2 days beforehand.15 Bowel cancer The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program (NBCSP) shows low levels of engagement across the entire population; only 40% of the eligible 6 million people invited to participate between January 2021 and December 2022 returned their envelopes.16 LGBTQ+ engagement is mostly unknown, though a 2017 Victorian survey found similar engagement levels to the non-LGBTQ+ population.19 The prevalence of colorectal cancer is not known to be different between LGBTQIA+ peoples and the rest of the population (except possibly for anal cancers12), so screening should be recommended for all LGBTQIA+ peoples per the program guidelines.6 Anal cancer Men who have sex with men (MSM) and who are also living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) have approximately 60 times the rate of anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) when compared with the general population. High-risk HPV (HRHPV) is detected in 88% of ASCC.28 In Australia, the availability of high-resolution anoscopy (HRA) is currently extremely limited. For at-risk individuals who do not have access to HRA, the Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine (ASHM) recommends that anal swabs for HPV and cytology should not be collected. Instead, it is recommended that there be annual assessment of history and symptoms, an annual digital anorectal examination (DARE) and annual examination of the peri-anal region.28 The screening recommendations apply to people living with HIV aged 18 years and over.28 Lung cancer Recently implemented, the National Lung Cancer Screening Program includes screening by a practitioner-referred low-dose computed tomography (CT) scan on the basis of age and smoking history.14 With higher smoking rates in Australian LGBT populations,29 screening should be recommended where appropriate, especially given this program is more practitioner directed than the other three. Cancer surveillance Neither prostate cancer nor skin cancer have a program of coordinated screening, though both are common, and the discussion of screening and surveillance is recommended. They are discussed here to provide support for patient education. Prostate With multiple possible symptoms (and asymptomatic presentation), and some challenges in using prostate-specific antigen (PSA) as a screening test, screening for prostate cancer among cisgender men is considered on a case-by-case basis after a thorough discussion of the relative risks and benefits.30 TGD people with prostate glands typically retain their prostate glands even following gender affirmative surgery (which many transgender people choose not to access, or are unable to access).31 If DARE is subsequently required, noting that this is no longer a recommended part of prostate cancer screening, the prostate gland may sometimes be palpable only via their neovagina.31 Feminising GAHT lowers the risk of prostate cancer,6,32,33 as anti-androgens used in GAHT may also be used in treating prostate cancer.34 Feminising GAHT can also lead to a marked reduction in PSA, which can make interpretation of PSA results difficult.31,35 TGD peoples with prostate glands who are not using GAHT have a risk of prostate cancer similar to cisgender counterparts.31 Counselling and the offer of PSA screening should be essentially the same as for cisgender men, though there is no clear cut-off for PSA.31,35 Skin LGBTQ+ peoples may have higher rates of sun exposure, ultraviolet tanning and sunburn when compared with the general population,36 though this may not translate to clear increases in skin cancer.37–39 International studies are unlikely to be generalisable to the Australian population because of their retrospective nature and our cumulative sun exposure and skin cancer risk profiles.38,39 In the absence of further information, annual self-checks are recommended (noting they will miss lesions out of view), more frequently for higher-risk patients, with medical skin checks performed as needed on the basis of risk profile or discovery of concerning lesions.40 Skin cancer prevention advice should be universal, especially for those at higher risk.40,41 A skin check for TGD patients may potentially provoke dysphoria, especially if requiring full exposure for whole-body photography; clear discussion of the examination and consideration of modifications, such as limited exposure of the body part being examined at the time, would be recommended. LGBTQIA+-specific screening and surveillance Some tumours merit special discussion in regard to LGBTQIA+ populations, as follows. Meningioma and prolactinoma Meningioma is a rare, usually benign, tumour of the meninges12 associated with use of cyproterone acetate, a synthetic progestin, especially (though not exclusively42) higher cumulative doses over the lifespan – they may exert mass effects requiring treatment.12,34 Transgender women taking cyproterone have a four times higher incidence of meningioma when compared with cisgender women.34 Prolactinomas, which are similarly rare tumours,5 have also been reported at four times the rate in transgender women when compared with cisgender counterparts.34 Cyproterone34 and a number of other medications (including GAHT) and health conditions43 are known to cause hyperprolactinaemia.44 No specific screening for either tumour is recommended,5,44 though patients and clinicians should be alert to the small increased risk as well as signs and symptoms of concern, such as visual field changes and galactorrhoea, with further investigation and referral as appropriate. Genital tract cancers Given some gender affirming surgeries may include oophorectomy, hysterectomy and orchidectomy, consideration of cancers of these organs and related tissues, such as the endometrium, needs to be discussed on an individual basis. There is little evidence to screen for endometrial or uterine cancer,6 though symptoms such as abnormal uterine bleeding, discharge, pain and masses should be investigated,17 ideally supported by an affirmative gynaecologist.45 Menstruation typically ceases 3–6 months after beginning masculinising GAHT,46 but it can persist past 12 months.4 After ensuring adequate testosterone levels (10–15 nmol/L4; common reasons for ongoing menses include inadequate serum testosterone and topical administration methods47,48), investigation for abnormal uterine bleeding should proceed.45 Ovarian cancer risk in TGD peoples is not considered higher than in their cisgender counterparts,6 but investigation of symptoms should occur as for non-TGD peoples.17 Masculinising GAHT may cause endometrial hyperplasia; while in theory this would increase the risk of subsequent endometrial cancer, this has not been supported by clinical evidence to date.12 For TGD women following gender affirmative surgery, neovaginal cancer has been reported, with squamous cell carcinomas and adenocarcinomas, depending on tissue source (skin or gastrointestinal tract, respectively); some are associated with HPV.6 Screening, such as via self-examination, at routine intervals is recommended in the US.6 Routine testicular self-examination is recommended for people with testes, though the risk of cancer in transgender women is approximately similar to that in cisgender men.37 Supporting increased screening Higher screening rates are, at least in part, linked to higher rates of patient engagement. This depends on creating safer spaces for LGBTQIA+ individuals – both through inclusive environments and through practitioner training and confidence. Promotion of a safer environment may be by posters and signs; practice forms and paperwork; the practice website; visible iconography, such as flags; and inclusiveness training for practice staff, including reception and administrative staff.26 Training to improve cancer screening and prevention at a practice level for all communities is available,10 for example, via the Primary Care Cancer Control Quality Improvement Toolkit.8 Cervical screening engagement resources were mentioned above, which would also be suitable for practice nurses.26 Clinician- and patient-centred information can be found via sites such as TransHub (www.transhub.org.au) and through work with communities of practice, in person or online. Practice nurses may also be an untapped resource with significant potential for patient contact. Upskilling practice nurses to support cancer (and overall) screening and prevention, during management planning and via patient education, may be an effective and time-saving method to share the load in general practice while improving nurse autonomy and scope of practice.1,18 Conclusion Cancer screening and prevention is a key function of the general practitioner in primary care. In LGBTQIA+ populations, including TGD peoples, this largely follows the same recommendations as the non-LGBTQIA+ population, although an individualised approach is required, with some specific caveats based on which organs and tissues the individual possesses. Multiple barriers to screening exist; these need to be explored on a case-by-case basis and addressed, where possible, via clinical flexibility and appropriate modifications, including upskilling of other practice staff. Improving uptake of appropriate cancer screening and prevention activities by patient education and recommendation, and by incorporating it within management plans, will better support early detection and improved cancer outcomes for LGBTQIA+ peoples. supplementary_news.content: Startups Tech Health Energy Impact More fighting cancer New statewide plan aims to eliminate cervical cancer in Texas by 2032 Laura Furr Mericas Oct 9, 2026, 8:30 am The five-year plan was launched during the CPRIT 2026 Innovations Conference in Galveston this month. Photo via Unsplash.com MD Anderson, on behalf of a coalition of health systems, has announced a new plan to eliminate cervical cancer in Texas. The five-year Texas Lone Star Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan was launched during the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT) 2026 Innovations Conference in Galveston this month. The plan focuses on three major pillars with goals to be achieved by 2032: HPV vaccination: Increase the percentage of Texas boys and girls up to date on human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination by age 15 from 50.5 percent to 80 percent Cervical cancer screening: Raise the share of Texas women up to date on cervical cancer screening from 64 percent to 80 percent Timely follow-up, diagnosis and treatment: Ensure 80 percent of women receive diagnostic follow-up and treatment when needed through community outreach, patient navigation, provider training and survivorship support Overall, the coalition wants to see fewer than four new cases of cervical cancer annually per 100,000 Texas women by 2032, according to a news release from MD Anderson. Currently, Texas has an incidence rate of 9.5 women per 100,000 diagnosed with cervical cancer, compared with 7.5 women per 100,000 nationally. “Texas has the tools to prevent nearly every case of cervical cancer, but tools can save lives only when people can utilize them,” Dr. Ernest Hawk, vice president and division head of Cancer Prevention and Population Sciences at MD Anderson, said in the release. “The Lone Star Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan gives us a shared roadmap to vaccinate more of our children, screen more of our women and make sure every abnormal result leads to care. With innovations like HPV self-collection and the commitment of partners across the state, elimination is within reach.” About 40 other hospitals, health care organizations and companies join MD Anderson in the coalition that launched the Lonestar Plan. Those based in Houston include Houston Methodist, Rice University, UTHealth Houston, Texas Children's Hospital, Houston Health Department and others. The CPRIT also announced its Texans Conquer Cancer Awards and its CPRIT Champion awards during the Innovations Conference this week. Several are based in Houston, including: Zhiqiang An, co-founder of CrossBridge Bio, Director of the Texas Therapeutics Institute, and Vice President of Drug Discovery at the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston Dr. Abbey Berenson, Director of the UTMB Center for Interdisciplinary Research in Women's Health Care Dr. Michael Taylor, Chair of Pediatric Neuro-Oncology at Texas Children's Cancer and Hematology Center and Director of Texas Children's Pediatric Brain Tumor Research Program To date, the CPRIT has awarded more than $4.2 billion in grants to fight cancer in the state. Over the summer, it awarded four $2 million grants to institutions in Houston and Bryan for the creation or expansion of “core” cancer research facilities. Texas Medical Center Innovation recently announced that its $2 million grant would renew its Accelerator for Cancer Therapeutics for five years. Read more from TMCi about the renewal here. supplementary_news.content: FILE – A patient receives a vaccine protecting against human papillomavirus (HPV) at a pharmacy in Miami, Sept. 9, 2025. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell, File) By Associated Press PUBLISHED: October 7, 2026 at 10:10 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... By MIKE STOBBE, AP Medical Writer NEW YORK (AP) — Preteens may soon have something to celebrate: Medical experts are discussing the possibility that one dose of a life-saving cancer vaccine, instead of two, may be enough to protect them. U.S. vaccination recommendations have become splintered in the past year, with federal officials and doctors’ organizations disagreeing over guidance and even battling each other in court. But both sides have been exploring revisions in longstanding HPV vaccine recommendations. “This would be a significant shift in terms of what has been communicated for many years about the best way to protect adolescents against HPV,” said Jason Schwartz, a Yale University vaccine policy researcher. Here’s a look at HPV shots, which debuted 20 years ago and may now be approaching a crossroads. HPV is linked to thousands of cancer cases HPV, human papillomavirus, is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the U.S. More than 40 HPV types can infect the genital areas of men and women, plus the lining of the mouth and throat. Certain strains are responsible for most cases of genital warts. HPV also is a leading cause of the nearly 50,000 cancer cases diagnosed in the U.S. each year that affect those parts of the body. Indeed, about 90% of cervical cancer and anal cancers are attributed to HPV infections , according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In 2006, federal health officials approved the first HPV vaccine, Merck & Co.’s Gardasil. A second vaccine was approved in 2009, GlaxoSmithKline’s Cervarix. Both vaccines are approved for use in males and females, available for kids as young as 9 to adults in their 20s. But they were prioritized for 11- and 12-year-olds, because the shots work best if given before someone is sexually active. HPV vaccination recommendations have changed before Initially, in 2006, HPV vaccinations were recommended only for girls and given as a series of three shots over six months. Boys were added in 2011, a move largely intended to stop them from spreading a virus to girls that could cause cervical cancer. Ten years ago, the government changed the dosing recommendations. It dropped the number of recommended doses from three to two after studies showed that amount offered sufficient protection. Research also suggested two doses worked better when spaced six to 12 months apart, meaning they could be given at annual checkups. Since then, studies in multiple countries have shown dramatic decreases in infections, genital warts cases and precancerous cervical lesions. In 2020, the American Cancer Society updated its guidelines for women, raising the age at which screenings should start to 25, from 21. The organization attributed the change to data indicating vaccinations had led to a drop in rates of cervical changes that are seen as precursors to cancer. Evidence has continued to be favorable. The University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project this year published a research review that found that HPV vaccines had lowered the risk of genital-area cancers in women. And a study published in April in the journal JAMA Oncology found vaccinated males are nearly 50% less likely to develop cancers of the head and neck, esophagus, anus or penis. What’s more, “the duration of protection is long,” said Angela Ulrich, who led the Vaccine Integrity Project review. “We have people who are 20, 30, 40 years old who are seeing protection from the HPV vaccine.” HPV vaccination rates are lower than for other vaccines A recent CDC report found vaccination rates against HPV were lower than the rates for some other shots adolescents get, at least partly because most states don’t require HPV vaccinations as a condition of school attendance. Still, the HPV vaccination rate has been flat for four years in a row, with about 63% of teenagers getting both doses. It doesn’t help that HPV shots are known to have a sharper sting. (Doctors have noted fainting is more common after HPV shots.) Questions about pain are common, said Dr. Scott Hadland, who works at a Boston clinic that treats adolescents and young adults. “Some of my patients tell me it hurts more than other vaccines they’ve received, but only for a moment,” he said. Also not helping lately, perhaps, is the elevation of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to U.S. health secretary. Before he was appointed to oversee federal health agencies last year, Kennedy was an attorney and consultant in lawsuits against Merck over the Gardasil vaccine, and falsely claimed the vaccine increases cervical cancer risk. Research suggests one shot may be enough for girls In January, Kennedy ordered the number of recommended HPV doses to be reduced to one, as part of a unilateral reduction of the childhood vaccination schedule. That change was blocked by a federal judge’s order, but it actually is something that medical experts had been considering for some time. The idea gained attention late last year with the publication of a study in Costa Rica that tracked more than 20,000 girls over five years. It found a single HPV shot provided about 97% protection against cervical cancer, similar to two doses. A year earlier, in 2024, research developments prompted a CDC advisory committee to form a work group to explore the possibility of a revised recommendation. That work was interrupted when Kennedy dismissed the members of the committee. The American Academy of Pediatrics — one of the medical groups that sued Kennedy — makes its own vaccination recommendations. It has been considering a guidance change, exploring questions such as whether one dose is sufficient for at least some people and at what age vaccination should begin, said Dr. James Campbell, chair of the organization’s committee on infectious diseases. Should kids get one shot or two? Recommendations are evolving. But right now, experts advise that kids get two shots. While there is evidence showing one shot was sufficient for girls in preventing cervical cancer, there is less evidence about other kinds of cancer in girls. Also lacking is data on whether one shot is sufficient protection for boys against the HPV-related cancers they are at risk for, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project review. Whether the recommendation remains two shots or is changed to one, it’s important that kids get vaccinated, Hadland said. “The benefits are very clear. It prevents cancer,” he said. But they were prioritized for 11- and 12-year-olds, because the shots work best if given before someone is sexually active. HPV vaccination recommendations have changed before Initially, in 2006, HPV vaccinations were recommended only for girls and given as a series of three shots over six months. Boys were added in 2011, a move largely intended to stop them from spreading a virus to girls that could cause cervical cancer. Ten years ago, the government changed the dosing recommendations. It dropped the number of recommended doses from three to two after studies showed that amount offered sufficient protection. Research also suggested two doses worked better when spaced six to 12 months apart, meaning they could be given at annual checkups. Since then, studies in multiple countries have shown dramatic decreases in infections, genital warts cases and precancerous cervical lesions. In 2020, the American Cancer Society updated its guidelines for women, raising the age at which screenings should start to 25, from 21. The organization attributed the change to data indicating vaccinations had led to a drop in rates of cervical changes that are seen as precursors to cancer. Evidence has continued to be favorable. The University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project this year published a research review that found that HPV vaccines had lowered the risk of genital-area cancers in women. And a study published in April in the journal JAMA Oncology found vaccinated males are nearly 50% less likely to develop cancers of the head and neck, esophagus, anus or penis. What’s more, “the duration of protection is long,” said Angela Ulrich, who led the Vaccine Integrity Project review. “We have people who are 20, 30, 40 years old who are seeing protection from the HPV vaccine.” HPV vaccination rates are lower than for other vaccines A recent CDC report found vaccination rates against HPV were lower than the rates for some other shots adolescents get, at least partly because most states don’t require HPV vaccinations as a condition of school attendance. Still, the HPV vaccination rate has been flat for four years in a row, with about 63% of teenagers getting both doses. It doesn’t help that HPV shots are known to have a sharper sting. (Doctors have noted fainting is more common after HPV shots.) Questions about pain are common, said Dr. Scott Hadland, who works at a Boston clinic that treats adolescents and young adults. “Some of my patients tell me it hurts more than other vaccines they’ve received, but only for a moment,” he said. Also not helping lately, perhaps, is the elevation of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to U.S. health secretary. Before he was appointed to oversee federal health agencies last year, Kennedy was an attorney and consultant in lawsuits against Merck over the Gardasil vaccine, and falsely claimed the vaccine increases cervical cancer risk. Research suggests one shot may be enough for girls In January, Kennedy ordered the number of recommended HPV doses to be reduced to one, as part of a unilateral reduction of the childhood vaccination schedule. That change was blocked by a federal judge’s order, but it actually is something that medical experts had been considering for some time. The idea gained attention late last year with the publication of a study in Costa Rica that tracked more than 20,000 girls over five years. It found a single HPV shot provided about 97% protection against cervical cancer, similar to two doses. A year earlier, in 2024, research developments prompted a CDC advisory committee to form a work group to explore the possibility of a revised recommendation. That work was interrupted when Kennedy dismissed the members of the committee. The American Academy of Pediatrics — one of the medical groups that sued Kennedy — makes its own vaccination recommendations. It has been considering a guidance change, exploring questions such as whether one dose is sufficient for at least some people and at what age vaccination should begin, said Dr. James Campbell, chair of the organization’s committee on infectious diseases. Should kids get one shot or two? Recommendations are evolving. But right now, experts advise that kids get two shots. While there is evidence showing one shot was sufficient for girls in preventing cervical cancer, there is less evidence about other kinds of cancer in girls. Also lacking is data on whether one shot is sufficient protection for boys against the HPV-related cancers they are at risk for, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project review. Whether the recommendation remains two shots or is changed to one, it’s important that kids get vaccinated, Hadland said. “The benefits are very clear. It prevents cancer,” he said. supplementary_news.content_title: Reduction in HPV vaccine uptake ‘worrying’, Director of Public Health says
supplementary_news.content: Reduction in HPV vaccine uptake ‘worrying’, Director of Public Health says The reduction in uptake of the HPV vaccine is “worrying”, the Director of Public Health Dr Helen Carter has said, pointing that uptake is aimed at 90% under World Health Organisation guidelines. By contrast the uptake in Gibraltar last year was 63%. The HPV (Human Papillomavirus) vaccine prevents cervical cancer in women and genital cancers in men, and in countries where the vaccine had been administered earlier than in Gibraltar, like Australia where they are seeing “almost no” cases of cervical cancer in the age groups which have been vaccinated. Dr Carter said the number of students being vaccinated for HPV was reducing annually and encouraged parents to consider uptake even if they had missed the vaccine previously. The HPV vaccine is offered to boys and girls in school Year 8, aged approximately 12 to 13 years, and those who are older can still take up the vaccine. Dr Carter said the HPV used to be offered in three doses and is now in one vaccine, and encouraged parents to give consent to prevent cancer. “I would love to see cervical cancer eliminated in my lifetime,” she said. The vaccination programme began on October 2 in Gibraltar’s comprehensive schools, with Health Visitors attending Westside and Bayside Schools to commence vaccinations. HPV is a very common virus and while most HPV infections cause no symptoms and clear naturally, some types can cause cancers, including cancers of the cervix, anus, genital areas and head and neck, as well as genital warts. Vaccinating at an early age is most effective as this provides protection before young people are likely to come into contact with the virus. The HPV vaccine prevents cervical cancer because it targets the high-risk HPV strains responsible for the majority of cervical cancer cases. This makes HPV vaccination an important opportunity to protect future generations and work towards the elimination of cervical cancer altogether. The HPV vaccine has been used worldwide for many years and has a strong safety record. The impact of HPV vaccination has been demonstrated in countries with high vaccination uptake. In some countries the number of genital wart diagnoses among young people fell by more than 90% following the introduction of the national HPV vaccination programme. Members of the public under 25 years old who have missed their HPV vaccination when previously eligible may still be able to receive the vaccination, subject to the applicable eligibility criteria. Anyone who has missed their vaccination during the school vaccination programme is encouraged to call 20003351 or contact the CHC on 20007962 to book an appointment. For further information about the HPV vaccine, including eligibility, benefits and possible side effects, please visit the Gibraltar Health Authority – HPV Vaccine information page

supplementary_news.content_title: No, You Won't Catch HPV From a Train Seat
supplementary_news.content: No, You Won't Catch HPV From a Train Seat Doctors say the viral chart is misleading. Here's what is on the seat, and what helps. A chart has been going around online. It puts high-speed rail seats near the top of a table of HPV sources. Hotel toilet seats, armrests, and tray tables show up too. The chart has arrows, percentages, and a warning tone. That format makes it look like evidence. The science underneath is thin. The first problem is what a positive surface test means. Many of these charts lean on studies that used PCR to detect HPV DNA. PCR is sensitive. It can find a fragment of viral DNA. A fragment is not a whole virus. A whole virus is not always infectious. To infect someone, a virus has to be intact and able to enter a cell and copy itself. A positive swab on a seat can mean a DNA trace is there. It does not mean a live, infectious virus is waiting. Think of a fire that has burned out. Ash can still hold chemical traces of what burned. The ash cannot start the next fire. A PCR-positive surface is closer to that ash than to a live flame. Li Tongzeng is chief physician in the Department of Infectious Diseases at Beijing Youan Hospital, Capital Medical University. He said the chart is unreliable and the public does not need to panic. HPV is fragile outside the body, he said. It survives poorly on dry surfaces. On fabric or hard plastic, such as a train seat, it is very unlikely to stay intact and infectious. HPV spreads mainly through sexual contact or close, direct skin-to-skin contact. Indirect transmission through public objects is extremely low, almost negligible. What HPV is and how it spreads HPV is a small DNA virus. More than 200 types have been identified. They fall into two broad groups. Skin types infect the skin. They cause common warts, plantar warts, and flat warts. These can spread through skin contact, often when there is a small break in the skin. Mucosal types infect mucous membranes. Low-risk types can cause genital warts. High-risk types are linked to cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal cancers. HPV does not travel through the blood. It infects epithelial cells. For mucosal HPV to reach a train seat, a person would have to leave virus from genital, anal, or oral mucosa on the seat. Clothing blocks the genital and anal route. Spitting on a seat is not normal behavior. That leaves skin HPV as the only plausible source on a seat. Skin HPV can shed from a wart. Even then, the next passenger would need several things at once: enough active virus, a break in the skin, and prolonged rubbing or friction at the contact point. Sitting down for a moment does not meet those conditions. A quick brush against a seat does not meet them either. No official public health agency has reported a case of HPV infection linked to a public seat. What is on the seat This does not mean train seats are sterile. They are public surfaces. They can carry bacteria, fungi, and skin scales. A passenger with athlete's foot who takes off their shoes and steps on the seat can leave fungal scales behind. A passenger who puts feet on a tray table can leave dirt and skin cells there. These are reasons for basic hygiene. They are not reasons to fear HPV. Wang Chun is associate chief physician in the Department of Dermatology at Southwest Hospital, Army Medical University. Wang noted that the risk from indirect contact depends on the person. People with weaker immunity, diabetes, or other underlying conditions may be more likely to pick up bacteria or fungi from public objects. People with broken skin, recent shaving or friction wounds, or heavy sweating during long, hot rides may also face a slightly higher exposure risk. For them, physical barriers and hand hygiene can lower the chance of an accidental exposure. Do disposable seat covers help? For HPV, no. Li Tongzeng said alcohol wipes and disposable seat covers mainly provide psychological comfort. They may help against ordinary bacteria and fungi. They do very little to reduce HPV risk. A seat cover can block grease, dust, and some skin scales. If it makes a long trip feel cleaner, use one. Do not treat it as armor against HPV. The virus does not spread through a dry seat surface in the way the chart suggests. What works Get the HPV vaccine. It lowers the risk of high-risk HPV infection and precancerous changes. Wash your hands. Do it after touching handrails, seat belts, and tray tables. Do it before eating. Do not touch your mouth, nose, or eyes with unwashed hands. Cover cuts. If you have a fresh wound, put a bandage or sterile gauze over it. That keeps bacteria and fungi in the environment away from broken skin. Wear long pants or a long skirt if your skin is sensitive. It creates a simple physical barrier between you and the seat. Do not put your feet on the tray table or the back of the seat in front of you. Do not take off your shoes and stand or sit on the seat. Those habits leave skin scales, dirt, and fungi for the next passenger. They also make the ride worse for everyone around you. The cleaning standard Railway 12306 customer service has said that high-speed rail seat cushions are removed and sent for deep cleaning every 120 to 180 days. In sleeper cars, bedding is changed for each passenger. The railway says these practices meet its sanitation and disease-control standards. A train seat is not sterile. It is a public surface with a cleaning schedule. That schedule is not the same as an HPV hotspot. What to do The claim that high-speed rail seats are a leading source of HPV does not hold. A positive PCR result on a surface can be a DNA trace. It is not proof of a live, infectious virus. HPV spreads through sexual contact or close skin-to-skin contact. A dry seat is a poor route for it. Use a seat cover if it makes you comfortable. Wash your hands. Cover a cut. Get vaccinated. Keep your feet off the tray table and the seat. Those steps address the risks that are present. The HPV hotspot label is not one of them. About the Creator Jin Writer of reamstories https://reamstories.com/jin Enjoyed the story? supplementary_news.content: Search Academic Calendar Campus Services Faculties & Schools Library Maps Quicklinks Workday UBC Directory The University of British Columbia UBC - A Place of Mind The University of British Columbia UBC Search UBC Search Faculty of Medicine Home Admissions About Strategic Plan Vision & Values Land Acknowledgement Indigenous Health Leadership Academic & Research Units Campuses Facts & Figures Careers Contact News Feature Stories Pathways Magazine The Next Big Question Education Programs Faculty Development Health Education Scholarship Continuing Professional Development Research Priority Areas Canada’s Immuno-Engineering and Biomanufacturing Hub Academy of Translational Medicine UBC AI and Health Network Centres & Institutes National Prizes Transforming Health Insights Podcast Giving Impact of Giving By the Numbers Ways to Give Contact Us Prospective Students Current Learners Policies & Procedures Respectful Environments, Equity, Diversity & Inclusion Mistreatment Help MD & Undergrad Research Summer Student Research Program Multidisciplinary Research Program in Medicine Grad & Postdoc Education Faculty & Staff Clinical Faculty Becoming Clinical Faculty Appointment Policy & Compensation Reappointment & Promotion Teaching Tracking & Payment System Contacts Teaching Opportunities & Career Development Awards Celebrating Clinical Faculty Alumni » Home » News » HPV vaccine offers lasting protection for women living with HIV, study finds Contact Communications UBC Faculty of Medicine Email: communications.med@ubc.ca Office: 604.822.2421 HPV vaccine offers lasting protection for women living with HIV, study finds By Alex Hsuan Tsui | October 6, 2026 Longest study of its kind could help accelerate global efforts to eliminate cervical cancer The HPV vaccine provides strong, long-lasting protection for women living with HIV, according to new research from the UBC Faculty of Medicine. The findings provide important new evidence as countries work toward the World Health Organization’s goal of eliminating cervical cancer. Women living with HIV are six times more likely to be infected with HPV and twice as likely to die from invasive cervical cancer than those without HIV, making vaccination particularly important for this population. Published in The Lancet HIV, the study followed women living with HIV for up to nine years after HPV vaccination — the longest study to date examining how well the vaccine works in this population. Until now, researchers had little evidence about the vaccine’s effectiveness in women living with HIV beyond two years. Dr. Elisabeth McClymont “We’ve known for some time that HPV vaccines are safe and highly effective, but we didn’t have long-term evidence to show how lasting that protection is for women living with HIV,” said first author Dr. Elisabeth McClymont, assistant professor in the UBC Faculty of Medicine’s department of obstetrics and gynaecology and department of pediatrics. “Our findings are incredibly reassuring. Even in a population whose immune systems can be affected by HIV, vaccination provided strong protection against HPV infection and cervical cancer for many years.” The study included 293 women living with HIV in Canada and was conducted through 14 HIV and gynecological care clinics across the country. The researchers found that the vaccine produced a strong immune response that was sustained over time. Among women who received all three doses and did not already have the strains of HPV targeted by the vaccine, rates of HPV infection and genital warts were very low, and no participants developed serious precancerous changes to the cervix caused by those HPV strains. The researchers also found that maintaining an undetectable HIV viral load was important for sustaining HPV antibody levels over time, underscoring the importance of continued access to HIV treatment and care. Dr. Deborah Money The findings could have particular significance globally. Nearly 20 million women and girls are living with HIV worldwide, with a disproportionate burden in sub-Saharan Africa, where access to cervical cancer screening can also be limited. “Cervical cancer is preventable, yet it continues to take lives in Canada and around the world, particularly in places where HIV rates are higher and access to screening and prevention is limited,” said senior author Dr. Deborah Money, professor and head of the UBC Faculty of Medicine’s department of obstetrics and gynaecology. “We now have concrete evidence that HPV vaccination works very well for women living with HIV over the long term. Making this vaccine more accessible and acceptable for those who need it most can help us prevent unnecessary deaths and move closer to eliminating cervical cancer globally.” This study was supported by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the CIHR Canadian HIV Trials Network, and an in-kind contribution from Merck Canada. supplementary_news.content_title: Kovina Therapeutics Awarded $2.3 Million NCI Grant To Advance HPV Cancer Therapy
supplementary_news.content: Kovina Therapeutics has received a $2.3 million Direct-to-Phase II Small Business Innovation Research award from the National Cancer Institute to advance its lead oral small-molecule therapy targeting HPV-driven cancers. The two-year award will support Investigational New Drug-enabling development of Kovina’s lead program. Kovina is developing first-in-class small molecules designed to directly target the Human Papillomavirus E6 oncoprotein. E6 contributes to HPV-positive cancers by degrading the tumor suppressor p53 and is required for HPV-positive cancer cell survival. Kovina’s approach is intended to inhibit E6 and restore p53 function. The award follows publication of Kovina research in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that validated direct pharmacologic targeting of HPV E6. The research demonstrated restoration of p53 tumor suppressor activity, selective killing of HPV-positive cancer cells and tumor growth inhibition in HPV-positive preclinical models. The NCI funding will support chemistry, manufacturing and controls work, IND-enabling pharmacology and toxicology and other activities required to prepare an IND application. Kovina noted that HPV causes an estimated 39,300 cancers annually in the U.S. despite the availability of preventive vaccines. The company believes direct targeting of E6 could ultimately have applications across HPV-associated disease ranging from premalignant conditions to invasive cancers. KEY QUOTES: “This award comes at an important point for Kovina as we move from compelling preclinical science into formal development. Together with our recent PNAS publication, the NCI support gives us significant momentum as we advance our lead program through IND-enabling development and toward the clinic.” Kristin Sherman, Chief Executive Officer of Kovina Therapeutics “HPV E6 has long been recognized as a compelling cancer target but directly inhibiting it with a small molecule has been challenging. Our work demonstrates that E6 can be specifically targeted, restoring p53 and selectively killing HPV-positive cancer cells. This gives us a strong foundation for translating the biology into a new therapeutic approach.” Elliot Androphy, M.D., Founder and Chief Scientific Officer of Kovina Therapeutics Thank you for visiting Pulse 2.0. SII developed the vaccine in collaboration with DPT, BIRAC, WHO-IARC and the Gates Foundation. Online Bureau ET Pharma Published On Oct 5, 2026 at 07:06 PM IST Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Pune: Serum Institute of India (SII), announced that its Human Papillomavirus vaccine (qHPV), Cervavac has obtained pre-qualification status from the World Health Organization (WHO). The recombinant quadrivalent vaccine is approved in used for the prevention of, cervical, vulvar, vaginal, and anal cancers in girls and young women and anal cancer in boys and young men aged 9-26 years of age. It targets four HPV genotypes—6, 11, 16 and 18—and follows a two dose schedule, administered six months apart. "WHO prequalification of Cervavac is an important step in strengthening the global response to HPV. We are pleased to see this achievement, and look forward to contributing to immunisation coverage, advancing global healthcare." said Adar Poonawalla, CEO, SII. Advt Cervavac was developed in collaboration with the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), along with the WHO-IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) and the Gates Foundation. Under trials it demonstrated non-inferior efficacy compared with Merck’s (known as MSD in India) Gardasil, which provides close to 100 per cent protection against initial infection and precancerous lesions caused by the four HPV types. The two high-risk types 16 and 18, together account for more than 70 per cent of cervical cancer cases globally. A WHO pre-qualification certifies that a therapy is safe and effective for the intended patient population and allows its inclusion in public health programs run by UN agencies and other organizations. The ongoing HPV vaccination drive in India has adopted Merck’s Gardasil 4, which protects against four HPV types, similar to Cervavac. However, it requires a single administration, while the indigenous alternative follows a two-dose regimen. Additionally, the US giant shot is indicated for a broader age group from 9 to 45 years. supplementary_news.content: WhatsApp Home Daily Culture Sport Media GIBRALTAR · 10 OCT 2026 · 01:44| ☀️ 20,7°C · 5,5 m/s YesterdayGibraltar Presents Nature Positive Tourism Pilot In Seville YesterdayRGP And GDP Renew Policing Agreement YesterdayImmersive Poetry Programme For Year 9 Students To Be Led By Jonathan Teuma YesterdayAutumn Classical Concert Set For 21st October YesterdayConvent Christmas Fair Committee Fund Donates £1000 To MAG ThuWestview Park Play Areas Relocated During Reclamation Works ThuUpper Town Residential Parking Scheme Announced ThuOcean Village Supports University Of Gibraltar Marine Science Activities YesterdayGibraltar Presents Nature Positive Tourism Pilot In Seville YesterdayRGP And GDP Renew Policing Agreement YesterdayImmersive Poetry Programme For Year 9 Students To Be Led By Jonathan Teuma YesterdayAutumn Classical Concert Set For 21st October YesterdayConvent Christmas Fair Committee Fund Donates £1000 To MAG ThuWestview Park Play Areas Relocated During Reclamation Works ThuUpper Town Residential Parking Scheme Announced ThuOcean Village Supports University Of Gibraltar Marine Science Activities Daily HPV Vaccination Programme To Begin In Gibraltar Schools By YGTV Newsroom4 days ago The Gibraltar Health Authority will begin its HPV vaccination programme in Gibraltar’s comprehensive schools from Friday 2nd October. The vaccine will be offered to boys and girls in School Year 8, aged around 12 to 13. A statement from the GHA follows below: The Gibraltar Health Authority will begin its HPV vaccination programme in Gibraltar’s comprehensive schools on Friday 2 October 2026, with Health Visitors attending Westside and Bayside Schools to commence vaccinations. The HPV vaccine is being offered to boys and girls in School Year 8, aged approximately 12–13 years. HPV (Human Papillomavirus) is a very common virus. While most HPV infections cause no symptoms and clear naturally, some types can cause cancers, including cancers of the cervix, anus, genital areas and head and neck, as well as genital warts. HPV vaccination is not just for girls. Boys can also be affected by HPV and can develop HPV-related cancers. Vaccinating at an early age is most effective as this provides protection before young people are likely to come into contact with the virus. The HPV vaccine prevents cervical cancer because it targets the high-risk HPV strains responsible for the majority of cervical cancer cases. This makes HPV vaccination an important opportunity to protect future generations and work towards the elimination of cervical cancer altogether. The HPV vaccine has been used worldwide for many years and has a strong safety record. The impact of HPV vaccination has been demonstrated in countries with high vaccination uptake. In some countries the number of genital wart diagnoses among young people fell by more than 90% following the introduction of the national HPV vaccination programme. Members of the public under 25 years old who have missed their HPV vaccination when previously eligible may still be able to receive the vaccination, subject to the applicable eligibility criteria. Anyone who has missed their vaccination during the school vaccination programme is encouraged to call 20003351 or contact the CHC on 20007962 to book an appointment. For further information about the HPV vaccine, including eligibility, benefits and possible side effects, please visit the Gibraltar Health Authority – HPV Vaccine information page

Ten years ago, when she was diagnosed with cervical cancer at the age of 31, some of her joy was halted. A year earlier, she had been diagnosed with three strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), a common viral infection including many harmless strains and some that have a higher risk of progressing to cancer. She was told to see her OB/GYN in five years as it usually cleared up on its own. Something just didn’t feel right to Robles, so she followed up with a different OB/GYN, Lee Lowery, M.D., of FirstHealth OB/GYN, a year later. Her bloodwork was negative for cancer markers, but she still had HPV and had just experienced 27 straight days of menstrual bleeding. Lowery was concerned, and Robles knew something just wasn’t right. She believes in her own intuition and that women often put themselves last. “You have to advocate for your health and take care of yourself,” she says. Lowery agreed with her intuition and performed a colposcopy, which ultimately led to her cervical cancer diagnosis and treatment with gynecologic oncologist Michael Sundborg, M.D. According to Sundborg, HPV is detected in 99.7% of cervical cancers, and any cancer that could be potentially related to the HPV virus (cervical, vulvar, vaginal, anal, as well as some head and neck) is tested in their patients. Robles had a full hysterectomy, along with removing part of the vaginal canal and two lymph nodes. Four months following the surgery, Robles was able to return to work. The HPV vaccine had just come out when she was a youth, and she was just over the cut-off age to receive it. In her line of work, she talks with many young women and has been able to share her experience and how the HPV vaccine could have prevented her cancer had it been available for her. “In the United States, pre-cancerous disease is being closely monitored and rates of pre-cancerous changes (dysplasia) in 20–24-year-old women dropped by 79%, and high-grade dysplasia dropped by 80% between 2008 and 2022,” says Sundborg. “Cancer takes years to decades to develop and often dysplasia is appreciated first. It will be telling as these women age into peak cervical cancer years.” Robles returns annually for a check-up with Sundborg’s physician assistant Lindsey Huckbody, PA-C. She still considers herself “colorful” and is using that gift to return to school to study photography. “Even though you are cured, the journey is never done,” she says. “Find a good system for yourself because the idea of cancer stays with you, and you must choose whether you let it be a good lesson or a bad lesson. I learned to advocate for myself and, more than anything, to take care of and love myself.” “Not to minimize her experience because the diagnosis of cancer is a heavy one, but Nelka is fortunate to have her cancer found early,” says Huckbody. “The biggest risk factor for developing cervical cancer is not getting screened. I feel fortunate to be involved in her care because she is such an awesome human being.” In cervical cancer, precancerous changes can be completely asymptomatic, making screening especially important. Women ages 24 to 65 should be screened every 3 to 5 years. The incidence of cervical cancer in the United States is much lower than in many parts of the world due to the availability of screening and now the vaccine. In 2024, 13,820 new cases of cervical cancer were reported and sadly, 4,360 deaths. In the United States, cervical cancer’s peak incidence is 35-44 years of age. Women who aren’t sure when they were last screened or who have questions about the HPV vaccine should talk with their health care provider. Michael Sundborg, M.D., Brian Burgess, D.O., and Lindsey Huckbody, PA-C care for patients at FirstHealth Gynecologic Oncology in the FirstHealth Cancer Center on the campus of FirstHealth Moore Regional Hospital in Pinehurst. infections in 2024: a worldwide incidence analysis 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月04日 来源:The Lancet Oncology 33.7 编辑推荐: 背景:感染性病原体是全球癌症的重要可预防原因。为服务预防工作,研究人员提供了感染相关癌症负担的综合图景,纳入新确立的致癌感染性病原体及最新全球癌症发病估计。方法:本项全球发病分析中,研究人员使用全球癌症观测站Cancer Today(GLOBOCAN)数据库中 点击免费下载【综合性的体外药效评价解决方案】,全方位支持您的抗体药研发项目,快速地完成体外药效试验以及获得优质药效的先导分子。 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Open access 背景:感染性病原体是全球癌症的重要可预防原因。为服务预防工作,研究人员提供了感染相关癌症负担的综合图景,纳入新确立的致癌感染性病原体及最新全球癌症发病估计。方法:本项全球发病分析中,研究人员使用全球癌症观测站Cancer Today(GLOBOCAN)数据库中2024年癌症发病数据,估算12种被IARC(International Agency for Research on Cancer)专论项目列为1类致癌物的感染性病原体所对应的新发癌症病例的人群归因分数(PAF)、绝对例数及年龄标准化发病率(ASIR):幽门螺杆菌(Helicobacter pylori)、人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)、乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)、丙型肝炎病毒(HCV)、EB病毒(EBV)、卡波西肉瘤相关疱疹病毒(KSHV)、埃及血吸虫(Schistosoma haematobium)、人类T细胞白血病病毒(HTLV)、麝猫后睾吸虫(Opisthorchis viverrini)、华支睾吸虫(Clonorchis sinensis)、默克尔细胞多瘤病毒(MCV)和HIV。按性别、国家、年龄组分层后的估计值被汇总至联合国地理亚区与世界银行收入组。发现:2024年全球估计2·3百万新发癌症病例可归因于感染,相当于全部癌症的12%。病例数最多者为H pylori(n=760?000,PAF 4%),其后为HPV(n=750?000,4%)、HBV(n=360?000,2%)、EBV(n=260?000,1%)与HCV(n=160?000,<1%)。感染相关癌症最大负担在东亚:990?000例(占全球42%,ASIR 31·9/100?000)。撒哈拉以南非洲(28·5)、中东欧(24·3)与东南亚(23·1)的ASIR亦高于全球均值(22·7)。对EBV相关癌症的重点分析显示癌种分布存在地区差异。解读:结果凸显感染控制对癌症预防的重要性。已有科学证据但常未充分利用的策略包括HPV与HBV疫苗接种;HIV、H pylori、HBV、HCV的检测和治疗;安全注射;避孕套与暴露前预防(PrEP)防HIV;以及HPV驱动宫颈癌与肛门癌的癌前病变筛查。结果亦为EBV等新预防工具的研发投资提供依据。 研究背景方面,全球癌症负担预计将从2024年约20百万新发病例增至2050年35百万,人口老龄化为主要驱动因素。癌症的经济与社会成本巨大,预防投入至关重要。感染性病原体是重要的可预防癌症原因,在141个国家是女性、58个国家是男性的首要可改变风险因素。IARC(International Agency for Research on Cancer,国际癌症研究机构)已把若干病毒、细菌与寄生虫列为1类致癌物。既往2018年全球估计约13%癌症病例、2·2百万例归因于感染;此后证据增强,HIV与默克尔细胞多瘤病毒(MCV,Merkel cell polyomavirus)等被纳入1类致癌物,EBV(Epstein–Barr virus)与胃癌等新的感染—癌种关联也被强化。因此研究人员开展本研究,利用最新GLOBOCAN 2024发病数据与更新后的归因分数,给出感染相关癌症负担的更新图景。 点击马上免费下载【间充质干细胞的分离培养、三系分化与鉴定的全面指南】!领 取 研究人员开展的研究为一项全球发病分析,基于GLOBOCAN 2024,估算12种IARC 1类致癌感染性病原体对应新发癌症的人群归因分数(PAF,population-attributable fraction)、绝对例数与年龄标准化发病率(ASIR,age-standardised incidence rate)。结论为全球2024年约2·3百万新发癌症可归因于感染,占全部癌症12%;东亚、撒哈拉以南非洲、东南亚与中东欧为高发区域;H pylori、HPV、HBV、EBV、HCV为最主要病原。该文发表于《The Lancet Oncology》,意义在于为HPV/HBV疫苗扩种、H pylori与病毒检测治疗、HIV预防、EBV疫苗研发及中低收入国家公平防控提供政策依据。 关键方法上,研究人员以GLOBOCAN 2024提取主要癌种发病数,部分亚型依据Cancer Incidence in Five Continents第10—12卷登记数据按比例拆分;共纳入12种IARC 1类致癌感染性病原体与37个感染—癌种对,其中21对沿用既往方法,16对采用新发表方法或本研究新建方法;HIV因免疫抑制机制不计入总感染负担以免与HPV、EBV、KSHV重复,仅结膜鳞癌单独计入;PAF主要由癌症患者中感染患病情况推算,HIV用人群感染患病率;ASIR采用Segi–Doll 1966世界标准;分析按国家、性别、年龄组分层后聚合至联合国地理亚区与世界银行2022收入组;用R 4.3.2完成,未给出不确定性区间。 Results 全球2024年感染相关癌症2·3百万例,总PAF 12%,总ASIR 22·7/100?000。H pylori致非贲门胃癌为主,HPV致宫颈癌为主,HBV与HCV主要致肝细胞癌,EBV主要致鼻咽癌,KSHV主要致卡波西肉瘤。东亚990?000例、PAF 15%、ASIR 31·9;撒哈拉以南非洲PAF 25%、ASIR 28·5;东南亚PAF 16%、ASIR 23·1;中东欧ASIR 24·3。低收入与中低收入国占全部感染相关癌症77%。男性在除HPV外各病原ASIR均高于女性;撒哈拉以南非洲女性HPV-ASIR 30·8、男性0·9。 EBV-attributable cancers的区域分析显示,东南亚、北非、东亚、西亚ASIR最高;东亚鼻咽癌与胃癌几乎各半,东南亚以鼻咽癌为主,撒哈拉以南非洲见霍奇金淋巴瘤与伯基特淋巴瘤,其他地区以胃癌和淋巴瘤为主。 Discussion 研究人员指出H pylori仍为全球重要致癌感染,东亚负担最重,日本、韩国、中国有筛查项目,但H pylori疫苗与高效疗法仍不足。HPV在撒哈拉以南非洲负担突出,单剂疫苗有助覆盖,性别中立接种适用于资源充足国家。HBV/HCV相关肝癌在东亚、东南亚、北非最重,蒙古与埃及尤为突出;HDV虽2025年列1类致癌物,但是HBV子集,不额外增加总负担。EBV升至第四位,因新增胃癌与特定淋巴瘤证据,几乎普遍感染但癌种分布受遗传、环境、共感染与免疫抑制影响,EBV疫苗与鼻咽癌血清学筛查具价值。HIV首次纳入总估计,主要通过免疫抑制放大HPV/KSHV/EBV所致癌症,南部与东部非洲最重;KSHV相关卡波西肉瘤71%与HIV共归因。血吸虫靠吡喹酮与饮水卫生等控制。研究局限包括GLOBOCAN覆盖不均、无年龄别稳健估计、无不确定性区间、部分PAF用总体均值忽略性别差异。 结论部分译为:研究人员总结,结果强调加快控制感染性病原体以实现癌症预防目标的重要性。虽然投资开发EBV、H pylori与卡波西肉瘤的新预防疫苗是关键,但许多预防策略已被证明显效且具成本效果。遗憾的是,这些策略常因社会、资金与政治障碍而未充分利用,往往在最亟需地区更为突出。全球与地方预防工作因此是公平性问题,应纳入全民预防策略:HPV与HBV疫苗接种;H pylori、HIV、HBV、HCV检测和治疗;安全注射;避孕套与暴露前预防防HIV;以及HPV驱动宫颈癌与肛门癌癌前病变的筛查与治疗。 打赏 展开全文 开通VIP 享海量文章 全站开放获取+解锁超过 200万篇新闻全文+每日更新 2000+篇,学术前沿动态全时追踪! 从2000到2026,27载全因有您;您的每一分支持,都给予我们无穷的动力! 公测期:打赏8元解锁30天免费阅读!
